events.title: feat(716.3-716.5): a runtime beside the package, and an install that says all three parts
events.message:
feat(716.3-716.5): a runtime beside the package, and an install that says all three parts

An installed C64RE had no machine, and every way it could find one was a CHECKOUT
shape: two environment variables somebody has to know about, and a sibling
directory that only exists next to a clone. The recipe a user met opened with
`cd ../TRX64 && cargo build --release`.

716.3 — the runtime. install-daemon.ts maps platform → release asset, verifies
the .sha256 TRX64 already publishes beside every archive, and unpacks into a
per-version cache (an upgrade is a new directory; a rollback is the old one still
being there). `runtime_install` and `npx c64re-mcp runtime install` are one
implementation. Resolution gained that cache and PATH — cache first, because it
holds exactly the pinned release while PATH holds whatever the machine happens to
carry; PATH is still consulted, because ignoring a deliberate `brew install`
would be its own surprise.

Fetched on FIRST USE, never a postinstall. `npx -y @c64re/mcp` has to start
immediately, and a postinstall that pulls 27 MB is also the first thing an
`--ignore-scripts` install silently skips.

The pin is the subtle part. EXPECTED_RUNTIME_PROTOCOL demands an exact match, so
the fetch may never resolve "latest" — REQUIRED_TRX64_VERSION sits beside it and
the gate cross-checks both against the sibling checkout's workspace version and
the daemon's own RUNTIME_VERSION string, because two hand-maintained numbers that
can silently disagree would only surface on someone else's machine.

Proved live rather than only in unit form: the fetched 0.9.2 daemon reports 0.9.2
and speaks trx64-runtime/2.

716.1 — the Node floor is not a version number, it is `node:sqlite`. engines is a
warning at install time and nothing at run time, and picking the exact 22.x that
first carried the module unflagged would be guessed rather than measured. So
startup checks whether THIS Node can import it, and says which Node it is.

716.4/716.5 — INSTALL.md leads with the thing nobody warns about: the install has
three parts and the third is the user's, because ROMs are Commodore's property
and will never be in a package. Three audiences, five routes, the version
contract, and a troubleshooting list of failures that actually happen. README
keeps a quick-start and links to it.

One gate had to change rather than be worked around: smoke:825 asserted the five
explorer packages were `dependencies`. 716.2 moved them, because the published
package needs four packages at run time and none of them are these — the explorer
is a Vite bundle that inlines sigma and graphology, and the tarball ships dist/,
not ui/. The invariant it protects is that the five are declared; that is what it
checks now.

e2e:716-package 26/0, e2e:716-runtime 39/0, both wired into gates.yml.
Full local gate 82/82 green in 324s.

Not proved, and §10 of the spec says so: Windows PowerShell and WSL2 are written
from the shape of the problem and have not been run on those shells; the Intel
Mac cross build has not been through a release run; and nothing named @c64re/mcp
exists until 716.6, which waits on an explicit approval.

events.title: ci(release): build for Intel Macs, by cross-compiling rather than by runner label
events.message:
ci(release): build for Intel Macs, by cross-compiling rather than by runner label

C64RE's Spec 716 runtime installer maps darwin-x64 to a macos-x86_64 release
asset. Its gate went red on its own finding: this matrix builds no such target,
so every Intel Mac was told "no asset for your platform".

Cross-built from macos-latest with --target x86_64-apple-darwin, not taken from
a macos-13 entry. The reason is the one already written against the Linux entry
here: a runner label is not a floor to build on. GitHub is retiring macos-13, and
an entry that disappears with it would take Intel Mac users along. Apple's clang
cross-compiles between the two arches by default and cc-rs passes the target
through, so reSID and the bundled DuckDB come with it.

Three mechanical consequences:

  - `rustup target add` and `--target` when the matrix names one.
  - One $BINDIR, computed once from the matrix, read by every step below it.
    A cross build writes to target/<triple>/release/, and four steps had
    target/release/ hard-coded.
  - The proof step is static for a cross entry. An arm64 runner has no Rosetta by
    default, so the binary cannot be run here; asking for Rosetta would trade a
    measured check for a slow unmeasured one. It asserts what the binary IS
    instead, and the version equality is already proved by the native entries of
    this same matrix from this same source tree.

Six targets: macos-arm64, macos-x86_64, linux-x86_64, linux-arm64,
windows-x86_64, windows-arm64.

Not yet measured: this entry has not been through a release run. The first v*
tag after this is where it is.

events.title: feat(716.2): a tarball that starts, proved from an empty directory
events.message:
feat(716.2): a tarball that starts, proved from an empty directory

The package gate runs against a PACKED TARBALL installed into an empty
directory, never against this checkout. That distinction is the point: C64RE has
always worked from a source tree, and every way it quietly depends on one is
invisible from inside the tree and fatal outside it.

Red first, and it was red in the way that matters — 17 failures ending in
"cannot load module", because `dist/` is gitignored, so the tarball carried the
TypeScript sources and no server at all.

  before  1373 files  23.2 MB unpacked  9.4 MB tarball  (nothing in it starts)
  after    642 files   8.2 MB unpacked  1.8 MB tarball

Manifest: `bin` → c64re-mcp, `main`, `engines.node >=22`, `prepack` → build so a
tarball cannot be cut from a stale tree, and a `files` allowlist that names what
is needed rather than an ignore list that has to be remembered. resources/ is
allowed by FILE, not by directory — only platform-kb.sqlite and the bundled
fingerprints are read at runtime; dos1541-source/ is reference material and the
27 MB c64ref JSON is a build input.

Runtime dependencies 13 → 4. react, react-dom, sigma and the four graphology
packages have zero importers in src/ or pipeline/src/ and 49 in ui/src/ — they
are UI-only, and a Vite bundle inlines them anyway, so they are devDependencies.
@types/ws is a types package. pngjs had no consumer anywhere at all.

One real defect the gate surfaced, which is exactly what it is for: c64ref_lookup
required a 27 MB derived snapshot that is gitignored, so it is in no package, and
whose builder FETCHES FROM THE NETWORK. Every install answered "knowledge_missing"
for every address. The platform KB is seeded from the same sources, ships at
1.4 MB, and both fallbacks already existed in that file — they were simply
unreachable, because the branch returned before anything consulted them. It now
answers from what shipped and offers the snapshot as the enrichment it is.

The gate also caught two of its own: `analyze` takes `path` since 866, not
`prg_path`, and project_init scaffolds the project and sweeps loose files into
it, so the payload is written after it, not before.

26 pass, 0 fail.

spec(716): decided — the npm route is supported, and Intel Macs with it

Someone who already has a harness on their own machine installs the package and
is a first-class user. The image from 880 is a second route, not the only one.

So INSTALL.md is written in full — macOS, Windows PowerShell, Windows + WSL2,
Linux and container, each validated on its shell or in CI before it may be called
supported — and macos-x86_64 joins TRX64's release matrix.

One caveat recorded before someone calls that a one-line change: macos-latest is
arm64, so the entry is either macos-13, the last Intel runner and one GitHub is
retiring, or a cross-build from macos-latest with --target x86_64-apple-darwin.
The second is right, and it is what that workflow's own comments already argue
for on Linux — keep the floor independent of runner labels GitHub may drop. It
costs slightly more than a row: the Package step copies from a hard-coded
target/release/, and a cross-build writes to target/<triple>/release/, so the
path has to come from the matrix. Carried as slice 716.3b in TRX64, not deferred
to anyone.

Deciding that npm is supported is not deciding to publish. 716.6 still needs its
own approval.

events.title: spec(716): pulled straight — what died, what was measured, what is left to decide
events.message:
spec(716): pulled straight — what died, what was measured, what is left to decide

The reSID clauses are cut, not rewritten. The spec required Emscripten docs, a
committed resid.wasm and GPL provenance for third_party/resid/. None of it
exists: 806 deleted the TypeScript emulator and its vendored reSID on
2026-08-12, one day after this spec was scoped. A spec describing a world that
no longer exists is what doctrine rule 9 is for.

Measured rather than assumed. npm pack today: 1373 files, 23.2 MB unpacked, and
no dist/ — it is gitignored, so the tarball would carry the TypeScript sources
and no built server, alongside 261 specs, 269 scripts, 68 bug records and the
git hooks. The commercial corpus stays out, so there is no leak. The manifest
has no bin, main, files, engines or prepack. @c64re/mcp is free.

Three things already work and should not be "fixed": run-cli.ts resolves the
pipeline child relative to its own module, so it survives node_modules as soon
as dist ships; resources/platform-kb.sqlite is tracked; tsx is a devDependency.

The runtime beside it is now decided rather than open: fetch on FIRST USE, never
a postinstall, because npx -y @c64re/mcp has to start immediately and a
postinstall turns a cold start into a 27 MB download. PATH and a cache directory
join the resolve chain, which is needed under 880 too. And the pin gets a gate:
EXPECTED_RUNTIME_PROTOCOL = 2 demands an exact match, so the fetch may never
resolve "latest", and two hand-maintained numbers that can silently disagree is
a defect that only surfaces on someone else's machine.

Two gaps code does not close, stated rather than buried: macos-x86_64 is missing
from TRX64's release matrix, and ROMs are Commodore's property, are gitignored,
and are never in a package — the install is three-part and the third part must
not be given a technical answer.

716.2 (the package gate) and 716.3 (the runtime) depend on no open decision and
are the whole of the risk. 880 consumes this package, so they are unconditional.

One decision is left, and it is a product decision: is the bare npm route a
supported, documented path, or only the thing the image installs? It decides
whether INSTALL.md's five-platform matrix is written at all.

events.title: spec(880): the sandbox — an environment you cannot step outside
events.message:
spec(880): the sandbox — an environment you cannot step outside

Everything built for autonomy so far reaches a session through a tool call, and
a session that does not call the tool is not reached. Measured twice.

Seven unattended runs put a number on every channel: a `paths:` glob fires on a
native read, and an RE session reads through read_artifact / graph_find / disasm,
so run 4 made four native accesses in 102 turns and fired zero rules. Carrying
the contract's blockers back on every write did work — model_assert 0 → 12,
orphans 62 % → 9.1 % — and then stopped working at exactly one place: run 7 read
its three blockers repeatedly and left anyway. Nothing inside a session can gate
a stop, because a stop is not a tool call.

The two supervised runs showed the other half. 877's footer delivered the debt
verbatim and the run carried on; and where the tooling was not obviously there,
the run was never refused — it went around. Its own daemon, its own WebSocket
driver, a regex parser for our own monitor's text dump, a `step` macro in 6502
beside runtime_step_into, 103 shell reads of one listing against 5 disasm calls.

A door only bites what passes through it. That is the sentence this spec exists
for, and it is where 877 had to stop: an MCP server has one lever and no purchase
at all on a session that declines to pull it.

So the harness moves into the container beside C64RE and the daemon, and four
estates are held strictly apart:

  guardrails   what must not happen anywhere — the doors, and what the image lacks
  agents       who is working: role and voice, and NO reach whatsoever
  graph        nodes with an exit proof checkable from the graph; no edge is
               traversed on a claim
  grants       the only enforced estate — tools, exec+filesystem, environment

A guardrail is what you must not do. A grant is what you cannot do. One is refused
at a door; the other is arranged by construction and has no door to go around.

Named as limits rather than hidden: the environment grant removes acquisition, not
invention — node is present because the harness needs it, so a session can still
write a 6502 interpreter, exactly as one wrote a stepper in 6502. And the tool
grant is the weakest today, because the server has no notifications/tools/
list_changed and DEFAULT_TOOLS is static.

One thing it closes: 877 could not enforce that a run may not waive its own
contract, because MCP carries no caller identity. In the sandbox the plugin sits
between harness and server and knows which is which.

Open for the owner: the tool-grant mechanism, how much of 716 this actually
retires (the image installs C64RE from the registry, so the packaging gate is a
prerequisite — what goes is the platform matrix and the downloader), local exec
vs a remote workbench on the NAS, and whether the workflow graph belongs to C64RE
or to the plugin.

events.title: Amiga: DblPAL display mode
events.message:
Amiga: DblPAL display mode

display=dblpal-hires: 640 x 512 without interlace on AGA and a 27 kHz
monitor, the geometry of pal-hireslace with a steady picture.

- Built for the 68020, which every AGA machine has.
- Super-hires with FMODE's 32-bit fetch, on a programmed beam with
  DblPAL.monitor's AA timing.
- The window opens where Workbench puts a DblPAL screen, the driver's
  default view position, and the Copper list sets the window and data
  fetch before it opens.
- The VBL server writes back the VTOTAL, VBSTRT and VBSTOP that
  graphics.library overwrites every field; without it the game and its
  music ran at half speed behind a Workbench on another monitor.
- Frame times read the whole beam line, V10-V8 above V7-V0, and take
  the line length and lines per field from the programmed beam.
- On a machine without AGA or a 68020 it says what is missing, in the
  shell or in a window from Workbench, and quits.
- Its screens are allocated after that check, so an A500 with 512 KB of
  Chip RAM still loads it and gets the message; the other modes keep
  their Chip RAM hunks.

Reports from 2MB machines keep running out of memory at level

spare. The TOS version does not change that - TOS 1.x leaves just

still recommended. The custom palettes table is re-aligned too.

events.title: fix(import): expanded archives keep their own dates, not the import day
events.message:
fix(import): expanded archives keep their own dates, not the import day

Indexing the NeXTSTEP discs showed files with their 1990s dates but most
directories dated the day the discs were built. Anything an archive does
not date itself fell back to "now":

- the folder an archive unpacks into (`pkg.tar.gz` -> `pkg/`),
- implicit parents a tar lists only through `a/b/file`,
- every member of a classic-Mac archive: `copy_into` never carried dates.

Now, for every archive expansion and every target filesystem:

- Undated directories take the archive file's own modification date
  (`Importer::implicit_dir_times`, `ensure_dir_at` takes a date).
- Mac archive members keep their Mac dates: `CopyOptions::preserve_times`,
  on for archive expansion only, so `cp` / Commander still stamp the copy
  time.
- `--expand-gunzip` output takes the original date recorded in the gzip
  header, else the .gz file's date.

Directories and files that carry a date in the archive were already kept,
and still are.

events.title: A drop shadow on the title menu, as the originals have
events.message:
A drop shadow on the title menu, as the originals have

The Amiga and Archimedes title menus draw their text with a
one-pixel black shadow down and to the right. The ST's menu now
does the same: each line goes down once in the title palette's black
at (x+1, y+1), every letter's shadow first, then the colour on top,
so no shadow lands on a neighbouring letter's ink.

A line and its shadow are nine rows - the font uses all eight for
descenders - so the list moves down to row 21. There each line and
its shadow sit inside one of Fit's ten-row runs; from row 12, the
shadow's last row was the one Fit drops at 20. Row 21 is still on
screen in Fill, and ten lines end at 128, clear of the FLASHBACK
logo. The picture strip kept under each line grows to nine rows, so
a shorter label or a change of page leaves no stale shadow behind.
events.author: neilrackett

events.title: fix(gui): start Linux ARM / RISC-V on OpenGL; keep renderer overrides through elevation
events.message:
fix(gui): start Linux ARM / RISC-V on OpenGL; keep renderer overrides through elevation

On an Orange Pi RV2 (SpacemiT/Ky X1, PowerVR BXE-2-32, Ubuntu 24.04) the
GUI segfaults on launch: eframe prefers wgpu, wgpu picks the PowerVR
B-Series Vulkan driver (24.2@6603887), and the driver crashes. A segfault
kills the process, so the wgpu -> glow -> software fallback never runs.
Measured on the board: default (wgpu/Vulkan) segfaults every time;
WGPU_BACKEND=gl and RUSTY_BACKUP_RENDERER=glow both run clean. wgpu is
also reported very slow on the Raspberry Pi 5's V3D.

- Linux on aarch64 / arm / riscv64 now tries OpenGL (glow) first, then
  wgpu, then software (`GL_FIRST`). Every other platform keeps wgpu first.
  The chain is one ordered loop instead of nested matches.
- pkexec strips the environment, and the elevated relaunch passed through
  neither RUSTY_BACKUP_RENDERER nor WGPU_BACKEND, so "Unlock Physical

events.title: Fit drops rows 9, 20, 31 so Conrad keeps his hair
events.message:
Fit drops rows 9, 20, 31 so Conrad keeps his hair

A player saw Conrad go bald on top as he walked. Fit shows 200 of
the 224 rows by dropping every eleventh, and it dropped 12, 23, 34
... 177: Conrad's head starts at row 33 or 34 on a room's top floor,
bobbing a row as he walks, and 177 or 178 on the bottom one, and the
top of his hair is a single row. On every frame it landed on 34 or
177 it went, leaving hair at the sides and skin on top.

Scored against the rows that matter on each floor (the top of his
head, either side of the bob, and his feet), the old placement was
the worst of the eleven: it hit two floors of three. Five avoid all
of them; the drops now start at 9 (kFitFirstDrop), so they fall at 9,
20, 31 ... 218. Checked in Hatari over fourteen walking frames on the
top floor: the hair is there in every one.

The squash and ST_textRow read the same geometry, so text placed
through TEXT_ROW follows on its own; ST_textRow also skips the short
runs the new pattern leaves at either end. The three placements made
by hand move with it: the title menu one row up to 12 (still Fill's
first visible row), the Escape panel's lines two up to 100, and the
inventory icon in Fit to row 10, where it loses one row low in the
circle - the overscan modes show every row and keep the engine's 8.

events.title: ci(riscv64): ask apt-cache madison for the riscv64 glib, not the native one
events.message:
ci(riscv64): ask apt-cache madison for the riscv64 glib, not the native one

c4b3a2c5's candidate loop ran `apt-cache madison libglib2.0-dev`, which
lists only the native (amd64) architecture, so the riscv64 filter found
nothing, no version was tried, and the job stopped at "no glib version
resolves". Qualify both queries by architecture (`:riscv64`, `:amd64`).

The failed run's unpinned dry-run confirms the approach: apt resolves
2.80.0-6ubuntu3.9 on both arches today. The 74 packages it removes (the
runner's python3 / LLVM / cloud-init stack) match the last green run on
main, so they are the job's existing behaviour, not a regression.

events.title: ci(riscv64): pick one glib version both arches can install, instead of a pocket
events.message:
ci(riscv64): pick one glib version both arches can install, instead of a pocket

The RISC-V GUI job failed with "dconf-gsettings-backend : Depends:
libglib2.0-0t64 (>= 2.79.0) but it is not installable". glib is
Multi-Arch: same, so libglib2.0-0t64:riscv64 must be the exact version of
the runner's installed libglib2.0-0t64:amd64. 87905288 pinned riscv64 glib
to the release pocket to dodge a ports-mirror lag (2.80.0-6ubuntu3.8's new
libglib2.0-dev-bin-linux had no riscv64 build), but the runner image's
amd64 glib follows noble-updates on its own schedule, so the release
version stops matching whenever the image moves: the intermittent
failures on main (2026-09-10) and on PR #84.

The install step now tries each glib version that has a riscv64
libglib2.0-dev and an amd64 libglib2.0-0t64, newest first, pins it on both
arches, and keeps the first one `apt-get install -s` resolves for the full
package list, downgrading amd64 glib if needed. That covers both the
ports lag and the runner skew without hard-coding a version, and fails
with a clear error if no version works.

events.title: Options on the title menu, with music, volume and 50/60Hz
events.message:
Options on the title menu, with music, volume and 50/60Hz

The title menu was full: eight levels, Skill, Screen and Quit at the
11-row pitch Fit keeps whole, and a twelfth line would run into the
FLASHBACK logo. The settings move to a page of their own: the main
list is the levels, Options and QUIT, and Options holds Skill,
Screen, Music, Music Volume, Refresh and Back. Left, right or fire
changes a setting; Back, Escape or Backspace returns with the cursor
on Options. Changes last for the run, RS.CFG sets where they start.

The title plays the menu track, so Music and Music Volume act at
once: On starts it, Off stops it, and each volume step (tens,
wrapping, so fire alone reaches every level) is heard as it is
chosen. With no MUSIC\ folder the line says Not Installed rather
than offering a switch that could do nothing.

Refresh switches the display between 50 and 60Hz. Play runs at the
same speed either way - all pacing is on the 200Hz timer - but at
60Hz most monitors draw the picture taller, and Fit comes close to
the height the overscan modes give. An open border holds 50Hz
regardless and the rate comes in when it closes. refresh_rate in
RS.CFG (50 or 60) sets the start; without it the machine's own rate
stands.

QUIT is the DOS menu's own string now, localised with the rest of
the engine's menus, in place of the port's "Quit Game". Each line
keeps the picture strip beneath it so a page change or a longer
label never leaves old text behind. Music, volume and refresh are
ST-only; the desktop build's Options page is Skill, Screen and Back.

events.title: Bump STDL to 16972e5: ST RAM for the hardware, voice tick at 60Hz
events.message:
Bump STDL to 16972e5: ST RAM for the hardware, voice tick at 60Hz

v1.10.1 allocates everything the Shifter and the sound DMA read in
ST RAM. On a machine with alt-RAM, a screen page could land where
the Shifter cannot see it and the game showed garbage with a border
open; overscan=false was the workaround and is no longer needed.

16972e5 keeps the voice sequencer at 50 ticks a second when the
display runs at 60Hz. The STE action music is driven from it and
played 20% fast at 60Hz; the YM music, through STDL_Music, never
did. Measured on target over the first two seconds of an action
track: 101 sequencer ticks at 50Hz, 100 at 60Hz.
events.author: neilrackett

events.title: The voice sequencer keeps 50 ticks a second at 60Hz
events.message:
The voice sequencer keeps 50 ticks a second at 60Hz

STDL_SetVoiceTick's hook ran once per VBL, so after
STDL_SetRefresh(60) it ran 60 times a second and a song written for
the 50Hz VBL played 20% fast. STDL_Music already divides by the rate
in effect; the voice tick now uses the same accumulator, so at 60Hz
one VBL in six passes it by and the sequencer stays at 50 a second.
At 50Hz nothing changes: the accumulator lets every VBL through.

Found in a port that offers 60Hz as a display setting: its sample-
based action music ran fast while its YM music, going through
STDL_Music, did not. Measured on target, a sequencer counting ticks
over the first two seconds of a song reads 101 at 50Hz and 100 at
60Hz with this change, against 120 without.

tests/host/test_voice.c runs 60 VBLs at a 60Hz rate and expects 50
ticks; it fails without the change (60) and passes with it. The
headers, porting guide, skill and README now list the voice tick
alongside STDL_Music as rate-aware.

events.title: Say what $B6F1 really does: nothing ever sets it, so Elrond puts the road back every time
events.message:
Say what $B6F1 really does: nothing ever sets it, so Elrond puts the road back every time

Its description said "Elrond has read the map and the shut road is open
again", but no instruction writes it except NEW_GAME_CHOICES, which clears
it -- the only other F1 B6 in memory is POP AF then OR (HL) in the picture
code. So ELROND_READS_MAP's "already put back?" test never passes and the
road is rewritten, to the same three bytes, each time Elrond reads the map.

Watched live over MCP on the original tape, played to Rivendell: the
treeless opening's west exit ($BCF8) was zeroed by NEW_GAME_CHOICES and came
back as $04 $00 $14 from ELROND_READS_MAP when Elrond examined the map, and
$B6F1 was still 0 afterwards.

events.title: fix(879): a hook's stdin belongs to git, and is ours to read once
events.message:
fix(879): a hook's stdin belongs to git, and is ours to read once

The gate went green, the hook printed "push allowed", and git push then died
with exit 141 — SIGPIPE — without the commit reaching the remote. Twice.

Git hands a pre-push hook its ref lines on stdin, and every child the hook
starts inherits that pipe. The gate's eighty node steps inherited it, one of
them drank from it, and the pipe broke under git. The hook was reporting on a
push it had just killed.

The refs are now read once, at the top, and everything downstream — gate.sh, and
inside it every step — starts with </dev/null.

TRX64's hook never hit this because cargo does not read stdin. Eighty npm
scripts are a different animal.

events.title: fix(fs): keep raw file-name bytes to NeXT volumes; spool hard-link copies
events.message:
fix(fs): keep raw file-name bytes to NeXT volumes; spool hard-link copies

ab6c13ff carried non-UTF-8 name bytes through every UFS and every tar
import, which reached further than intended: FreeBSD / Solaris / SunOS
UFS names changed from U+FFFD to placeholders, and a tar import into
FAT, HFS or ext stored the placeholder code points themselves, since
only UFS turns them back into bytes (ext4 got four bytes of junk each).

`EditableFilesystem::stores_raw_names` (default false) now gates it, in
the same single-predicate shape as `supports_symlinks`. Only a NeXT UFS
volume (4.3BSD cylinder groups) says yes:

- UFS: raw bytes on NeXT; every other UFS flavour keeps its old lossy
  UTF-8 reading and writes names as given.
- tar import: placeholders only when the target stores raw names; any
  other target gets `%XX` for a byte that is not UTF-8, as in a84c107a.

Hard-link copies now stream through `tempfile::spooled_tempfile` at the
shared `fs::copy::SPOOL_THRESHOLD` instead of `read_file` into RAM, per
CONTRIBUTING's streaming rule.

events.title: feat(879): a report nobody reads is not a gate
events.message:
feat(879): a report nobody reads is not a gate

e2e:839-media went red at 7dfb3c5f — the commit that brought runtime_monitor's
description in line with TRX64 0.9.2 and, among other things, taught eject to
take a unit. It then stayed red through 877's push and 878's, and nobody saw.

The rule is not the problem. "CI reports, never gates" stands: a PR is read and
judged by a human, and branch protection blocks only force-push and delete. What
the rule assumes is that someone reads the report. Nobody does, so it was not a
weaker gate — it was not a gate, and it had been standing in for one.

Nor was the existing hook going to catch it. .githooks/pre-commit regenerates
docs/tool-surface-inventory.json on a src/ change and does nothing else. The gate
hook that was remembered is TRX64's hooks/pre-push, which says in its own header
that nothing else runs those tests. C64RE never got one.

scripts/gate.sh runs the gates locally and runs EXACTLY the ones CI runs. It
carries no list of its own: it parses .github/workflows/gates.yml and executes
that workflow's steps, in its order, under its names, skipping npm ci. A second
list is how this went wrong, so there is no second list. It stops at the first
red, names the step, prints the one command that re-runs it, and exits 2 rather
than report green on a run that did nothing.

.githooks/pre-push decides the tier from what the push carries:

  not master          → nothing; a feature branch gates when it merges
  prose + pictures    → the 3 document gates, 5s
  anything else       → all 80, 331s

Markdown is not inert here the way it is in TRX64: this repo has gates that judge
documents, and doctrine rule 9 is one of them. The file test is a whitelist of
inert files, not a blacklist of code — a package.json, a workflow, an unlisted
file type all run the full gate, because guessing wrong that way costs minutes and
guessing wrong the other way ships red to master.

GATE_SKIP=1 bypasses one push behind a loud banner. GATE_DRYRUN=1 prints the tier
and the files and runs nothing. package.json's prepare already points
core.hooksPath at .githooks, so npm install installs it.

Proved: dry-run on a feature branch → NOTHING, on a specs-only range → DOCS naming
its three files, on scripts/e2e-839-media.mjs → ALL. Full gate 80/80 green in 331s
on master, which is CI's 5m32s to the second.

CI still reports and does not gate. Branch protection untouched.

matrix, which generates the document that tells a session which tool to reach
for. Two artifact registrations recorded producedByTool: "disasm_prg" for work
the live door had done.

The cost was never cosmetic. A run reaches for the name the tooling just
recommended, gets the alias notice, and spends the detour we sent it on. And an
alias that keeps being recommended is not on its way out — it is a second name,
permanently, which is what 866 set out to end.

The rule: a comment may name a retired door, because "there used to be four"
is history and history keeps the name it had. Description, refusal, hint, error
and generated documentation name the live door.

check:tool-names enforces that line and nothing wider. It reads the retired set
from ALIAS_SUCCESSOR rather than a list of its own, so the next alias is covered
the day it is added; it scans string literals only, tracking quotes, cross-line
templates and block comments; and it takes // retired-name-ok: <reason> on the
sites that exist because of the alias — the registration, the map, DEFAULT_TOOLS,
the phase lists, and the notice that explains to a caller what the name they used
did. A reason under 12 characters is a mute and fails, same shape as 877 D3's
deliberate-limitation mark.

Proved red on a name reintroduced into a refusal body, red again on that site
marked with a 4-character reason, then green: 14 marked sites, 346 files.

Gates: e2e:866 77/0 (the aliases still answer and still say what they are),
e2e-tooling-defects 107/0, 727 matrix probe 17/0, check:docs-current and
check:doc-capability-claims green. Wired into gates.yml beside 877 D3.

Left undone on purpose: ~45 comments still name a retired door. Most are history
and correct, some are stale, and separating them is a reading job, not a
substitution. The gate does not check comments and says so in its own header.

events.title: feat(fs): carry non-UTF-8 file names byte for byte onto UFS
events.message:
feat(fs): carry non-UTF-8 file names byte for byte onto UFS

NeXTSTEP wrote file names in its own 8-bit NeXTSTEP encoding (0xF6 is
u-diaeresis, 0xBC an ellipsis; Unicode VENDORS/NEXT/NEXTSTEP.TXT) and
NeXTSTEP-J in EUC-JP. Neither is UTF-8 and a disk does not record which
it used, so the only faithful thing is to keep the bytes. Our filesystem
API passes names as `String`, which forced lossy decoding on read and a
%XX escape on tar import, so a NeXT saw "Steroidgrundger%F6st.lookMol"
instead of "Steroidgrundgerust" with its umlaut.

`fs::raw_name` maps each byte that is not UTF-8 to a placeholder in the
last 256 code points of Supplementary Private Use Area-B (U+10FF00 + b):
`decode` on the way in, `encode` back to the exact bytes on the way out.

- UFS: dirent names and symlink targets decode on read and encode on
  create / mkdir / symlink / rename / delete, so a name read off one NeXT
  disk and written to another lands byte for byte.
- tar import: member names go through `decode` instead of `%XX`.
- `rb-cli ls` prints the raw bytes as `\xNN` rather than placeholder glyphs.
- A host file extracted with placeholders in its name re-imports the same.

Tests pin the round trip for NeXTSTEP, EUC-JP and 0xFE/0xFF bytes, and that
a UFS dirent holds the raw 0xF6 with no placeholder bytes on disk.

events.title: fix(import): read old NeXT tarballs the way GNU tar does
events.message:
fix(import): read old NeXT tarballs the way GNU tar does

Three more archive shapes from the NeXT software mirror aborted an
--expand-archives import:

- Old NeXT tar records a hard link's target size in the link header with
  no data behind it. GNU tar ignores the size on link / device / dir
  headers; the tar crate skipped that many bytes and then failed on a
  "header" in the middle of file data (eval.3.3.s.tar.gz). A small reader
  (`NormalizedTar`) now zeroes the size on those headers before the tar
  crate sees them, for import, measure and preflight alike.
- Member names in EUC-JP or Latin-1 were refused ("only Unicode paths are
  supported on Windows"). Names now come from the raw bytes, and bytes
  that are not UTF-8 become `%XX`, so they stay distinct and ASCII-safe
  (Steroidgrundger%FCst.lookMol).
- A member stored twice in one archive stopped the import on a name
  conflict (edsnd.1.42). As with GNU tar, the later copy now replaces the
  earlier one; conflicts with anything outside the archive still follow
  the caller's policy.

events.title: fix(import): tar hard links land as copies; restore GNU tar 1.11 long names
events.message:
fix(import): tar hard links land as copies; restore GNU tar 1.11 long names

Building NeXTSTEP CDs from the NeXT software mirror dropped ~60 members
and misnamed more:

- Hard links were skipped as unrepresentable, so Opener.app lost its
  gzip / gunzip / toast tools, gcc its i386- / m68k-next-nextstep3-gcc
  drivers, and several .rtfd help documents their images. A link now
  lands as a copy of its already-imported target (`Importer::lookup`
  resolves it); a link whose target never landed is still skipped.
- GNU tar 1.11 stores members with names past 100 bytes as
  `@@MaNgLeD.N` and names them in a trailing type-`N` entry
  ("Rename @@MaNgLeD.N to <path>", "Symlink <target> to <path>").
  Those members were written under their placeholders, leaving e.g.
  UsingCalendarPalette.nib empty. They are now held (up to 256 MiB) until
  the list arrives and written under their real names; any it never
  names keep the placeholder.

`ImportStats` gains `hardlinks_copied` / `mangled_renamed`, reported by
`rb-cli import`; the preflight counts a hard link as the file it becomes.

events.title: Stamp TOC packets at delivery and drain MMIO hits at interrupt entry
events.message:
Stamp TOC packets at delivery and drain MMIO hits at interrupt entry

A TOC dump entry counted as delivered, and the last one ended the dump,
when the drive built the packet, before RX DMA or the PIO port handed it
to the host. A host that left the receive channel stalled saw a
first_sector stamp for data it never had. The trace now tracks the TOC
packet in flight and counts it (and ends the dump) when the packet reaches
the host, where command replies were already stamped.

When an interrupt woke a stopped CPU with a catch or breakpoint armed
alongside an MMIO watch on the vector table, the higher-priority stop left
the dispatch's MMIO hit pending, and resuming stopped a second time on the
handler's first instruction for the old vector fetch. Drain the hit before
choosing the stop, as the post-instruction check already does.

events.title: merge: Spec 877 — a promise with teeth, and the documents that lie about us
events.message:
merge: Spec 877 — a promise with teeth, and the documents that lie about us

Six decisions, each proved red before it was built.

The contract machinery worked to the last inch and then stopped: it stored
"ALL code … semantically annotated" and 90 %, computed the shortfall and
delivered it on the write path — and a run read that and kept building a
cartridge with 0 of 171 routines named. The doors that PUBLISH refuse now
while a promise is owed, and never the work that would clear it. The human
waives with a reason that is recorded; a run may not waive its own, which
cannot be enforced from inside and says so rather than pretending.

A document of ours forbade tools of ours in bold, and a run duly grew its
own daemon, driver, monitor-text parser and a 50-frame until. A gate fails
now when a doc denies a capability the surface has, with a marked escape
for the limits that are real.

A retired door name said the wrong thing on every answer — naming the
successor where it meant the alias, which reads as "the new door wants a
PRG" and is exactly the belief that fabricated 2-byte load headers four
days after 865 abolished them. Once per session now, re-armed by onboard,
and every note ends with the rule that was broken.

Listings carry equates for the names the graph holds outside their own
image, so a name is where people look. Two latent defects that would have
broken a rebuild came out with it.

And two doors write meaning instead of five hand-rolled generators: a
writer, and a merger that refuses a contradiction by naming both sides and
records the resolution as a finding — because who was right at $82E6 is
what the project exists to remember.

`aliasNotice()` had been in byte-doors.ts since 866 and `e2e:866` had asserted it

a PRG and nothing else", which read straight says the new door wants a PRG, which

and so does the board row, which repeated the same claim.

New §6 as-built: what each of D1-D6 became, file by file, with its gate and that
gate's count. And the limits, stated rather than implied:

    inside — MCP carries no caller identity and the harness relays the human and

    channel-stamped, lapsing, never laundering the measurement.
  • `save_artifact` is off DEFAULT_TOOLS, so one of D1's three teeth cannot bite
    a normal session at all.
  • The teeth are at delivery, not in the loop; D4's "once" depends on
    onboarding; D3's gate scans the agent-facing documents, not every document.

this. It now also asserts that `agent_onboard` re-arms every retired name, that
"once" still holds inside the re-armed session, and that a SECOND server process
over the same project behaves the same — the answer this is all about is the one
a different process gives.

events.title: feat(disasm): 877 D5 — the listing equates the names it references
events.message:
feat(disasm): 877 D5 — the listing equates the names it references

Six participants of the Binky run searched a rendered listing for `$F2A3`
instead of for its name — 103 shell reads against 5 disasm calls — while the
graph had held `game_state` for that address the whole time. The name existed;
it was just not where anybody was looking.

Every name the project knows for an address OUTSIDE the rendered image that the
listing REFERENCES is now an equate at its head, in both dialects
(`.label game_state = $F2A3`, `game_state = $F2A3`). Which addresses is read
back off the rendered lines — the operands actually printed, never `.byte`
values and never the `#$01` of an immediate. Which name comes from the 804
resolver through one door, so the three layers and their precedence stay decided
in the one place that decides them; `staticNameAt` is the resolver's answer with
no machine to ask about residency, exact hits only.

A name that cannot win says so instead of vanishing: one already used by this
listing for another address, one over the project's `maxLabelLength`, one that
is a 6502 mnemonic, or an address the graph gives two different names — each
gets a line naming the address and the name. A name the rendered text already
defines is skipped silently; that is the `.pseudopc` case, and a second
definition would stop the rebuild.

An equate emits no bytes: the rebuild is byte-identical before and after, and
the new gate asserts it through disasm_prg's own verification, for the plain and
the relocated listing.

Two defects found on the way, fixed here because the gate goes red on them:

- the undefined-symbol backstop matched a code label only at column 0, so the
  indented label inside a `.pseudopc` block read as undefined and was equated a
  second time — "The symbol 'reloc_entry' is already defined", the one thing
  that backstop exists to prevent;
- the 64tass converter passed an equate's tail through verbatim, so a `//`
  comment on a `.label` line survived into the `.tas`.

And one comment: 832's note claimed `renderExternalLabelEquates` writes an
equate for an annotated address outside the mapping. It never could — that
address is kept out of `labelSet`, which is all that renderer reads. The comment
now says what happens, and names what finally prints such a name.

events.title: feat(877 D6): one door merges fragments, and the judgement survives
events.message:
feat(877 D6): one door merges fragments, and the judgement survives

The merge script the five fragments went through carried its judgements as
Python literals in a scratchpad that dies with the session:

    order   = ["C","D","B","E","A"]
    segpref = {"82E6": "E"}
    rename  = {("D","64BF"): "exit_door_probe"}

Who was right at $82E6 and why is exactly what the project exists to remember.
It was lost, and the graph received the merged result without ever learning the
merge was contested.

merge_annotations takes N fragments, each with a name — the name is the WHO in
"who claimed what". Fragments that agree collapse into one and nobody is asked
anything: five readers annotating one entry point is the normal case, not a
contradiction. Fragments that disagree are REFUSED by naming the key, every
claimant and what each of them claimed. There is no priority order, because an
order is a judgement with the reasoning deleted — it says which fragment usually
wins and nothing about THIS address, which is the only thing anyone will want to
know later.

The caller answers with resolutions: [{ key, winner | value, why }]. `winner` is
a fragment name; `value` is an entry neither side proposed, stating only what it
changes, which is the `rename` table as an argument; `why` is required, because
the reason IS the record. Each one is written into the project as a finding
carrying both readings, which won, and why, before the file is written — the
file is reproducible from the fragments, the judgement is not.

Refused as well: a resolution for a key nothing disputes (a recorded judgement
about a dispute that did not happen reads later as if there had been two
readings), a winner that claimed nothing there, both a winner and a value, and a
resolution with no reason.

One name at two addresses is its own contest, keyed by the name — it is the
annotation defect that fails in the assembler rather than quietly in the
listing. A site is (kind, address) and not the address alone: resolving it takes
the name from the losing site only, so the routine that happens to sit at a
label's address is untouched, and a segment keeps its range and kind and loses
only the name.

e2e:877-merge, hermetic over stdio, 40 checks: the control that agreement is
silent, the refusal naming both sides, the three bad-resolution refusals, the
half-resolved case, the dry run that writes and records nothing, the value
resolution, one spelling out of three in, the name contest and what it leaves
alone, the recorded findings read back through read_finding, and the round trip
— fragments in, one file out, the real importer accepts it, and the listing
rebuilds byte-identical.

events.title: feat(877): D2 — the human overrules, and it is recorded
events.message:
feat(877): D2 — the human overrules, and it is recorded

`contract_set waive:["namedRatio"]` releases an owed promise so the three
doors open again. It must be signed and it must say why: no `waived_by`, no
waiver; a reason under ten characters is a shrug, not a reason. What lands is
a record — the standing file and the project timeline both carry who waived
what, why, when, and the number that was actually shipped.

A waiver does not launder anything. `project_critique` and the 849 footer
keep measuring and keep reporting the shortfall: this opens the DOOR, not the
number. While any other promise is owed the refusal names every waiver
already granted, so a waiver cannot make itself invisible. `agent_onboard`'s
reset forgets what the session said and keeps what the human decided.

And it lapses. Waive at 90 %, then quietly ask for 95 %, and the door refuses
again rather than inheriting a release nobody granted.

"A run may not waive its own promise" is NOT enforced, and src/contract/waive.ts
says so at the top rather than pretending. contract_set is an MCP tool: the
human's call and the run's call arrive on the same channel, from the same
client, and MCP carries no caller identity — the permission prompt that might
tell them apart happens outside this server and is never reported back. Every
test that would distinguish them (a name that looks human, an env var, a
confirmation file) is a string a run with a shell can also produce. So the
waiver is not made impossible, it is made expensive to hide: signed, channel
recorded verbatim as what the server actually saw, never silencing the
measurement, and lapsing on its own. What is left over — a run that signs a
human's name and ships — is visible from outside in one glance, which is
where 849 says this enforcement belongs.

Gate: npm run e2e:877-teeth — 72 checks, red before (no dist/contract/waive.js),
green after. 848-contract, 844-slots, 844-teeth, 846-critic, 847-docs,
849-rules, 849-standing and check:text-only-tools stay green.

events.title: feat(877 D4): a retired name says its successor once per process, and means it
events.message:
feat(877 D4): a retired name says its successor once per process, and means it

The comment at `analysis-workflow.ts` claimed each old name "says so once in its
own answer". It did — every answer, forever — and the sentence it said was part of
the defect. `analyze_prg`'s note read "analyze took a PRG and nothing else",
naming the SUCCESSOR where it meant the alias, so a reader came away believing the
new door still wants a header. Four days after 866 shipped a run reached for
`analyze_prg`/`disasm_prg`, found they want a PRG header, and wrote
`struct.pack('<H', addr) + data` in front of every block it extracted — the fake
load headers Spec 865 exists to abolish.

Three changes, one sentence each:

  • ONCE PER PROCESS. `aliasNotice` holds the flag; the first answer under a
    retired name carries the note and says it is "the last answer that will say
    so", every later one is clean. Repeated on every listing the sentence becomes
    furniture, and furniture is not read.
  • The note names the OLD door — "analyze_prg took a PRG and nothing else" —
    so nobody concludes the successor wants a header.
  • Every note ends with the rule the run broke: never invent a 2-byte load
    header to get headerless bytes through a door, pass load_address. "A
    fabricated header is two bytes that are not in the original, and everything
    downstream believes them."

holds it up rather than asserting a behaviour on its own word.

repeated the note, no note announced itself as the last, the analyze note named
`analyze` as the door that took a PRG, and none of the three warned against a
fabricated header.

events.title: feat(877 D6): one door writes the annotations file
events.message:
feat(877 D6): one door writes the annotations file

Nothing took "here are 40 segments and 60 routines, write the file", so on
one run five subagents wrote five generators — genA.py, B_gen.py, C_gen.py,
D_gen.py, E_gen.py — and agreed on neither a file name nor the spelling of an
address. The step that combined them then had to undo both, with
s["start"].upper().lstrip("$").

write_annotations takes the sections as arguments and produces the file the
importer accepts. $43a8, 0x43A8 and 43a8 all come out 43A8, so nothing
downstream has to normalise. And it refuses BEFORE the file exists, in the
loader's own terms and naming the entry by its own index: two segments on one
start (BUG-060's id collision), a routine with no name, one address with two
names, one name at two addresses, a name past the project's length limit, an
output path the importer could not read a stem off. One offender means nothing
is written — the tolerant skip is for a file a human wrote by hand, not for one
a tool is writing.

The section schemas document the fields and enforce none of them, which was
measured here: with `name` declared required, a routine that forgot it came
back as `MCP error -32602 … "expected":"string"` and the caller learned nothing
about which routine or which key it had mistyped.

e2e:877-write, hermetic over stdio: W1 the door is on the default surface, W2
the file lands at <stem>_annotations.json, W3 one spelling out of three in, W4
the four refusals each leaving no file, W5 the round trip — written here, the
real importer takes all three entries, and the listing rebuilds byte-identical.

events.title: feat(877): D1 — an owed promise refuses the doors that finish the work
events.message:
feat(877): D1 — an owed promise refuses the doors that finish the work

The run was told, on the footer of a slot_record answer, in as many words:
"**Contract: now owed** — named 0.0 % (0/171 nodes) is below the 90 % the
contract asks for". It read that and carried on building the cartridge — 21
payloads extracted, 2 analysed, 0 annotated, 105 files under ef/. The
machinery was right to the last inch; nothing made it cost anything.

Three doors now refuse while a promise the human wrote down is owed:
render_docs, save_artifact with a release role, and agent_record_step for a
step that claims a phase is closed. The refusal is 844's: a heading, the
promise with the number asked and the number measured, the shortest way to
close the gap, and the way out. One voice, not a second one.

And never the work that would clear it. 37 doors — analyze, disasm,
save_finding, slot_record, model_assert, every runtime and sandbox door,
every read — are asserted open door by door in the gate, not promised in a
comment. The two conditional doors are narrow on purpose: a rebuild's
build-output is not a release, and "annotated 12 routines" does not close a
phase.

The promises are records now (contract/promises.ts), because a door that
refuses on one needs the id a waiver can name, the value asked, the value
measured and the path out — a blocker string carries none of that. The
critic renders its contract blockers from there, word for word unchanged:
that text is what the 849 footer quotes and what e2e:848-contract asserts.

Gate: npm run e2e:877-teeth — 38 checks, red before (no dist/contract/teeth.js),
green after. 848-contract, 844-slots, 844-teeth, 846-critic, 847-docs,
849-rules and 849-standing stay green.

events.title: feat(877 D3): a document may not deny what a tool does, and a gate says so
events.message:
feat(877 D3): a document may not deny what a tool does, and a gate says so

`docs/runtime-sandbox.md` told agents in bold that "The MCP `runtime_*` tools
cannot give you that" and "Do NOT use the MCP `runtime_*` tools for this". True
when it was written; false since `runtime_sandbox_run` shipped — that tool IS a
private daemon on its own port, started as a child of the call. A run read the
document, believed it, and grew a parallel surface out of it: its own daemon, its
own WebSocket driver, a regex parsing the monitor's text dump back into bytes, and
an `until` loop polling the PC every 50 frames where a breakpoint stops on the
instruction.

The document now leads with `runtime_sandbox_run` — one call, its own machine,
its own budget — and keeps the raw-WebSocket recipe for the one thing that tool
genuinely cannot be: a machine that is still there after the call. An interactive
loop (step, breakpoint, monitor, trace) on a machine that is not the shared one
is the remaining case, and the recipe now says so where it used to say "do not
use the MCP tools". `docs/agent-doctrine.md` §1.2 points at the tool first and
keeps the raw recipe as the exception.

The gate: `check:doc-capability-claims` greps the agent-facing docs
(`agent-doctrine.md`, `runtime-sandbox.md`, `docs/tools/**` — the ones an agent
is pointed at and reads as instruction; the generated surfaces are excluded
because their sentences are the tools' own) for a capability denial standing in
the same sentence as a tool name, and fails when that tool exists in the
regenerated surface inventory. A denial that is TRUE is marked and must say why:

  <!-- deliberate-limitation: runtime_sandbox_run — it returns no session id ... -->

A mark with no reason (under 30 chars) fails, and so does a mark whose sentence
has gone. Two self-tests run the detector over the exact paragraph this gate was
written for, so widening a regex to silence a false positive cannot quietly
disarm it.

Red before: 4 claims (agent-doctrine 202/235, runtime-sandbox 5/15).
Green after: 12 docs, 296 tools, 3 marks, 3 covered denials, 2 self-tests.

events.title: docs: 877 — a promise with teeth, and the documents that lie about us
events.message:
docs: 877 — a promise with teeth, and the documents that lie about us

The contract machinery works to the last inch and then stops. It stored
"ALL code … semantically annotated" and 90 %, computed the shortfall, and
delivered it on the write path — "Contract: now owed — named 0.0 %
(0/171 nodes)". The run read that and kept building the cartridge.

849 named the gap itself: a stop is not a tool call. So the doors that
publish refuse while a promise is owed, and never the work that would
clear it. The human waives with a reason; a run may not waive its own.

Four more from the same two runs, all measured rather than supposed: a
doc of ours forbids tools of ours in bold, and a run duly grew its own
daemon, driver, monitor-text parser and a 50-frame `until`; the retired
door names never say their successor although the comment claims they
do, so fake load headers came back four days after 865 abolished them;
the listing prints bare addresses the graph has names for, which is what
103 shell reads against 5 disasm calls are made of; and nothing writes an
annotation file, so five agents wrote five writers and the merge kept its
judgements in a scratchpad.

events.title: grm-rd6h: a direct-site read-back of a live-bank mirror is a RESTORED_BANK note, not a warning
events.message:
grm-rd6h: a direct-site read-back of a live-bank mirror is a RESTORED_BANK note, not a warning

grm-yflf classified a caller-side read-back of a write-through / ROM-identifying
mirror as RESTORED_BANK, but only through OracleHooks on the call-site path; each
strategy's direct-site hooks kept isLiveBankMirror's default false, so the same
LDA <shadow> / STA <latch> shape at a direct mechanism write still warned.

- BankMirrors.isLiveBankMirror: the one shared kind test; OracleHooks and the
  MemoryLatch / SerialShift / SelectData direct-site hooks all use it. Probe
  hooks untouched (JUnit guards their "consulted a mirror" signal).
- SwitchOutcome / engine SwitchResult carry the scan's ReadBack, so the direct
  note names the shadow cell and read address (shared restoreDetail core with
  the call-site wording). evaluateLatchScan no longer drops readBack.
- BankAnnotationAdapter.setBookmarkClearingOther: setBookmark only replaces a
  SAME-type bookmark, so a site that warned in an early round (mirrors not yet
  derived) and noted in a later one kept both. Now the stale other-type
  bookmark in our own category is removed first.

Blessed (owner-approved): megaman d571 (warnings 31->30), wizwarr ffa6 + 034b
(5->3; ff9e keeps bank -> 0), ironsword 040a (6->5), nesmirrortest c122,
nesnmitest c022 -- each a one-site WARNING->NOTE swap, no values moved.
megaman/wizwarr on 12.1.3 + GP-6936 local patch. check nes: pass=29, the
other fails dodge/lwings per realrom-current-fails.

project.display_title: ZX Spectrum game disassemblies — reproducible SkoolKit archaeology
project.notes: Independent reproducible disassemblies of six ZX Spectrum games: Atic Atac, Manic Miner, Fairlight, Knight Lore, The Hobbit and Ant Attack. Build scripts take user-supplied original media, generate commented/source-level-debuggable disassemblies and snapshots, and verify reassembly against the original bytes. Ant Attack is documented as 100% covered (41,984/41,984 bytes), with every routine named and every instruction but three observed to execute; its build reassembles byte-for-byte. The Hobbit also has an optional verified-source fast-draw patch whose 22 pictures are compared against the original run with whole-memory equality checks.

events.title: grm-ic5.1: a curated prg_mode hint is a known layout mode -- suppress the other modes' overlays
events.message:
grm-ic5.1: a curated prg_mode hint is a known layout mode -- suppress the other modes' overlays

DescriptorSupport.gameHintedLayoutMode returns a game descriptor's hint for the
board's layout mode field (null whenever applyGameInitialStateHint would refuse
it); NesRomLoader lets it win over scanImageMode for liveMode, so planWindows
drops the other modes' overlay blocks, as its javadoc already claimed.

Re-blessed drmario, tetris (38 -> 12 blocks, removals only) and rcproam
(14 -> 6 blocks). rcproam is a 32 KiB cart, so its M3 overlays were byte copies
of base: 4826 duplicate overlay instructions go away; follow-ups grm-yjiq
(helper now named caseD_1d) and grm-6ild (prg_bank=0? precision).

events.title: native-par: fixed-buffer modes fit a small source to the buffer
events.message:
native-par: fixed-buffer modes fit a small source to the buffer

With --native-par and no explicit size, the target width was
min(buffer width, source width) unless the mode was flagged hires, so
any source narrower than the buffer stayed at its own size inside black
bars on all four sides.  cpc-mode2 (640x200, not flagged hires) hit it
for every source under 640 px: a 540x360 photo came out 540x180 in the
middle of the buffer.  TED, Thomson, GBA, SMS/GG and the other CPC modes
did the same for sources smaller than their buffers; the Atari/CGA/EGA
640-wide modes escaped only because they are flagged hires.

A fixed-buffer mode now always takes the full buffer width and then
letterboxes or pillarboxes as before, in both the CLI (main.cpp) and the
API/web path (api.cpp).  Amiga lores keeps its don't-upscale rule.

ctest native-par-small-source-{cpc-mode2,cpc-mode1,stf-med}: photo.jpg
must come out 600x200, 300x200 and 640x178.  Full suite passes.

events.title: Add Sega Master System / Game Gear and Amstrad CPC output modes (#14)
events.message:
Add Sega Master System / Game Gear and Amstrad CPC output modes (#14)

New fixed-buffer modes:
  sms-mode4        256x192, VDP mode 4, 2 x 16 of 64 (RGB222), <= 448 tiles
  gg-mode4         160x144, VDP mode 4, 2 x 16 of 4096 (RGB444)
  cpc-mode0/1/2    160/320/640 x 200, 16/4/2 inks of the 27-color palette
  cpc-plus-mode0/1/2  same, 4096-color RGB444 ASIC palette

SMS/GG (src/sms.*): genesis::cluster_tiles (K=2) -> per-cluster palette
(ega_histogram; RGB222 is the EGA gamut, OCS brute-force for RGB444) ->
dither::diffuse_cells_mirrored -> genesis::dedup_tiles (H/V flips) ->
tile_merge::merge_to_budget + Lloyd refit (single-palette slots) -> planar
tiles, u16 tilemap (bit 9/10 flips, bit 11 palette), CRAM. Preview decoded
from the packed data. Output: PNG, devkitSMS .h, .bin (tiles ++ tilemap ++
CRAM).

CPC (src/cpc.*): 16 KB &C000 screen, pen bit order and hardware color
numbers from MAME amstrad_m.cpp. Inks via gamut_histogram (16) or an
exhaustive C(27,K) search scored on a dithered proxy (K <= 4); Plus via OCS
brute-force. Output: PNG, .h (screen + firmware/hardware inks or Plus
0x0GRB words + ASIC bytes), .bin, AMSDOS .scr, companion .pal.

Shared pieces extracted (byte-identical output for Genesis, SNES Mode 7,
EGA verified against main):
  dither::diffuse_cells_mirrored  per-cell mirrored ED (was inline in the
                                   Genesis branch)
  tile_merge::merge_to_budget      greedy merger (was inline in the SNES
                                   Mode 7 packer)
  quantize::gamut_histogram        EGA histogram picker over any gamut
  genesis::cluster_tiles           tile k-means with a palette count

Gates: --depth/--chipset no-ops, lock/pin/palette/reserve, copper/strips/
dpf, --best, .iff and viewer outputs rejected. Web: sms/cpc/cpcplus
chipsets, preview scales, PAR, export buttons (convertScr binding).
Tests: smoke outputs + sizes/AMSDOS checks, rejections, and a bit-exact
decode round-trip per mode (tools/check_sms_cpc_roundtrip.py).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: iff: web IFF export sets HIRES and LACE in CAMG (#13)
events.message:
iff: web IFF export sets HIRES and LACE in CAMG (#13)

api::convert_iff, the path the web app's IFF export takes, never set
IffOptions::hires (nor has_transparency), so a hires or ham6-hires
conversion saved from png2amiga.app opened on a lores screen in AMOS and
other loaders.  The CLI set it; the API did not.  The transparency mask
export had the same gap for hires.

make_camg also ORs in the mode's own is_hires / is_interlaced, so a
caller that passes only the mode still gets the right viewport bits.

iff_camg_check (ctest iff-camg-web-export) converts through
api::convert_iff for lores, lores-lace, hires, hires-lace, ham6,
ham6-hires, ham6-hires-lace and ehb-lace and checks HIRES, LACE and HAM
in CAMG.  Without the api.cpp fix, ham6-hires and ham6-hires-lace fail.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: Review fixes for the palette and sprite work, and no jacket pin
events.message:
Review fixes for the palette and sprite work, and no jacket pin

The inventory icon is put into the background before the sprites are
drawn, not after: copying it onto the visible layer after them wiped
any sprite in that corner for a frame on a change of item. It goes in
without priority marks, so a sprite crossing it keeps the fast path,
and is drawn back on top only when something was drawn over it that
frame - the engine always draws it over everything.

New palette weights no longer force a full requantise on their own;
only turning them on or off does. A room that loads a slot with
another palette number, or the same colours under another, paused
~620ms on its way in instead of taking the patch path. In play the
patch path gives a copied colour - an enemy's half of the object
palette - the slot of the identical colour, and otherwise compares in
CIELAB like the rebuild. The Amiga demo data gets no weights; they
were measured on the full game.

The halves of the object palette a level's enemies use are worked out
from Game::_monsterListLevels rather than a hand-copied list in the
table generator. prioUnder checked one group too many for an aligned
sprite (foreground next to it sent it down the slow blit) and now
scans unrolled, eight rows at a time. The row copies share one
width dispatch (copyRowN, 1-5 groups or a whole row) between the
screen copy and the restore, and the quantiser skips work it did not
need, with identical output.

The jacket pin is gone. Since the weighted palette it only acted on
the title, where entry 0x17 is a title colour: holding it exact cost
the flare its highlights, and measured against the Amiga original the
title's mean colour error is 7.66 without it against 7.91 with.
events.author: neilrackett

events.title: Disassemble Ant Attack from its tape, every routine named and nearly every instruction seen to run
events.message:
Disassemble Ant Attack from its tape, every routine named and nearly every instruction seen to run

scripts/build_antattack.py loads the original Quicksilva tape in SkoolKit's
simulator, plays it to find the code, and disassembles everything the one
tape block loads -- $5C00 to $FFFF, the system variables and the game's own
BASIC included, each BASIC line a block described by its listing and each of
the seventeen scripts a labelled block. The build fails unless all 41984
bytes reassemble byte for byte.

The playthrough is random play plus staged scenes: a rescue, running out of
time, the ending (BASIC's fin set to 1), bites, grenade hits and near misses,
landings on an ant, a wall and each other. Each scene only places things on
the simulated machine; what follows is the game's own code. Between them they
run every instruction but three -- FALL's branch for flag bit 3, which
nothing sets.

scripts/antattack_annotations.ctl names, describes and comments every
routine, and labels every variable and record field the code touches, so the
assembly has no numeric addresses left and skool2asm no warnings.
scripts/antattack.ref and --html add pages on how the game works, the city
(drawn whole with the block picture DRAW_BLOCK itself paints), the levels, the
sprites and the scripts, each script screenshotted as it runs. The pages that
quote the game are generated, not committed.

publish_pages.py takes --game antattack, and the landing page and README list
it. Not done: sound for the scripts.

events.title: docs: BUG-065 — the Binky run, from inside and from outside
events.message:
docs: BUG-065 — the Binky run, from inside and from outside

A run watched live from outside while it happened, then compared against
its own field report. Both halves are in the record because they disagree.

The run reports eleven frictions, all real: a sandbox that says LOAD → RUN
and lands at READY, a CPU-reached wait that never fires on a polling loop,
a length parsed as hex without saying so, no mid-run capture and no
breakpoint step, the shared session occupied by another project, and — the
one that explains the most — a listing that prints bare addresses for
everything outside the image while the names sit in the graph.

It does not report the other half: 103 shell reads of that listing against
5 disasm calls, a foreign disassembler used eight times with a wrapper
built around it, 21 runtime runs with zero steps and a hand-built 6502
tracer, five self-invented annotation writers, and a merge script holding
the judgements as Python literals in a scratchpad that dies with the
session.

Friction is remembered. A detour is not — from the inside it feels like
working.

events.title: A busy room at full pace on a plain ST
events.message:
A busy room at full pace on a plain ST

Level 1's room 45 with enemies on screen ran at 20.5fps on an STE and
20.9 on a plain ST. Both now reach 28.3, the same as the Mega STE
(28.5) and the ceiling of the 30Hz pacing, so the room plays no
slower than an empty one.

The inventory icon is drawn into the room's background layer once,
when it changes, instead of being blitted and restored every frame.
A sprite whose rectangle has no foreground in the priority plane
skips the masked path that checks it pixel by pixel. Dirty runs of
2-5 groups are copied to the screen and restored from the background
a row at a time with movem, where the word loop cost ~50 cycles a
group, and the squashed screen modes read each row's screen offset
from a table instead of multiplying.

RS.LOG was costing ~130ms a line: a text-mode write makes MiNTLib
emulate fstat, which converts the file's DOS date through mktime. It
is now opened in binary mode with an explicit CRLF, so the file reads
the same. With logging=true that was a visible hitch whenever
anything logged, and every log_fps average carried one, so fps
figures measured before this read about 5% low.

events.title: Flow Control Macros: Allow pre-increment/decrement in typed compares
events.message:
Flow Control Macros: Allow pre-increment/decrement in typed compares

You can now replace:

    WHILE inc var : u8 var < #kMax

With:

    WHILE u8 ++var < #kMax

This only works as a prefix for the LHS of the expression, and works
for u8, u16/s16, and u24 expressions (although dec24 is NYI)

Note that to ca65, ++var and --var are just the unary positive and
unary negative operators repeated, so effectively no-ops. Therefore
the Flow conditional expression parser will flag those when in
unexpected locations.

Also, added test coverage for u24 expressions.

events.title: docs: NeXTSTEP CD builder and --expand-gunzip
events.message:
docs: NeXTSTEP CD builder and --expand-gunzip

- README: `optical new next-ufs` examples, the NeXT-label row explains the CD
  shape (2048-byte sectors, not ISO 9660), the UFS row notes the fixed 1024
  DIRBLKSIZ on NeXT CDs, and `--expand-gunzip` beside `--expand-archives`.
- cli-examples: a "Build a NeXTSTEP CD-ROM" section covering both archive
  depths and why they default off (.pkg / .tar.Z stay for NeXT's Installer).
- OPEN-WORK: §3.3 follow-ups (tail-fragment packing, bootable discs, RISC
  hybrids, a real-kernel size check under Previous), §6.2 the missing GUI
  path for creating any CD image, and a §10 audit entry.

No picker or MiSTer-matrix change: `.iso` is already in DISK_IMAGE_EXTS and
NeXT CDs were already readable.

`--include-appledouble`, plus `--expand-gunzip` and `--bytes-per-inode`.

  each file's tail a full block, where NeXT packs tails into fragments.
- A size the builder refuses is caught before the output file is created.
- Discs past 700 MB are built, with an Info line that they will not burn.
- v7 tar: a typeflag-less entry ending in `/` is a directory (GNU tar reads
  it the same way). NeXT's 3.3_Int_68k_Patch1.tar failed to expand without it.

Tests: tests/cli_suite/cli_next_cdrom.rs covers both archive depths, the v7
directory, ls / fsck / get, and the refused-size path.

events.title: feat(import): --expand-gunzip strips one gzip layer; sniff pre-POSIX tars
events.message:
feat(import): --expand-gunzip strips one gzip layer; sniff pre-POSIX tars

`--expand-archives` unpacks a tarball fully. `--expand-gunzip` is the lighter
option: it strips only the gzip layer and keeps what is inside, so
`x.tar.gz` / `x.tgz` land as `x.tar` and `disk.iso.gz` as `disk.iso`. With
both, tarballs are unpacked and only non-tar gzip files are decompressed.
A file named `.gz` that is not gzip is copied through untouched.

The decompressed size is counted by streaming (MultiGzDecoder), not taken
from the trailer's ISIZE, which wraps at 4 GiB; `measure_dir_for` and the
preflight use the same count so `--size auto` sizes to the unpacked tree.

Tar detection also accepts pre-POSIX (v7) headers, which carry no `ustar`
magic and were silently copied in unexpanded: two of NeXT's own 3.3 patch
tarballs are this shape. The fallback requires a name, octal numeric fields
and a matching header checksum.

- `rb-cli import --expand-gunzip`; the CD/HD builders pass `false` for now.
- `ImportStats::gunzipped` counts it; `import` reports it.

events.title: feat(partition): build NeXT UFS CD-ROM images, pinned to NeXTSTEP 3.3's own CDs
events.message:
feat(partition): build NeXT UFS CD-ROM images, pinned to NeXTSTEP 3.3's own CDs

A NeXT "ISO" is not ISO 9660: every NeXTSTEP 3.x CISC disc is a dlV3 disk
label in 2048-byte sectors wrapping one 4.3BSD UFS partition. The new
`partition::next_cd_builder` streams that shape from scratch, reusing the
existing label writer and 4.3BSD formatter.

For a disc the size of NeXTTIME.iso, every derived superblock word, the label
header and slot 0 match the reference disc byte for byte; cylinder-group
headers and fs_postbl / fs_rotbl differ only where the reference holds files.

- ufs_format: `Bsd43Geometry` fixes ntrak / nsect / rps / maxcontig / maxbpg
  (preset `NEXT_CDROM`: 32 x 64, 5 rps, 20000, 512); HD behaviour unchanged.
- ufs: `DIRBLKSIZ` on NeXT is the kernel's compile-time 1024, not the media's
  device block. All 3168 directories on the 3.3 CISC CD chunk at 1024, while
  `fsize >> fsbtodb` said 2048, so editing a NeXT CD was writing chunks a NeXT
  kernel would call corrupt. `dir_block_size` caps it for reader + formatter.
- next: `NextPartitionSpec::cpg` (16 on disks, 2 on CDs); boot-block numbers
  are scaled to d_secsize (32/96 at 1024 is 16/48 at 2048).
- Scope: data discs only (no boot blocks); RISC hybrids not produced.

fix(os): stop compiling the Linux device-open message on Windows

Since c85fa9bf (R-068) Windows opens raw devices through

caller and `cargo clippy -D warnings` fails on a Windows host with
dead-code. Narrow its cfg to the platforms that call it and drop the
unreachable Windows arm.

events.title: An automatic palette measured against the Amiga original
events.message:
An automatic palette measured against the Amiga original

Every room of every level was rendered by the desktop build and the
ST's automatic palette scored against it, colour difference weighted
by pixels. It was far off - background dE 10-24 on most levels - for
two reasons: colours were weighed by how many palette entries shared
them rather than how much of the screen they cover, and compared in
RGB. The jungle's teal, a quarter of every screen, was merged with a
grey and Conrad's trousers into purple, which is also why the
trousers vanished against it; levels 6 and 7 lost their deep blue to
black.

In play the quantiser now compares colours in CIELAB (a table of all
4096 STE colours), weighs each by its average share of the level's
room pixels (a table measured from every room, tools/
gen-palette-tables.py) plus a fixed importance for the object palette,
Conrad's colours and the half of it the level's enemies are drawn
with, and keeps each merged cluster at its heaviest member rather than
an average. Background dE is now 0.7-3.4 and Conrad 0-3.2; the rooms
look like the original. Per-level palettes fitted offline by hand were
no better, so nothing is shipped but the weights. The title and the
cutscenes keep the old rule.

A colour no room shows is floored at weight 1, or it would merge at
no cost with the first colour in the list rather than the nearest.
Conrad's weight replaces the jacket pin in play; the pin was on the
wrong slot for most levels anyway (0x17, where Conrad draws from
0x47). And a merge no longer recomputes the nearest partner of every
colour pointing at a survivor that did not move: pixel weights point
most colours at the same few heavy ones, and that had made the
rebuild twice as slow. A full rebuild at a level start or a change of
room palettes takes about 620ms on a plain ST, against 540ms before.

On the Amiga data an enemy has no palette of its own: its slot is
loaded with half of the object palette. The README lists what each
of the 32 Amiga colours is used for, for custom palettes.

events.title: Stop the fast Hobbit crashing when anything is said in quotes
events.message:
Stop the fast Hobbit crashing when anything is said in quotes

Special word slot 0's handler, $82FD-$8390, is not code nothing can run, as
the disassembly had it: a quote mark comes through the tokeniser as the zero
word slot 0 holds, and the handler is the quote's -- it files what is said to
a character as orders. The fast-draw patch had put code over it, so the
patched game restarted the Spectrum at the first SAY "...". Found by
rewinding the emulator from the reset to the JP (HL) into $8315.

The handler is restored, and what the patch had there goes below the game,
to $5D00-$5DBF (FAST_LOW), saved as hobbit_fast_low.bin and written into the
snapshot. With $5CC0 up to the stack marked, thirty-odd commands in the
simulator -- quoted orders, a fight, walks through pictures -- touched nothing
below $5E85, nor anything from $5B00 to $5CBF. check_fast_draw.py's stack
marker moves up to $5DC0 to clear it: all 22 pictures still identical.
Checked on the emulator: SAY "HELLO" gets TALK TO WHAT ?, SAY TO THORIN
"CARRY ME" gets You talk to Thorin.

The disassembly now has ORDER_BEGINS and SPECIAL_QUOTE as code, the two bytes
after PLOT_INK they keep things in, and PARSE_ORDER; slot 0's handler is a
code seed like the others. The Patches and Bugs pages and the plan say what
was wrong. The keyboard patch's other borrowed stretches were checked again:
nothing points or jumps into them.

Flow the Hobbit Inspector's map out from where you are, so its exits point their own way

No fixed layout can put every exit on its own side -- the game's map
contradicts itself, and 30 of its 176 compass exits point the wrong way on any
layout. So the inspector lays the map out afresh around one place, the
player's or one clicked on (Follow you goes back): each exit's place in the
cell its direction names, working outwards, and further along the same line
where that cell is taken (map_flow.js). The focus's exits are drawn in the
accent colour and labelled N, E/N, U...; when the focus changes, the map glides
to the new layout.

own compass exits point their own way (bar a place reached two ways, which can
be on one side only); 77% of its neighbours' do too. Checked in headless Edge
by clicking the lonelands: W to Bag End, E/N to the trolls' clearing, NE to
the trolls' path. The fixed layout file and its script go.

The site's map keeps a fixed layout, now annealed for direction first and
length second: 45 wrong-way exits rather than 67, on the same size of grid.
