events.title: cpu: 68030 MMU — a frame $A RTE leaves the next opcode in IRC before replaying the write
events.message:
cpu: 68030 MMU — a frame $A RTE leaves the next opcode in IRC before replaying the write

When the pending write of a frame $A RTE faults again, the bus error
frame built for it stores regs.irc as the opcode of the instruction to
resume, but at that point IRC still holds this RTE's own opcode: the
frame $A path restores the stage B opcode into mmu030_opcode_stageb
only. So after the handler's RTE the CPU resumed the faulted
instruction by executing an RTE at its PC, on a stack that holds no
frame, and took a format error — the second panic Atari System V hit
at every copyin that straddles an unmapped kernel page, once the
first (stale stage B opcode) was fixed.

Load IRC with the stage B opcode from the frame before the replay so
a nested fault records the right instruction, and clear mmu030_opcode
so the RTE's own opcode is not written back over it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: slaapliedje

events.title: cpu: 68030 MMU — a deferred prefetch fault is taken when the word is consumed
events.message:
cpu: 68030 MMU — a deferred prefetch fault is taken when the word is consumed

get_word_030_prefetch() defers the bus error for an invalid pipeline
stage while a branch is in the pipe (pipeline_stop), on the grounds
that the words past a taken branch are never used. That is right for
the words after the branch, but the branch's own extension words are
also past the point where pipeline_stop is set: a BSR.L or Bcc.L whose
32-bit displacement straddles a page boundary, with the second page
not yet resident, had its low displacement word returned as $FFFF
instead of faulting. Under Atari System V that made every such call
into a PLT stub — the displacement's low word being the page's first
word — branch to an odd address (BSR.L with displacement $FFFFxxxx
read back as $FFFFFFFF, target PC+1) and the process died with an
address error; XFaceMaker2 was the first program with a PLT call at
exactly that spot.

Keep the deferral for the words ahead, but fault when the word being
returned is the one that never arrived: the instruction is using it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: slaapliedje

events.title: cpu: 68030 MMU — undo address register fixups when a prefetch fault restarts the instruction
events.message:
cpu: 68030 MMU — undo address register fixups when a prefetch fault restarts the instruction

A prefetch fault raised from inside an instruction — the next opcode's
fetch landing in an unmapped page — is reported with mmu030_opcode =
-1, the same as a fault while filling the pipe before the instruction
starts, and the run loop's handler discarded the mmufixup entries for
that case. But the generated MOVE handlers pre-decrement the address
register and record its fixup before the fetch of the next opcode, and
the write comes after: MOVE.L (d16,An),-(SP) at the last words of a
page faulted with SP already decremented, the fixup was thrown away,
the instruction restarted after the RTE and decremented SP again. The
result was one unwritten stack slot in the middle of an argument list;
in XFaceMaker2 that was XtCreateApplicationShell's num_args, which came
out as whatever the stack held, and Xt walked the ArgList off its end.

Restore the fixups in that case too. A completed instruction has
already cleared them, so a fault while filling the pipe for the next
one — or for a branch target — is unaffected; the condition codes are
deliberately not restored, since a completed RTE/RTR must keep the CCR
it loaded.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: Add The Hobbit Inspector, a VS Code extension that watches the game while it runs
events.message:
Add The Hobbit Inspector, a VS Code extension that watches the game while it runs

After Wilderland: a panel beside the emulator's debugger with a map of every
location and a dot for each character where it is, a table of all 61 objects
-- place, holder, size, weight, strength, defence and flags -- and a log of
everything the game says. The log comes from logpoints on PRINT_CHAR, where
words start and where the screen wraps, so it has the text of every
character's actions whether or not the player sees them, each line marked as
shown, done unseen, or only considered: the game tries an action out with
DOING_IT clear, and what it would have said passes PRINT_CHAR too (the warg
trying to follow each character in turn).

Everything shown is read from the running game -- memory by readMemory every
400ms, text as zxLog events -- so nothing of the game is committed; the map's
layout (map_layout.json) is the site map's, written by
scripts/hobbit_map_layout.py. hobbit_model.js has no vscode import and is
tested from Node, against the built snapshot when there is one. Checked by
running extension.js under a stand-in vscode module against a private
zx_server while playing, and its page in headless Edge.

Corrects the object flags note: bit 6 is on the player and seventeen others,
C-C, not twelve.

events.title: Read The Hobbit's keyboard under interrupt, so commands can be typed ahead
events.message:
Read The Hobbit's keyboard under interrupt, so commands can be typed ahead

patches/hobbit_keyboard.s, included by the fast-draw patch: an IM 2 interrupt,
set up once the title screen's key is pressed, runs the second half of the
game's own SCAN_KEYBOARD fifty times a second and keeps each new key in a
16-byte ring. SCAN_KEYBOARD keeps its debounce delay, since GET_KEY's patience
counts scans, and takes keys from the ring. The wait after a picture returns at
once when something has been typed ahead and leaves it to be read, and
otherwise throws its key away as before; NEW_KEYPRESS (PAUSE, SAVE) throws its
key away; the DIs after the tape routines become EIs.

The game never enables interrupts and borrows IY, so the ROM's IM 1 routine is
out: I = $39 takes the vector $FFFF from the ROM's unused $FF bytes, where a JR
lands on a JP at $FFF4, both in the UDG area the game never uses and written at
set-up. The ring and the start of the set-up go in UNREACHED_WALK_HELD and
UNREACHED_WIPE_EXIT; the rest in the space the drawing patch left.

Checked live on the emulator: a command typed while the last one's picture drew
was obeyed in full, PAUSE's key did not reach the next command, and the game
still typed WAIT when left idle. check_fast_draw.py (now over all the patch's
ranges): all 22 pictures still identical. 699 bytes change in all.

events.title: sana2: give transmit its own scratch buffer
events.message:
sana2: give transmit its own scratch buffer

createwritepacket() has the guest's CopyFromBuff() copy the outgoing
payload into pdev->tempbuf and then snapshots it into the host packet.
CopyFromBuff() is guest code; while it runs, the receive path can
deliver a packet, and handleread() writes that packet into the same
tempbuf. The outgoing frame then carries received bytes.

Allocate tempbuf at twice its size and use the second half for
transmit only. A write that starts while another one on the same
opener is still copying is refused instead of sharing that half.
events.author: RLH

events.title: sana2: don't let an unread packet hold up the receive queue
events.message:
sana2: don't let an unread packet hold up the receive queue

uaenet_int_handler2() only looked at the head of the read queue. When
no reader wanted that packet, for example a broadcast of an EtherType
nobody reads, it started the drop timer on every queued packet and
stopped, so packets behind it that did have a reader waited until the
head was dropped DELAYED_DROPPED_PACKET_FRAMES frames later.

Step over a packet that has no reader, keeping it queued with its own
drop timer, so later packets are still delivered.
events.author: RLH

events.title: sana2: accept multicast frames the guest registered
events.message:
sana2: accept multicast frames the guest registered

uaenet_gotdata() dropped every multicast frame unless the unit was
promiscuous, so the multicast filter in handleread(), which checks
frames against the S2_ADDMULTICASTADDRESS ranges, never saw one and
multicast protocols such as mDNS/DNS-SD received nothing.

Admit multicast frames in uaenet_gotdata() and drop those for
addresses nobody registered when the read queue is processed, where
the multicast list is already read. They then neither wait in the
queue nor reach S2_READORPHAN readers.
events.author: RLH

events.title: Draw The Hobbit's pictures nine times faster: rows beside the sweep in IX and IY, each cell coloured once, whole bytes filled at a time
events.message:
Draw The Hobbit's pictures nine times faster: rows beside the sweep in IX and IY, each cell coloured once, whole bytes filled at a time

The fill keeps the bytes above and below its sweep in IX and IY instead of
stepping the address up and down for every pixel; colours a cell only as the
sweep enters it, since the colouring writes the same byte every time; and fills
a whole byte at once at the start of a clear byte whose neighbours above and
below are each clear and seeded, all set and unseeded, or off the canvas --
where all eight pixels would push no seed and change no flag.

The loop along a sweep lives in the 165 zeros after the last picture
(-): no code refers to them, SAVE and START's world copy stop short
of them, and twenty turns of play left them zero. The game never enables
interrupts, so borrowing IY is safe.

check_fast_draw.py: all 22 pictures identical in the whole of memory, the
stack no deeper. 126.1 s of drawing originally, 33.1 s after the first pass,
13.4 s now (9.4x); Bag End 0.55 s, the slowest 1.04 s. The Patches page,
its GIFs' captions, the plan's record and the README say so.

events.title: Ctrl+Shift+P reloads the room's palette
events.message:
Ctrl+Shift+P reloads the room's palette

With palette_custom on, Ctrl+Shift+P forgets what PALETTE\ held and
which file was in use, and loads the room again - which is where the
palette is chosen - so an edited or newly added file shows at once,
without leaving the room. The room load only redraws it and its icon;
nothing about Conrad or the room's objects changes. Once the room is
back, the file now in use is shown on screen, or AUTOMATIC when none
applies. With the option off the key does nothing, like Ctrl+P.

events.title: Custom palettes can say which Amiga colour each of their 16 replaces
events.message:
Custom palettes can say which Amiga colour each of their 16 replaces

On the Amiga a room is drawn in 32 colours: 0-15 the background
palette, 16-31 the object palette that Conrad, items and the
inventory share. After any of a .hex file's 16 colours, "= 1,2,17"
now lists which of those 32 it replaces; anything not listed - and
enemies, level 2's extra palette and the text colours, which have no
number - still takes the nearest (or with palette_hue the closest
hue). The lists are optional, so plain 16-line files work as before.
It is how a palette whose only greens are bright keeps the jungle's
muted olives green: nearest colour sends them to grey.

The numbering is worked out per room from the game's own palette
setup (the background palette wherever it is loaded is 0-15, the
object palette 16-31), and the lists are honoured in the full rebuild
and in the few-entries update that palette animations take.

Ctrl+P's file now carries the room's 32 Amiga colours, numbered, in a
comment block, and each of its 16 lines already lists the ones it is
used for, so an author changes colours and moves numbers between
lines; reloaded unchanged it draws the room as the automatic palette
did. The parser reads a line at a time, so comments sit anywhere.

events.title: Draw The Hobbit's pictures four times faster, as a patch on the exact source
events.message:
Draw The Hobbit's pictures four times faster, as a patch on the exact source

patches/hobbit_fast_draw.s INCLUDEs the byte-exact hobbit.asm and rewrites the
plotting code in place: FLOOD_FILL and DRAW_LINE visit the same pixels in the
same order and push the same fill seeds, but carry each pixel's screen address
and bit mask along with the point instead of rebuilding it from (D,E) every
time -- PIXEL_ADDRESS was half of all drawing time. The attribute rule, the ink
flipped where it would match the paper, is kept, with its three values written
into the comparison's immediates once per line or fill.

The new code fits either side of the ATTR_ routines, which RUN_PICTURE's PAINT
calls and which stay put, and in special word slot 0's handler, $82FD-$8390,
which nothing can run. The plan's printer buffer was wrong: the game's PRINT
command uses it through the ROM.

build_hobbit.py --fast-draw assembles it after the byte-exact check and writes
hobbit_fast.sna with its SLD, refusing a patched image that differs outside
the three declared ranges (427 bytes change, all inside them).
scripts/check_fast_draw.py draws all 22 pictures from the same machine in both
and compares the whole of RAM afterwards: all identical, the stack never
deeper, 126.1 s of drawing down to 33.1 s, 3.81x; Bag End 6.7 s to 1.7 s.
Recorded on the emulator from the title screen, Bag End finishes after 7.0 s
in the original and 1.9 s patched.

The plan doc, uncommitted until now, records what was built and where the plan
was wrong; the README says how to build it.

events.title: Label every address Atic Atac's code and comments use
events.message:
Label every address Atic Atac's code and comments use

Every operand that is an address now assembles as a label or an equate, and
every address the prose mentions is a #R reference; what is left as a number is
a number -- pitches, sound-and-length pairs, pixel coordinates, the stack's top.

- The runtime records above the loaded block and the game's variables below
  it are equates: PLAYER, PLAYER_ROOM, WEAPON_X, SOUND_SLOT, LIVE_DOORS;
  FRAMES, TILE_SOURCE, ROOM_COLOUR, LIVES, FOOD_LEVEL, SCORE, CARRIED, CLOCK,
  ROOMS_SEEN and the rest, 73 in all.
- INITIAL_STATE's records the code names are labelled: the four keys by colour
  (a key is sprite $81, its colour its drawing mode), ACG_KEY_PARTS, FOOD,
  MUSHROOMS, each monster by name. The collectables $8C-$8E are the three
  pieces of the A.C.G. key: ACG_DOOR opens only when the three inventory slots
  hold them, in order.
- Code other code writes into, or reads a table less a bias from, is labelled
  and written as label plus offset: the eight blitters' combining opcodes,
  the outline's vertex fetches, two patched JRs, PLAYER_TEMPLATE's fields,
  the roast's height bytes, TEXT_FONT-$0100, ACTOR_HANDLERS+$0144. Each has a
  line comment saying which field, since the HTML shows the address.
- SPRITE_TABLE is words, split at FURNITURE_SPRITES and FURNITURE_COLOURS;
  SPAWN_TYPES is the sixteen creatures a new monster can become, running on
  into SPAWNABLE_SPRITES; the panel layout is one row to a line.
- The 59 numbered entry points other routines use, and L954D and L9565, are
  named (DOORWAY, DRAW_DOOR, OPEN_DOOR, SHUT_DOOR, STEP_ACTOR, BEEP_BC...).

Three routines were named for a guess and are renamed for what they do.
CYCLE_ROOM_COLOUR is PLACE_KEYS: it puts the green, red and cyan keys in
random rooms and the mummy with the red one. ESCAPE_SEQUENCE is TRAPDOOR_FALL:
reached only from the trapdoor's handler, it draws room $96, the fall's
outline, with a falling note, and ends in ENTER_ROOM to the room below; the
ending is reached instead by MAIN_LOOP finding the player in room $8E, and the
CONGRATULATIONT note now says so. CARRYING_8C is ACG_DOOR. SCAN_EB18 is
SCAN_COLLECTABLES. Two notes were a byte out ($9876, $934A) and one named a
caller ($9340) that does not call.

The room pictures no longer show room $8E overwritten by the end screen: the
render's own copy of MAIN_LOOP's CP $8E is pointed at a room there is none of.

Built from the tape: 30208 bytes reassemble byte-for-byte. skool2asm's only
warnings are 11 numbers in comments.

events.title: Decode every Atic Atac room list, and the records they name
events.message:
Decode every Atic Atac room list, and the records they name

Each room's list is a word per entry now, each assembling as the label of the
record it names -- DOOR_R03_R02, CYAN_DOOR_R6C_R03, TRAPDOOR_R03_R65,
SUIT_OF_ARMOUR_R01_R03 -- and linking to it, with a comment saying what the
half in this room is: a door and the room it leads to, a trapdoor and where it
falls, where a trapdoor from above lands, or which piece of furniture. The
rooms named link to their own lists. A room's page also lists the objects and
monsters that start there, which the list does not name: MAIN_LOOP finds them
by their own room byte.

INITIAL_STATE is generated a record to a line, each said in words: the three
slots a game fills in, every object and monster with its room and place, and
every sixteen-byte door or furniture record with its two rooms. A record's type
is read as its handler would: a door when DISPATCH_FROM_LIST's lookup reaches a
door routine, furniture when it reaches DOOR_1's draw-only tail, and named for
the picture it draws. Its old note called all 274 of the sixteen-byte records
doors; they are 205 doors and 69 pairs of furniture, 36 of the pairs two
different pieces, and it says so. The collectables are named by their code,
since the annotations name them only as a group.

events.title: Add a map of Atic Atac's castle, floor by floor
events.message:
Add a map of Atic Atac's castle, floor by floor

The game has no map and no idea of a floor, so the map is worked out from its
doors. Every room lists what is in it (ROOM_CONTENTS); a door is two records
eight bytes apart, one in each room, with its wall in its +$05; and a record's
type is a door exactly when its handler -- ACTOR_HANDLERS + 2 * ($A2 + type),
as DISPATCH_FROM_LIST looks it up -- is one of the door routines rather than
DOOR_1's draw-only tail. Rooms are placed beside the room they were reached
from, on the side of the door; trapdoors drop a floor, and each staircase's big
door frame is taken as a floor above its other end, the reading of the six
that leaves the fewest doors out of place. Each room then takes the floor most
of its doors agree on: 149 rooms on five floors, the lowest all caves, and 6 of
199 doors that no choice of floors satisfies, marked as links elsewhere. A room
whose square is taken goes to the nearest free one.

The page draws each floor as SVG: every room in its own outline and colour from
ROOM_TABLE and ROOM_SHAPES, linked to its contents list; doors grey, locked
doors in their colour, the character doors dashed; the ways to other floors
marked with the room they reach. read_shapes now keeps each outline's groups
for it. The landing page links it.

Checked in Edge, headless.

events.title: Amiga: empty the mirror during the transfer
events.message:
Amiga: empty the mirror during the transfer

The transfer zeroes each mirror piece it reads, so the next drawing
viewport arrives empty: clear_image skips the shadow and the row clear
marks are gone. A frame drawn but never carried is wiped whole.

Rows the target shows empty are tested eight longs at a time first.

pal-hireslace, 68020 26 MHz, ELITE title: work 45 -> 42 ms, clear
2 -> 0 ms.
events.author: pulchart

events.title: Amiga: sprites cost less Chip RAM time
events.message:
Amiga: sprites cost less Chip RAM time

The cursor, the compass, chart planets and panel icons are sprites
drawn straight on screen. Each plane word was read for the saved
background and then masked and drawn in place: three reads and two
writes. It is now read once, saved, masked and drawn in a register,
and written once.
events.author: pulchart

events.title: Amiga: plots cost less Chip RAM time
events.message:
Amiga: plots cost less Chip RAM time

Dots, line pixels and the edge words of each polygon row masked and
coloured the screen word in place: two reads and two writes per
plane. They now read it once and write it once, which matters where
drawing goes straight to Chip RAM: a 68020 without Fast RAM, the
panel, charts and menus.
events.author: pulchart

events.title: Amiga: the shadow carries only what changed to Chip RAM
events.message:
Amiga: the shadow carries only what changed to Chip RAM

Each Chip buffer has a Fast RAM copy of its view; frames draw into a
third. Only 16-byte pieces differing from the target's copy cross; rows
it shows empty skip the compare. Sums missed changes.

After crossing, the drawn view is the target's copy: the three rotate,
and the replaced one is cleared where it held data. One allocation holds
all of it.

Writes past the shadow into a flight view (primitives outside the live
window, shadowless frames, AMIGA_FLIP_ADDRESS users, the scroller) make
that copy unknown; its next transfer sends everything.

Frame time builds count crossed pieces.
events.author: pulchart

events.title: Amiga: load files through workspace buffers, not the second screen
events.message:
Amiga: load files through workspace buffers, not the second screen

On a 68040 (ACA1240) in pal-hireslace, BITMAPS.IMG read into the
second screen sometimes arrived wrong, and the loader then searched
its offset table forever: the machine froze on the loading picture.
The bitmaps now load through a 4 KB workspace buffer and the title
through the bitmap bank, both in Fast RAM when there is some. A read
that fails or ends early quits instead of hanging.
events.author: pulchart

events.title: Amiga: shadowcopy=changes|counter|all says what the shadow carries
events.message:
Amiga: shadowcopy=changes|counter|all says what the shadow carries

changes (default) carries changes, counts nothing. counter also shows
total/crossed in frame time builds. all carries every piece and shows
total/ALL, to measure the saving; only that decision differs.
events.author: pulchart

events.title: Amiga: the radar costs less Chip RAM time
events.message:
Amiga: the radar costs less Chip RAM time

Each frame the radar draws and erases a stick per ship directly on
screen, in Chip RAM, where every access waits for the slow bus. It
now reads and writes each screen word once instead of three reads
and two writes, and skips the right word when the stick's head does
not reach it.

events.title: packaging: give the AppStream component an icon and categories
events.message:
packaging: give the AppStream component an icon and categories

0.8.4's metainfo carried neither, and a component without an <icon> has no
icon at all: Ubuntu's App Center listed the installed package with a blank
space beside its name, while the menu entry - which reads Icon=pist from the
desktop file, not from AppStream - showed fine. <icon type="stock">pist</icon>
is exactly what appstream-generator records from a desktop entry's Icon key,
and <categories> mirrors the entry's Categories.

The categories also close a validation trap: appstreamcli only runs its
store-visibility checks, app-categories-missing among them, once an icon makes
the component qualify as an app, so the file validated clean while carrying
neither. Adding the icon alone turned validation red; adding both keeps it
green with only the intended developer_name notice.

Verified against a live install of a rebuilt deb: appstreamcli search pist
reports Name: PiST and Icon: pist, the hicolor cache the dpkg trigger rebuilds
contains pist, and removing the package leaves both clean again.

events.title: Watch MMIO accesses and trace CD32 drive commands in emulated time
events.message:
Watch MMIO accesses and trace CD32 drive commands in emulated time

Value-comparing watches cannot see a device register: they peek a word
before and after each instruction, and a register like Akiko's cannot be
peeked (reading its PIO port pops a byte), so every Akiko, CIA or Gayle
access looked like an unchanged 0000. An MMIO watch is taken at the CPU's
own bus access instead: every data access to the range (fetches
excluded) is recorded with its size, value, direction, PC, frame, beam
position and colour clock, stamped when the access completes. It stops
the machine from the Break tab ("MMIO +/-"), the console (MWATCH) and the
control protocol (break.add kind "mmio", whose stop carries the access);
COPPERLINE_DBG_MMIO logs every hit headlessly, and event.mmio streams them
without stopping.

The CD32 drive gains a host-side command trace. Each packet becomes a
record stamped when the host issued its first byte (TX DMA fetch or PIO
write, tracked through the drive's receive buffer), when the drive parsed
it, executed it and delivered its reply, when a read, play or TOC dump
delivered its first and latest unit, and when it ended, with the decoded
command, sector range, requested speed, reply status and outcome. The Bus
sets the trace clock before every register access and deferred tick, and
a countdown that expires inside a tick's batch is stamped where it
expired. The trace is an observer only: never serialized, carried across
state loads (ending what was in flight as abandoned), and it survives a
guest reset. It is the debugger's new CD tab, the console's CDTRACE,
COPPERLINE_DBG_CD, and the control protocol's cd.trace and event.cd.

Both are pure observers: a CD32 Kickstart boot with every Akiko access
logged and the trace on leaves chip RAM byte-identical at 70 s to an
uninstrumented run, and the debugger transparency test now arms MMIO
logging and streaming. An armed MMIO watch forces the precise CPU loop and
blocks run-ahead, like the other debugger hooks.

runtime_profiles.name: Atari ST / STE / Mega ST 68000 build
runtime_profiles.notes: The shipping ST/STE binary is compiled for a bare 68000 and is explicitly described as the safe run-on-anything Atari build; a stock non-e ST is verified.

evidence.excerpt: Atari ST / STE / Mega ST — openua-atari-st-*.zip, 2 MB, colour monitor; tested on TOS 2.06, EmuTOS and TOS 1.04.
A 68000 build runs on any Atari, and a stock non-e ST is verified too.

runtime_profiles.name: Atari Falcon030 / TT030
runtime_profiles.notes: One -m68020-60 binary serves both Falcon030 and TT030; the standard target machines documented here are 68030 systems.

evidence.excerpt: Atari Falcon030 / TT030 — openua-falcon-*.zip, 4 MB, TOS 4.04 (Falcon) or 3.0x (TT). One binary serves both.
The Macintosh 68k code is retargeted to machines including the target 68020/030 family; Falcon030 and TT030 are supported backends.

runtime_profiles.name: Accelerated Atari ST / STE 020+ build
runtime_profiles.os: No extra TOS floor documented; TOS 2.06 tested
runtime_profiles.notes: On an accelerated ST/STE the Falcon/TT -m68020-60 binary detects ST hardware and selects the native ST display backend. The documentation explicitly states an 020 or better is required for this variant.

evidence.excerpt: Run the Falcon/TT zip's binary; the Falcon/TT zip is -m68020-60. Requirements are just the accelerator: an 020 or better.

runtime_profiles.name: Amiga ECS/OCS
runtime_profiles.notes: Bare-68000 ECS/OCS build; Kickstart 1.3 will not launch it. The documentation describes 7 MHz as playable, with acceleration improving comfort.

evidence.excerpt: Amiga ECS/OCS (A500+ / A600 / A2000, bare 68000) — Kickstart 2.0 or later, 2 MB; playable at 7 MHz.

runtime_profiles.name: Amiga AGA / RTG
runtime_profiles.notes: One -m68020 Amiga binary serves AGA and Picasso96/CyberGraphX RTG, selecting the display path at runtime. The hardware guide describes memory as about 4 MB, so no exact minimum RAM value is asserted here.

evidence.excerpt: Amiga AGA (A1200 / A4000) and RTG — Kickstart 3.0+, about 4 MB; one frua serves AGA and Picasso96/CyberGraphX RTG.
The codebase is already GCC -std=gnu99 -m68020 C.

project.notes: Macintosh 68K FRUA engine reconstruction with Amiga and Atari-family targets.

events.title: palette_hue: match a custom palette by hue instead of nearest colour
events.message:
palette_hue: match a custom palette by hue instead of nearest colour

The jungle's greens are muted olives, and against a palette whose only
greens are saturated - EGA's - the nearest colour is a grey. With
palette_hue=true each colour is matched on hue weighted by the
saturation both share, then saturation, then brightness, so the
olives stay green; greys and pale colours come out noisier, which is
why it is an option and nearest colour stays the default. It applies
only to custom palettes: the automatic one is built from the room's
own colours, so every entry already has a near twin.

events.title: Custom room palettes from PALETTE\, and Ctrl+P to write one out
events.message:
Custom room palettes from PALETTE\, and Ctrl+P to write one out

palette_custom=true: for each room the game looks for
PALETTE\L1R45.HEX, then PALETTE\L1.HEX for the whole level, and uses
the file's 16 colours in place of the ones the quantiser would choose;
every logical colour takes the nearest of them. Level 2 is two level
files whose room numbers overlap, so its rooms carry the part too:
L2_1R17.HEX, L2_2R17.HEX. Neither file, and the room keeps the
automatic palette; the title and cutscenes always keep their own.

A file is 16 lines of RRGGBB, as Lospec and Aseprite export .hex
palettes, rounded to the STE's 4 bits a channel. Ctrl+P writes the
room's current colours to the game folder under the room's name and
says so on screen for a couple of seconds, so an author starts from
the game's own choice - or from the custom palette in use, which
round-trips exactly.

PALETTE\ is scanned once at startup, so a room change touches the disk
only when it has a file to load, and palette_st.cpp uses GEMDOS
directly: the C library's fopen converts the file date through mktime,
over 100ms a call on a 68000. The quantiser's closing steps - the
remap, its generation counters, the reconversion - are now one helper
shared by the automatic and custom paths.

events.title: Review fixes: SDL build, true level headroom, one VBL per push
events.message:
Review fixes: SDL build, true level headroom, one VBL per push

The memory log's hook in stepLogic was not fenced, so the SDL build
no longer compiled; and it ran before the level's first room was
decoded, which is what allocates the tile pool, so level 1's figure
left out 96K. Measured after the room, level 1 is the tightest at 2MB
with music and both borders. The README now says a 2MB machine is a
tight fit rather than putting a number on it.

With a border open, a scene's first push waited for the VBL twice -
once in stShow and again inside copyRectPlanar's full-page sync - a
lost frame per scene. stShow now leaves a full page to that sync.

double_buffer: Fill maps the rows outside its window to row 0, so a
copy running past the window recorded its damage as a backwards
range and the pages drifted apart; damage now covers the rows that
are displayed. And the palette is written after the flip, not before,
where it recoloured the old picture until the VBL.

Tidied from the review: ST_pageBand and a leftover include removed,
ST_copyPage's unreachable band copy and ST_pageShowRect's untracked
branch folded away, comments still describing the abandoned per-row
and per-block masks rewritten, the whole-rows threshold named,
pageTouch returns first when no scene is running (every in-game
sprite and fill called it), and the unused .prf track names left out
of the ST build.
events.author: neilrackett

events.title: Prepare the 1.6.0 release
events.message:
Prepare the 1.6.0 release

Records 1.6.0 in every place a release identifies itself: VERSION, the
pinned version test, the AppStream release history, the apt commands in the
README, the in-app Help and the installation and Linux desktop guides, the
HFE guide, the health-response example, the release-checklist example and
the documentation index.

A feature release, covering #31. Drives attached through USB open in place,
and can be exported to an image file or copied onto another drive. SFS, PFS3
and the FFS long-filename variants are read and written, Directory Cache
volumes keep their caches, and copying between panes works again for
floppies and now works for partitions.

The notes call out the changes to how images are written: Directory Cache
caches are now maintained, the long-filename variants are writable, and the
FFS hardfile repairs no longer touch SFS or PFS3 volumes. They also say
plainly that long-filename volumes have not been checked by a real AmigaOS
3.2 FastFileSystem.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: peteclarke-del

events.title: Open drives attached through USB, and fix copying between panes
events.message:
Open drives attached through USB, and fix copying between panes

A hard drive or memory card from an Amiga, attached through a USB adapter,
can now be opened where it is from Add Pane or File -> Open attached drive.
Only disks behind a USB controller are listed. A drive opens read-only, has
no undo, and takes changes only once Allow writes is chosen; one that Linux
has mounted is refused. Linux gives whole drives to the administrator, so
the package carries a udev rule for the desktop user, documented but not
installed.

A drive can be copied out and duplicated without passing through the page:

- File -> Export drive to image file streams the drive, as its partition
  table describes it or every byte of it, or one partition with a .geo
  sidecar, to a file chosen in a native Save dialog. Empty space is not
  written, and a stopped copy leaves no file behind.
- File -> Copy drive to another drive writes a verified copy over another
  attached drive. The target is chosen from the attached-drive list, must
  be large enough, unmounted and writable, and is named again before it is
  erased. Every byte is written, then read back from the drive and compared.

SFS and PFS3 volumes with no partition table open as single volumes, and
each volume and partition now reports its own filing system and name
limit, so SFS and PFS3 partitions allow long names in every dialog. A
partition for another system is refused with its DOS type rather than an
engine error. The FFS hardfile repairs that run when an image is saved no
longer touch SFS or PFS3 volumes, whose root block is not where FFS keeps
it.

Copying between panes is fixed:

- A copy whose target was a partition went to the engine's command line,
  which addresses the whole drive, and failed on its partition table.
- The direct copy used for floppies and single volumes called a method
  that did not exist, so it has failed since 1.1.1.
- Files are read one at a time rather than all before writing, and a copy
  that would replace a file, use a name the target cannot hold or overrun
  its free space is refused before anything is written.
- A drop is one tracked operation that shows each file and can be stopped
  from Jobs.
- In the Linux desktop a multi-file drag arrived as its first file alone,
  and its drag image stayed on screen. The GTK drop target now leaves drags
  that began in the window to the page, and the page keeps its own record
  of what is being dragged.
- Whole partitions can be dragged, from the partition table or a partition
  pane, into a drawer or onto another drive's partition, including another
  partition of the same drive.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: peteclarke-del

events.title: Read and write PFS3, long-filename and Directory Cache volumes
events.message:
Read and write PFS3, long-filename and Directory Cache volumes

Large Amiga partitions are usually PFS3 or SFS, and amiganut could only
name PFS3. It now reads and writes PFS3 volumes in place, bare or inside
an RDB partition, for the PFS\1, PFS\2, PFS\3 and PDS\3 DOS types. Changes
are made copy-on-write in the handler's own order, with the root block
written last, and a volume the handler left with a postponed operation is
opened read-only. Deleted files are freed at once rather than moved to
the deleted-files drawer, and new links are not created. The work was
checked against pfs3aio 19.2 on an emulated A1200: DiskValid passed every
volume built and changed here, and every change pfs3aio then made read
back and validated.

Directory Cache volumes (DOS\4, DOS\5) were listed as writable, but no
change updated the cache, so a real machine listed a drawer as it used to
be. Every change now keeps each directory's cache blocks exact, validate
compares them with the hash chains, and rebuild_dircache repairs a volume
left stale. The Kickstart 3.1 FastFileSystem listed volumes written here
without a difference, and its own changes validated cleanly afterwards.

Long-filename volumes (DOS\6, DOS\7) are read and written with names of
up to 107 characters, following the layout amitools documents. No AmigaOS
3.2 FastFileSystem has yet checked a volume written here. is_dircache no
longer reports these two types as Directory Cache.

Also:

- The Kickstart probe declines anything larger than a ROM can be before
  reading it. It read its whole input, and mounting a partition of a
  256 GB drive attached over USB read the drive into memory.
- The FFS bitmap is decoded and encoded a long at a time, and only the
  bitmap blocks that changed are written back. Rewriting every one on
  each flush made copying many files take longer the larger the volume.
- Copy collection can carry each file's size instead of its bytes, so a
  tree from a hard-drive partition is not held in memory before writing.
- A block device is accepted wherever an image file is.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: build: give the installer licence a name CPack can use, and no dmg SLA
events.message:
build: give the installer licence a name CPack can use, and no dmg SLA

Pointing CPACK_RESOURCE_FILE_LICENSE at the repository's LICENSE broke both
non-Linux legs of the 0.8.4 release, in two different ways, and neither is
visible from Linux.

CPackWIX converts the licence resource to RTF by extension and accepts .txt or
.rtf. LICENSE has no extension at all, so the MSI failed with "unsupported WiX
License file extension ''" - it only ever worked before because CMake's own
placeholder is named CPack.GenericLicense.txt. It is now copied to license.txt
in the build tree at configure time: one licence text to maintain, and an
extension CPack understands.

CPack.cmake:880 enables a dmg Software Licence Agreement whenever the licence
resource is anything other than that placeholder and CMP0133 is not NEW. An SLA
cannot be accepted headlessly, so hdiutil attach answered "attach canceled" and
the macOS leg could neither verify nor publish its dmg. The first response to
that was a five-attempt retry, which is the wrong answer to a deterministic
error; the retry is gone and the SLA is off. The licence still travels inside
the bundle - LICENSE, NOTICE and the generated THIRD-PARTY.txt - which the dmg
step already asserts.

events.title: build: narrow the /usr/lib guard to shared objects, and retry hdiutil attach
events.message:
build: narrow the /usr/lib guard to shared objects, and retry hdiutil attach

Two failures from the 0.8.4 release attempt, both in verification rather than
in what ships.

The /usr/lib guard fired on /usr/lib/.build-id, which rpmbuild adds for its
debuginfo links on the runner - the local rpmbuild does not, which is why the
dry run of this step passed. A directory is not cached by ldconfig and cannot
be handed to another application, so the check now matches shared objects,
which is the actual hazard: it still fires on the 0.8.3 layout it exists to
prevent, and passes on the private prefix with .build-id beside it.

hdiutil attach died with "attach canceled" on a dmg CPack had just reported as
generated, eleven seconds earlier. CPack's DragNDrop generator attaches the
image itself to write its .DS_Store and detaches it again, and the device can
still be busy a moment later, so the attach is retried at an absolute
mountpoint. A genuinely broken image fails all five attempts, so the retry
cannot mask one.

events.title: release: 0.8.4
events.message:
release: 0.8.4

0.8.3's deb could not be installed at all: it carried the build host's
copyright file for every library the bundle links, into paths dpkg knows
belong to installed packages, and dpkg refuses to take a file from another
package. The packages also installed their Qt, glib and D-Bus into /usr/lib,
where ldconfig hands them to every other application on the machine, and no
package stated a name, an author or a licence that a software centre could
read. All three are fixed here: the installers stage a private prefix, the
release workflow installs the deb to prove it, and PiST ships AppStream
metadata, a DEP-5 copyright and its own licence text as the installer
licence. Assets are named PiST-<version>-<platform>.
events.author: idontwantyourspamthanks

events.title: docs: record the installer layout, and what an AppImage cannot do
events.message:
docs: record the installer layout, and what an AppImage cannot do

The install text named an AppImage without a version, because that is what the
workflow produced. It carries one now, so the snippets use a glob rather than a
literal file name: naming an artifact a release does not actually ship has been
a defect here before, and the release body is published verbatim with nothing
in the release checklist that would remind anyone to bump it.

Both the README and the release body now say what an AppImage cannot do -
register itself with the desktop - and name what can: AppImageLauncher,
appimaged, or the deb and rpm. That is what makes the packages the recommended
route on Linux, and it is the answer to "installing the AppImage works but
nothing appears in the menu".

PLAN.md Phase 4 records the facts the packaging now rests on: the dpkg rule
that made 0.8.3 uninstallable, the ldconfig precedence that made /usr/lib
unsafe, the private prefix and why moving the subtree rigidly preserves the
rpath and qt.conf, the AppStream id choice, the empty CFBundleIdentifier, and
the measured portal behaviour behind the conditional desktop-file name. NOTICE
records where the relocated distro copyright texts live, and why the AppImage
keeps them where linuxdeploy put them.
events.author: idontwantyourspamthanks

events.title: ui: state the desktop-file name so Wayland groups the window
events.message:
ui: state the desktop-file name so Wayland groups the window

On Wayland the app_id came from the application name, "PiST", which matches no
desktop entry, so the taskbar showed a generic icon and would not group the
window under the launcher. Under X11 nothing was wrong: xprop on the 0.8.3
binary reports WM_CLASS "pist", "PiST", because Qt derives res_name from the
executable name rather than from setApplicationName. pist.desktop now states
that with StartupWMClass=pist.

setDesktopFileName() is called before the application object exists, which is
when Qt reads it, and only when an entry is actually installed - pist.desktop,
or the appimagekit_pist.desktop that AppImageLauncher generates for an
integrated AppImage. An unconditional call was measured to make the desktop
portal fail to register the app ID on every build-tree and unintegrated-AppImage
start, which is a warning printed for a name nothing on that system can
resolve. With the guard, a run that has no entry stays silent and a run that
has one claims exactly that name.
events.author: idontwantyourspamthanks

events.title: packaging: name the product PiST, its author Koala Software, and its licence
events.message:
packaging: name the product PiST, its author Koala Software, and its licence

A software centre had nothing to read. The deb reported the name its file
happened to carry and "Unknown Author", and no licence anywhere: the package
had no AppStream metadata at all, CPACK_RESOURCE_FILE_LICENSE was still CMake's
CPack.GenericLicense.txt placeholder, and there was no DEP-5 copyright file,
which is where Debian policy puts the statement. The RPM's vendor was the
literal string "unknown", CPACK_PACKAGE_VENDOR being the product name rather
than an author.

CPACK_PACKAGE_NAME is now the product name an installer shows - PiST, in the
MSI product name, the NSIS/STGZ install directory and the dmg volume - and
CPACK_PACKAGE_VENDOR the author, which is what WIX.template.in writes as the
MSI Manufacturer and CPackRPM as the Vendor. The distro package names are
spelled out lowercase, as Debian policy requires; CPackDeb lowercases whatever
it is given and CPackRPM does not. On macOS the bundle presented itself as
"pist" and shipped an empty CFBundleIdentifier, because neither
MACOSX_BUNDLE_BUNDLE_NAME nor MACOSX_BUNDLE_GUI_IDENTIFIER was ever set.

packaging/io.github.idontwantyourspamthanks.pist.metainfo.xml carries the name,
the developer and the licence a store displays. Its id is reverse-DNS and the
menu entry stays pist.desktop, joined by <launchable>: a flat id also merges,
but appstreamcli then fails validation, which is a trap for whoever adds a CI
gate later. The developer is stated twice, because Ubuntu 22.04's AppStream
0.16 - the oldest release these packages support - cannot read the 1.0 tag.

packaging/copyright is the DEP-5 statement, installed beside LICENSE and
NOTICE. Its Files patterns are layout-agnostic (*/vasmm68k_mot, */libQt6*)
because that one file ships in packages with three different layouts, and a
pattern naming usr/bin/ would silently stop matching the installers' private
prefix - leaving the non-free assembler and linker claimed by the GPL-2+
catch-all, which is the one thing the file exists to prevent.

The deb's description was mangled too: it was assembled from five adjacent
quoted arguments, which set() joins into a list, so the semicolons reached the
control file as a literal "; " at the head of every continuation line. It is
one multi-line string now, shared with the rpm so the two cannot drift.

The icons are installed at 128, 256 and 512 px instead of leaving the hicolor
directories the AppImage deployer creates empty.
events.author: idontwantyourspamthanks

events.title: build: stage the deb and rpm from a private prefix
events.message:
build: stage the deb and rpm from a private prefix

The 0.8.3 deb could not be installed. It was staged straight from the AppDir
the AppImage is built from, and linuxdeploy copies the build host's copyright
file for every library it bundles into usr/share/doc/<package>/. Inside an
AppImage that is attribution; inside a .deb those are paths dpkg knows belong
to libglib2.0-0, libpulse0, libxcb-* and fifty more installed packages, and
dpkg will not take a file away from another package:

  trying to overwrite '/usr/share/doc/libglib2.0-0/copyright', which is also
  in package libglib2.0-0

Nothing in the workflow could see it: the verification extracted the package
with dpkg-deb -x and ran the binary from the extracted tree, which never asks
dpkg whether the files are free to take.

Two more defects came out of the same stage. The AppImage's own plumbing was
installed into / - AppRun, AppRun.wrapped, .DirIcon, apprun-hooks/ and the
root-level pist.desktop and pist.svg symlinks. And the bundle's 74 libraries
sat in /usr/lib, which ldconfig scans before the multiarch directory: with two
copies of a soname in the cache the /usr/lib one is listed first and is what
ld.so resolves, so the package made itself the system-wide provider of
libQt6Core.so.6, libglib-2.0.so.0 and libdbus-1.so.3 for every other
application on the machine.

The installers now stage /usr/lib/pist - Debian's private-library convention,
and a directory ldconfig does not recurse into - holding bin/, lib/, plugins/
and the ROM, with only pist and pist-mcp symlinked into /usr/bin so the bundled
hatari, vasm and vlink cannot shadow a user's own. The subtree moves rigidly,
which is what keeps it working: the $ORIGIN/../lib rpath and the qt.conf
linuxdeploy wrote beside the binary (Prefix = ../, Plugins = plugins) resolve
inside the prefix unchanged, and the ROM walk finds share/emutos two levels up.
The foreign copyright texts move to doc/pist/licenses/distro/ rather than being
dropped: they are the only licence texts for the transitive system libraries
the bundle carries, which collect-notices.py does not attest.

Verified against the 0.8.3 artifact. The packaged binary runs from the new
layout under xvfb, resolving the assembler, linker, hrdb emulator and EmuTOS
inside it; a Prefix one level deeper aborts with "Could not find the Qt
platform plugin xcb", which is why this runs under xvfb rather than offscreen,
the offscreen plugin not being bundled. Rebuilt from the same content, the
package installs into a dpkg database that owns the colliding path, where
0.8.3's does not.

The step now installs the deb on the runner and removes it again. The runner
has the very packages whose copyright files used to collide, so that is the
check that fails if a distro-owned path ever returns to the stage. It also
asserts the control fields, the rpm's name, licence and vendor, and that
nothing is owned directly under /usr/lib.

Asset names lose the tag's "v": github.ref_name interpolated verbatim is what
produced pist-v0.8.3-linux-amd64.deb, and a store truncating that at the first
dot is what reported a package called "pist-v0". Every artifact is now

events.title: Label every address The Hobbit's code and comments use
events.message:
Label every address The Hobbit's code and comments use

Every operand that is an address now assembles as a label, and every address
the comments mention is a #R reference, so the asm reads it as a label and the
HTML links it. What is left as a number is a number: word references, a port,
constants and negative offsets.

- The variables at $B6DA-$B71E, 48 of them, each labelled (ACTION, TARGET,
  PLAYER_AT, DOING_IT...), and the work areas the generated control file took
  for unused -- the AND checkpoint, the two windows' cursors, the fill's seed
  flags, MOVE's and CHARACTERS_ACT's bytes -- given blocks and labels. PHRASES
  is worked out field by field; ENDINGS is 24 bytes, followed by ORDER_COUNT;
  the frames below COMMAND_FRAME are a block of their own.
- The generators label any record field the code or a comment names: object
  fields (PLAYER_WHERE, RED_GOLDEN_DRAGON_FLAGS), room descriptions and exits,
  the characters' slots, Bard's rewritten script step. Room descriptions are
  DEFWs to their messages. The timers are laid out field by field, their
  routines as DEFWs.
- Messages are named from their text (MSG_YOU_HEAR_A_NOISE), including the
  ways into the middle of one; $ADC4 is a sixth. Script jump targets are named
  after their table (GANDALF_F, GOBLINS_A). The printed-word list is decoded a
  word to a line, by PRINT_WORD's own rule for a third letter.
- Code other code writes into, or enters part-way, is labelled and written as
  label plus offset (LOCK_BIT_OP+3, SHUT_ROAD+2, OBJECT_INDEX-3); the 83
  numbered entry points other routines use are named (RUN_MESSAGE_HL,
  PRINT_WORD_DE, NEXT_CHARACTER).
- Three comment addresses were off: the title screen waits at $6C6D, not
  $6C60; PRINT_WORD's second entry is $74C1 and the class dispatch $75C1.
  ROOM_PREPOSITIONS held OUTSIDE as a wrong label, now kept a number.
- The HTML links LD operands too.

Rebuilt from the tape: 40000 bytes reassemble byte-for-byte. The only
skool2asm warnings left are USR 27648 and 26000 T-states in comments.

events.title: Flow Control Macros: Introduce typed comparisons
events.message:
Flow Control Macros: Introduce typed comparisons

Instead of:

  IF scmp16 var1, var2 : NEG

... where you need to remember that NEG means "less than" for 16-bit
signed comparisons, and that you need to use ecmp16 if you want equality,
you can now write:

  IF s16 var1 < var2

The microsyntax is:

  IF <type> <arg1> <op> <arg2>

Where type is one of: u8 u16 s16

And op is: = <> < >=

This plugs into the existing parser so NOT, OR and AND work too.

No binary changes (except for the tests)

events.title: fix(drive): VIA2 port B is live without a disk (BUG-062)
events.message:
fix(drive): VIA2 port B is live without a disk (BUG-062)

TRX64 skipped VIA2's store_prb and undump_prb while the drive had no disk, a
guard from the TS port; VICE's drive is live either way. The DOS's power-on
"motor off" was lost whenever the disk came later, so the rotation ran while
the pin said off, and a restore (which re-derives the motor from the pin)
left the straight run. Head steps and zone changes made with no disk in were
lost the same way.

New gate: a drive that never spun restores cycle for cycle (red before: apart
after frame 47). snapshot_roundtrip_fidelity's drive-active scenario never
pressed RETURN (nine keys for a ten-key buffer) and passed only through this
bug; it now enters the command and the drive really seeks.

events.title: Animate The Hobbit's pictures as the game draws them, and decode their commands
events.message:
Animate The Hobbit's pictures as the game draws them, and decode their commands

Each location's picture is now captured frame by frame while the game's own
DRAW_LOCATION_PICTURE draws it in the simulator, one frame per 50 Hz frame
interrupt, and saved as a GIF that loops at the game's own speed -- slow
fills and all -- holding the finished picture for three seconds before it
starts again. The Locations page shows these (a click restarts one) with
how long each takes to draw, and each picture's block in the disassembly
opens with its animation.

The picture streams, which were rows of bytes, are now a line per command
in words: the border and starting attribute, MOVE to x, y, LINE of n
pixels in a direction (diagonally, or stepping the other way every n),
FILL with a colour from a point, PAINT a colour along a path of cells, and
the end. Each block's title names its location.

Frames are made with PIL's own operations -- the bitmap as a mask choosing
between ink and paper layers blown up from the attributes -- since there
are some hundreds per picture.

Checked: rebuilds byte-for-byte; Bag End's animation sampled -- walls,
door, then the floor filling -- and drawn in 6.8 s, as measured earlier.

events.title: Decode The Hobbit's character scripts, as editable source and on the Characters page
events.message:
Decode The Hobbit's character scripts, as editable source and on the Characters page

The scripts region ($C82D up to TIMERS) is now generated by script_blocks,
like the rooms and objects: each script table and every step on a line of
its own, commented in words ("TAKE", "GIVE TO: curious map, the player",
"Switch to one of its first 4 scripts at random"), with a block per
character's table and one for the scripts several share. Every address in
them -- a table's scripts, a step's fallback, a jump, a routine a step calls
-- is a DEFW, and so a label in the generated source (GANDALF_A,
ON_ATTACK_WITH, GANDALF_WHATS_THIS...), which makes a script editable there
with the addresses following. The CHARACTERS slots are decoded field by
field the same way, their script pointers labels too. script_program checks
that every byte of the region is a table or a step, and stops the build if
not; 13 tables and 148 steps cover it exactly.

The Characters page writes every character's scripts out step by step,
linked to the source, a script that runs on into another saying so.

Checked: rebuilds byte-for-byte; the generated asm read to confirm the
DEFWs are labels; the page read in a browser.

events.title: feat(872): a 1581 on the wire — drive_type, D81 media, status and monitor
events.message:
feat(872): a 1581 on the wire — drive_type, D81 media, status and monitor

- session/drive_type {unit, type}: refused while that drive is powered,
  naming the position; off, the board is built fresh; a medium that does
  not fit is written back, ejected and named in the reply.
- media/ingress|mount|swap|open and swap_disk_and_continue accept D81 (one

- session/state drives[] and session/drive_status carry the type; a
  1581's status is its CIA glue and WD registers.
- Restores set the board types before the media go back in
  (prepare_drive_types); a C64 power cycle keeps each position's board.
- Monitor: device drive<unit> on a 1581 — its map through m/d, and r
  shows head, side and the WD.

events.title: feat(872): the 1581 board — drive CIA, WD1772 + MFM surface, D81, checkpoints
events.message:
feat(872): the 1581 board — drive CIA, WD1772 + MFM surface, D81, checkpoints

A drive position holds a 1541 or a 1581 (Spec 872 D1-D5):

- ciacore.rs: VICE core/ciacore.c ported 1:1 for the drive CIA — IFR and
  SDR delay lines, FLAG, SDR/CNT/SP, port hooks, the IRQ line as
  cia_set_int_clk drives it — with the 8520 TOD as a binary event counter
  on a pin held high (WD1772 board, J1 open). The C64's CIAs are untouched.
- fdd.rs / wd177x.rs: fdd.c and wd1770.c ported 1:1; is1772 = 1; a sector is
  always built from its own bytes (D81 error bytes kept and ignored).
- drive1581.rs: the board — own 6502 at 2 MHz, 8 KiB RAM, open bus at
  $2000-$3FFF, CIA/WD mirrors, 32 KiB ROM, CIA-port glue (cia1581d.c).
- drive.rs: the position carries the board; the 870/871 part rules apply
  unchanged; set_board_type refused while powered; D81 media; lazy
  write-back; pair_* fold and deliver ATN per type (FLAG for a 1581).
- iec.rs: type-aware fold; conf3 reads unit_type by slot.
- drive_snapshot.rs / c64re_snapshot.rs: DRIVE8 (type 1581), DRIVECPU0
  (0x2000 RAM), CIA1581D0, WD17700, FDD0, IMAGE0; drivePart.boardType
  (absent = 1541, not written for a 1541).
- tests/drive1581_gate.rs: §9 tests 1-10 over the real KERNAL and DOS.

events.title: Give The Hobbit's HTML disassembly locations, objects, characters and actions pages
events.message:
Give The Hobbit's HTML disassembly locations, objects, characters and actions pages

The index now has a "The game" section. Locations lists all 79 places with
the game's own description, exits linked to where they lead, what starts
there, the first-visit score, the arrival hook and the HELP hint -- and,
for the 22 that have one, the picture, drawn by the game's own
DRAW_LOCATION_PICTURE in the simulator and saved as a PNG. Objects,
Characters and Actions are tables of every record's size, weight,
strength, defence, flags, side, script slot, order limit, reactions and own
handlers, and of all 59 sentence patterns with their handlers and options,
cross-linked to each other and to the code. A Reference section has Bugs
and Credits.

The four game pages are the game's own text and art, so
scripts/hobbit_pages.py generates them on each --html build into
game_disassembly/ (gitignored); scripts/hobbit.ref, committed, holds only
the layout and prose. Tables are read from the tape's data, not the running
game, which by its first prompt has already had Gandalf give the player the
map.

Hobbit.message's scratch stack moves from $BF00, in the room records, to
$5E80 below the game's own stack: the flood fill's queue on it had been
landing on the rooms and breaking the next picture.

Checked: pages rendered and looked at in a browser; each picture drawn from
a clean machine.

events.title: Amiga: the credit scroller is as tall as the text on an interlaced screen
events.message:
Amiga: the credit scroller is as tall as the text on an interlaced screen

It blitted its eight lines onto eight rows of the screen and started ten
rows above the panel, which is right while a text line is eight rows. On
an interlaced screen a line of text is sixteen, so the scroll came out
half height and crowded against the panel. Each of its lines now covers
zoom_y rows, and it starts ten text rows up.

events.title: Leave out the code and tables the ST can never use
events.message:
Leave out the code and tables the ST can never use

The ST plays Amiga data and has no software mixer, so the other
versions' loaders (Mac, PC98, the DOS demo archives and their
decompressors), the DOS SEQ cutscene player and the digital music
players (.mod, .ogg, CD-i, .prf and its MIDI parser) can never run -
but the engine still names them, from resource-type switches and as
members of Mixer and Game, so they were linked in and loaded into
memory with the rest. st_stubs.cpp stands in for them with the few
entry points the engine links against, all left idle, and the upstream
sources are untouched. The toolchain's TOS target cannot drop unused
functions at link time, which is why this is done by hand.

staticres.cpp: on the ST the Japanese font, strings and texts, the
DOS credits and the DOS language-menu flags become one-byte
placeholders - their call sites only run for Japanese, PC98 or DOS
data and stay as upstream wrote them - and the tables only the
removed players used are left out.

The font cache kept each 8x8 glyph in the decoded cell's 16-byte
rows; it keeps 8-byte rows now, and the half that was padding, 6K,
is gone.

The program's code is 510,412 -> 467,928 bytes and its fixed buffers
107,936 -> 101,792, 48K in all. In Hatari on a 2MB STE with music and
both borders open, the title has 432K free where it had 391K, each
level about 40K more, and the intro, every level, the credits and
dying back to the title all run.

events.title: feat(873): a folder on the bus — the line-level device, its DOS and its checkpoint
events.message:
feat(873): a folder on the bus — the line-level device, its DOS and its checkpoint

A third kind of thing on the IEC bus beside the two 1541 positions: no CPU, a
timed state machine (VICE serial-iec-device.c states, the Ultimate's timing by
default, VICE's as the second profile) that pulls CLK and DATA in its own slot,
and a DOS serving a host folder through the FolderSource trait. Advanced at every
sync point the drives have, event-driven on the C64 clock; the device map marks
its slot IECDEVICE (conf3). Refused beside a drive at the same unit. The
checkpoint carries the device (line state, channels as host path + position,
status, cwd, listing), never the folder's contents; rewind never touches the host.

Gate: tests/folder_device_gate.rs — directory bytes, KERNAL load/save, command
channel, SEQ + the 8→9 copy, not-in-the-way, refusals, read-only, checkpoints
mid-LOAD/mid-SAVE (500-frame lockstep), timing against the KERNAL read off the ROM.

events.message:
Describe the last of The Hobbit: the main loop, the font, and the code nothing reaches

START runs on into MAIN_LOOP, now commented: the title screen and the N key
that turns pictures off, the divider, the first turn's "> LOOK", and each
turn's read, tokenise -- quotes making an order, an unknown word echoed in
"i do not know the word ..." -- parse and obey. The story's FONT, both key
maps, CONTROL_CODES, ENDINGS, the character SCRIPTS and the two word
buffers are single blocks now, through `; span`.

Seven stretches read as code but nothing leads to them -- special word slot
0's handler, an OPEN for the wood elf alone, a routine that would wipe an
exit, and some fragments. They are left as data with what they would do said
beside them, keeping to the rule of marking as code only what there is
evidence runs.

With that no block is left untitled, and the README says 100%. The
character scripts are described as one block, not yet entry by entry.

Macros: Introduce ucmp8 as shorthand for LDA/CMP

This probably seems silly, but the intent is to align with the
domain-specific language introduced by the 16-bit macros like
cmp16/scmp16/etc, just like there is copy8 and copy16.

This is not used when the load into A has side effects. A common case
is when it is the first in a chain e.g. LDA / CMP / BEQ / CMP / BEQ.

No binary changes.

events.message:
Describe every one of The Hobbit's variables

VARIABLES ($B6DA-$B71E) now has a comment on every byte: the parser's place

events.title: Name the rest of The Hobbit's parser: PARSE_ACTION and the replies to names that do not fit
events.message:
Name the rest of The Hobbit's parser: PARSE_ACTION and the replies to names that do not fit

PARSE_ACTION turns a parsed sentence into an action code, sets the
pattern's options, and hands a pattern with objects to MATCH_AND_TRY --
going round again for each object with ALL, past those an EXCEPT names
(EXCEPTED, believed, not traced in play). What the parser says when a name
does not lead anywhere is TARGET_TROUBLE and INSTRUMENT_TROUBLE: "which
... ?" when several fit (ASK_WHICH, which keeps the sentence so the next
line can answer), "i do not see the ... here", "... what ?", and
UNKNOWN_VERB. Also TRY_INSTRUMENTS, PRINT_NOW, KEEP_QUESTION, NO_INSTRUMENT
and PUSH_PATTERN_WORDS, which picks words by rewriting its own jumps.

ASSIGN_PHRASES no longer claims an example it had not been checked on, and
MATCH_AND_TRY no longer states which way its flag goes.

Checked: rebuilds byte-for-byte; the spans in PARSE_ACTION checked against
the decoder.

events.title: Name how The Hobbit matches a sentence to its action pattern
events.message:
Name how The Hobbit matches a sentence to its action pattern

MATCH_PATTERN gathers the verb and the phrases' particle and preposition
into a probe and searches ACTION_PATTERNS with NAME_MATCHES; with no match
the verb does nothing, "you ... . time passes...". ASSIGN_PHRASES uses the
pattern's preposition to decide which noun phrase is the target and which
the instrument, so word order in the sentence does not matter, and keeps
the target's name for IT. Also PICK_WORD, NAME_OF_NUMBER and SEARCH_START
(the last marked as not worked out further).

events.title: Load no samples a machine cannot play, and no music it cannot either
events.message:
Load no samples a machine cannot play, and no music it cannot either

A plain ST has neither the voice device nor DMA sound, so its sound
effects are never heard - yet every level loaded its sample file,
119-152K, and each effect the game asked for then logged "Unknown
sound num" once none were loaded. The samples are now loaded only
where they can play (and not with ste_sound=false), and the effects
are dropped silently without them. On a 2MB ST the first level leaves
271K free where it left 127K; the STE is unchanged.

When a track has no .STM - every track with music=false, the default
- playMusic fell through to upstream's .ogg, CD-i, .mod and .prf
players, none of which can make a sound on the ST: a file probe at
every track change, and a .mod left in DATA\ would have been loaded,
a hundred K or more, and never heard. The ST stops at its YM player.

events.title: Unload the level on the way back to the title
events.message:
Unload the level on the way back to the title

The title needs a 70K block for its picture, and on a 2MB machine it
could not find one with level 5 or 7 still in memory and music or a
border open: dying and returning to the title stopped the game with
"Failed to allocate screen buffer". Nothing a level loads is needed
until the next level loads it again, so leaving one now frees it all -
the level files, the sprite positions, the sound effects (up to 152K),
the rewind states and the port's sprite, slab and tile caches - after
stopping the effects, so a playing sample is not read from freed
memory.

load_SPC kept the previous level's table on every level load after
the first; it frees it now.

With logging on, RS.LOG records the largest block TOS can still hand
out at the title and when a level has loaded and unloaded. It asks
TOS rather than probing with malloc: the library keeps the big blocks
a probe takes and splits them later, and that alone stopped level 1
finding room for its tile pool at 2MB.

In Hatari at 2MB with music and both borders open, every level starts
(119K free at the tightest), dying on 2, 5 and 7 gets back to the
title, and a second trip round leaves the title with the same 192K

events.title: Decode The Hobbit's fighting: strength, defence, sides, and who can kill the dragon
events.message:
Decode The Hobbit's fighting: strength, defence, sides, and who can kill the dragon

DO_ATTACK weighs the attacker's strength (byte 5 of its record, plus the
weapon's -- a bare FIST otherwise) against the target's defence (byte 6),
each jostled by -10 to +10. A blow no stronger is wasted, one more than 16
stronger kills, and anything between picks a message from WOUNDS and wears
the target down. KILL marks a character dead (flag bit 3), drops what it
held and ends its script. Byte 4's high bits are sides: SAME_SIDE stops
anyone attacking its own, and the player attacking a friend turns it into
an enemy.

DO_SHOOT needs the bow; Bard never misses, anyone else misses the dragon
every time -- only Bard can kill it -- and everything else a third of the
time. DO_GIVE and DO_EXAMINE are named too, and IS_ALIVE.

That closes two open items: object bytes 5 and 6, and what reads byte 4's
high bits; and it confirms flag bit 3 as dead or broken.

events.title: support: one rule for writing a file the user already has
events.message:
support: one rule for writing a file the user already has

Every path that replaces a file the user already had opened its destination
with Truncate and checked the byte count afterwards, which reports a failed
write honestly and still leaves the file empty: on a full disk or a quota,
the only copy of the source being edited, the sprite document, an export or a
floppy image is gone. The project file had moved to QSaveFile and was still
exposed, because Qt 6.8.1 - the Qt every release archive bundles - checks
only its own writeError before the rename, and a flush that fails inside
commit() never sets it, so the truncated temporary file goes over the
destination and commit() returns true. Qt 6.10 folds the device error in
first, which is why a development machine never saw it.

files::write() is that rule in one place: stage in the destination's own
directory, flush, check the device error, cancel the temporary when any of
them fails, and only then let it take the destination's place. The editor's
source save, ImageDocument (.pim), the ST image exports, the bitplane export,
the floppy extraction, FloppyImage::saveRaw and ProjectSettings::save all go
through it now. The files PiST generates for a session - the discovery file,
the debugger bootstrap script, the AUTO-folder image - are not user data and
keep their plain write.

Pinned by aFailedWriteKeepsThePreviousBytes, beside the project-level
saveFailureKeepsPreviousFile and sharing its RLIMIT_FSIZE fixture: with the
naive truncate-and-check body both fail on Qt 6.8.1, and both pass with the
rule. Full suite green on 6.8.1, the Qt the archives bundle.

events.title: Carry out file changes inside hard-drive partitions
events.message:
Carry out file changes inside hard-drive partitions

Deleting and renaming inside a partition of a hard drive failed whatever
the partition held: those changes were sent to the engine's command line,
which addresses a whole image, and a drive with a partition table has no
single volume there to act on. The same applied to replacing a file from
the editor, applying a patch and installing into a partition.

When a partition is selected, the remove, move and make-drawer commands
now run through that partition's own mount, so they work for FFS and SFS
partitions alike, and Validate checks the partition on screen rather than
every partition of the drive.

Opening one partition also no longer leaves a handle open on the whole
drive, which matters once the drive is a real device rather than a file.

events.title: Read and write Smart File System volumes
events.message:
Read and write Smart File System volumes

Amiga drives prepared for large partitions often use SFS rather than FFS,
and the workbench could list such a partition in the drive's Rigid Disk
Block but not open it. Amiganut now reads and writes SFS 1.x volumes,
whether bare or inside an RDB partition, and can format new ones.

Changes follow SFS's own crash protocol. File data goes only into blocks
free both on disk and in the pending change; changed metadata is logged
to free space, a TRFA marker points at the log, the blocks are written
in place and the marker returns to TROK, with a flush between stages.
Power lost at any point leaves the old volume or the new one, and a
volume SFS left mid-change is read as SFS would replay it.

Validate now checks what SFScheck checks, and runs in seconds on a
60 GB partition. The work was checked against real SFS 1.277 on an
emulated A1200: SFScheck accepted volumes built and changed here, and
every change real SFS then made read back intact.

Also fixes RDB partition placement when a partition groups several
sectors into one filesystem block, as SFS partitions often do: the
offset was scaled by SectorPerBlock a second time, putting such
partitions at twice their real position.

events.title: Decode The Hobbit's character scripts, the orders the player gives, and the win
events.message:
Decode The Hobbit's character scripts, the orders the player gives, and the win

Every other character is driven by a script, walked each turn by
CHARACTERS_ACT ($980E) from a 7-byte slot in CHARACTERS ($CACB). A step is an
action tried exactly as the player's sentences are -- the action code and its
objects in $B6E7-$B6E9, carried out through ACTION_TABLE -- or a routine, a
pause, a jump, or a switch to another script from the character's own
FIND_RECORD table, at random or by key. The keys past the ordinary scripts are
reactions: REACT sends a character to the script it keeps for whatever the
player has just done to it. An order the player has given (ORDERS, $B738)
replaces the step unless the step is marked uninterruptible.

ACTION_PATTERNS ($AB53) is the key to all of it: 59 sentence patterns whose
place in the list is the action code, so every code in the scripts and in
ACTION_TABLE now has a name. CHECK_WON ($A9D6) is the ending: the treasure in
the wooden chest.

The routines the scripts call are reached only through JP (HL), so the build
walks the scripts the way the game does and seeds them: 6720 instruction
starts, from 6567.

Checked: rebuilds byte-for-byte; over twelve WAIT turns in the simulator, 166
of 168 script pointers landed on steps as decoded, and the two that did not
were the warg's, past a pause the test walker had wrongly taken for an end --
which is what the SCRIPT_BARE description now says. Not yet worked out: the
sentence printing in ACTOR_TRIES, byte 6 of a slot, and how RANDOM uses A.

events.message:
Decode The Hobbit's timers: the barrel, the bog, the magic door and the rest

END_OF_TURN ($96B3) counts down ten 7-byte timers at $CA84 once a turn,
running each one's routine when it reaches zero and a warning routine in the
turns before, with at most one firing a turn. Those routines are reached only
through $9B80's JP (HL), so they are now code-map seeds (6567 instruction
starts, from 6440), and every one is named and commented: the barrel thrown
up on the long lake, the spider web, the goblins' door, the deep bog, the
magic door and the elf, the wine wearing off (which clears DRUNK, so
WINE_DRUNK's last step is starting timer 7), the eyes in the forest and the
hole in the mountain's side. Also START ($6C00), which saves the changeable
state aside and restores it on each new game, and the helpers the timers use:
RUN_ROUTINE, MOVE_CONTENTS, MOVE_HELD and EMPTY_OUT.

A misaligned annotation now stops the build instead of logging a line that
is easy to miss: one did exactly that here, and the only other symptom was a
40002-byte assembly.

change, timer 6's ring check and $B6F3 are described as read, not seen in play.

events.title: test: make the Windows leg's three checks honest
events.message:
test: make the Windows leg's three checks honest

All three were test defects, not product ones; the Windows leg had been
reporting them as failures since the review batch landed.

- gitDiscoveryFollowsTheOpenedProject: the cmd.exe fake recorded
  `<cwd> ^& <args>` while the checker it feeds splits on `|`, so field 0
  was the whole line, canonicalFilePath() of it was empty, and every
  invocation read as git running outside the project. Record `<cwd>^|<args>`
  with the redirection in front of echo, so no space can be echoed into
  either field. %CD% was already the scratch tree: GitService's working
  directory was right all along.
- settingErrorLinesRepaintsTheGutter: the error mark is a "!" glyph and
  the runner has no fonts at all (Qt ships none and the offscreen
  platform loads none), so drawText puts down no pixels and `marked`
  cannot differ from `plain`. Assert the breakpoint dot instead - drawn
  as geometry precisely so it does not depend on a font - keep every
  paint-count and clear-restores-plain check unconditional, and skip the
  glyph comparison last, naming the environment fact.
- floppyUpdateKeepsForeignNamesByteIdentical: the expected name was
  QStringLiteral("caf\xE9.txt"), and QStringLiteral pastes its narrow
  text after u"", which leaves the UTF-16 meaning of that byte to the
  compiler's mixed-literal interpretation - MSVC's is not U+00E9. Spell
  it QString::fromLatin1, the decode the product itself applies to the
  field, so the expectation is compiler-independent.
events.author: idontwantyourspamthanks

events.title: emu: widen the owed-prompt drain to a tail still on its way
events.message:
emu: widen the owed-prompt drain to a tail still on its way

drainStderr() waits 20 ms, which suits the completion path: Hatari
flushes a response before it prints the prompt that closes it, so the
bytes are in the pipe and the wait only collects them. The owed-prompt
path is different - the command was abandoned at its 10 s timeout with
the emulator still running it, so the rest of its output can be written
after the prompt we swallow for it. 20 ms lost that race on the macOS
runner, and the dead command's tail landed in the next command's
response (aTimedOutCommandsTailDoesNotContaminateTheNext, red in CI
while green on Linux).

Give that one path 200 ms and leave the completion path at 20: nothing
is waiting on an owed prompt, since its command was reported failed ten
seconds earlier. The fake's gap goes from 10 ms to 50 ms so the margin
is the assertion's, not the scheduler's - narrowing the window back now
fails deterministically, which is what the old 10 ms gap could not do.
events.author: idontwantyourspamthanks

events.title: settings: keep the project file when a save cannot reach the disk
events.message:
settings: keep the project file when a save cannot reach the disk

QSaveFile's atomicity depends on commit() noticing that the write failed,
and on Qt 6.8.1 - the Qt every release archive bundles - it does not: the
payload is buffered, so write() reports success and the failure surfaces
in the flush commit() performs internally, which sets the device error but
not the writeError commit() checks. It then renames the empty temporary
file over the project and returns true. Qt 6.10 checks the device error
there, so a development machine on a newer Qt is green either way - which
is how 0.8.2 shipped this.

Flush explicitly and check QFileDevice::error() before committing, and
cancelWriting() when either is wrong so the commit discards the temporary
file instead of renaming it. Reproduced on both versions side by side
under RLIMIT_FSIZE=0, and pinned by saveFailureKeepsPreviousFile, which
fails on 6.8.1 without the check and passes on both with it.
