events.title: Read the tokeniser: abbreviations, and punctuation as words
events.message:
Read the tokeniser: abbreviations, and punctuation as words

TOKENISE is commented step by step, and reading it through shows two
things about what a player may type.

Words can be shortened, and within limits lengthened. A candidate is
taken when it and the typed word agree over the shorter of their lengths
(LETTERS_AGREE, $6FBA) and the typed word is the shorter; when the typed
word is the longer, only if the entry has at least four letters and the
next candidate does not agree as well. Tried through the game: EXAM gives
EXAMINE, INV gives INVENTORY, SWORDS gives SWORD, INT gives INTO because
IN is too short to stretch, and EXAMINING is unknown.

And punctuation is tokenised as words (PUNCTUATION_TOKEN, $6F30): a full
stop takes THEN's class and a comma AND's, so they parse exactly as the
words they stand for.

It also confirms the word classes at the code level: the class nibble is
built from bits 5-6 of an entry's first byte above bits 5-6 of its
second, the rule found earlier from captured tokens.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: jonsole

events.title: Read how the parser ends a command, handles AND, and dispatches special words
events.message:
Read how the parser ends a command, handles AND, and dispatches special words

PARSE_THEN is where a command is finished. It refuses one with no verb --
"what ?", outside a quotation -- sets the ALL bit when $B719 says ALL was
used, counts the frame, and carries on into the next frame when it was an
AND that ended this one. Then it shares words between frames: a frame with
no verb takes the one before's, so TAKE THE MAP AND THE KEY is two TAKEs,
and a frame with the same verb but no second phrase borrows the previous
frame's, so PUT THE MAP AND THE KEY IN THE CHEST puts both in the chest.
It also fits the words of a reply into a command left unfinished, filling
whichever of the old noun and adjectives are empty. More on the line is
left to the main loop, except inside a quotation, where orders to a
character are parsed in one go.

PARSE_AND saves the checkpoint a following verb goes back to, which is
what makes AND separate commands as well as join nouns.

PARSE_SPECIAL searches SPECIAL_WORDS ($8271) and jumps to a handler for
each: ALL, EXCEPT, IT and ONE, and the game's own commands -- SAVE, LOAD,
QUIT, PAUSE, HELP, SCORE, PRINT and NOPRINT. The handlers are seeds now,
since nothing branches to them and the playthrough never types SAVE or
LOAD; the code map gains 157 instruction starts, to 6440.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: jonsole

events.title: Read the parser's verb, noun and preposition handlers
events.message:
Read the parser's verb, noun and preposition handlers

A preposition gathers any more prepositions, lets one article through,
and hands on to the adjective or noun handler; a noun goes into PHRASE,
which FILE_PHRASE then copies into the frame's first empty noun phrase --
E's bits 6 and 7 say which are still empty -- and a third phrase is an
error. PHRASE's first byte, left open before, counts its prepositions.

A verb is stored at the head of the frame by STORE_VERB, which clears E
bit 1 so that a second verb, not joined by AND, gets "what ?". It first
looks ahead past any adverbs for a direction, so RUN QUICKLY WEST puts
WEST at offset 2. And straight after AND a verb ends the command at the
checkpoint PARSE_AND saved and begins another, so TAKE THE MAP AND DROP
IT is two commands.

That last point corrects this commit's first draft, which read E bit 3
the wrong way round: E starts as $FF, so the bit is set for an ordinary
command and PARSE_AND is what clears it.

events.title: Read the parser's loop and its small class handlers
events.message:
Read the parser's loop and its small class handlers

PARSE_COMMAND starts each command at the first frame and keeps in E a set
of flags for what may come next -- bit 1 a verb, bit 2 an adverb, bit 4 an
article -- fetching each token with NEXT_TOKEN and jumping to its class's
handler. A command left unfinished, as after "which key?", is entered in a
different state so the new words are fitted into the old frame.

The small handlers fall through into one another, and that is the
grammar: a direction where a verb could start is the verb, so NORTHEAST on
its own is a command, and anywhere else it takes the adverb's place, as
after GO; GO and RUN are verbs; IN is a preposition except straight after
AND at the start of a command, where it is a verb; an article is noted and
dropped; an adjective goes into the phrase being built, PHRASE ($757A),
which refuses a third. STORE_WORD writes words into the frame low byte
first, which is why frames and object names hold them little-endian while
tokens do not. A word in the wrong place goes to NOT_ALLOWED_HERE, which
says "what ?" -- printed through the game to check -- unless it is inside
a quotation, where orders to other characters are let off.

events.title: Comment the message printer, and find that words have more than one ending
events.message:
Comment the message printer, and find that words have more than one ending

RUN_MESSAGE, PRINT_WORD and PRINT_LITERAL are commented step by step.

The full reading of PRINT_WORD corrects an assumption: an inflected word
does not always take "s". Bits 5-7 of its third dictionary byte choose one
of eight four-character endings in ENDINGS ($B71F): "s" for fifty verbs,
"es" for GO, CROSS, PUSH, SLASH, SMASH and TORCH, "ies", "d", "ing" -- and
a backspace followed by "ies", which is how CARRY prints as CARRIES: the
backspace takes the Y back off. EMPTY is given plain "ies", which would
print EMPTYIES if it were ever inflected; that is noted, not checked.

PRINT_WORD also starts a new line when a word will not fit on the current
one, and puts a space before a word when one is wanted.

events.title: Comment the input routines, and describe the keyboard's own tables
events.message:
Comment the input routines, and describe the keyboard's own tables

READ_LINE, GET_KEY, SCAN_KEYBOARD, WAIT_FOR_ANY_KEY and MATCH_WORD are
commented step by step. Reading them through added three things.

SCAN_KEYBOARD turns keys into characters itself, through two 40-entry
maps -- KEY_MAP ($8BFB), and KEY_MAP_SHIFTED ($8C23) when either shift is
held -- after masking out keys that never count as a keypress, the shifts
among them. Shifted, the keyboard gives the @ that READ_LINE takes on an
empty line as "do the last command again", and the $18 that clears the
line.

GET_KEY's patience adapts: the next wait is what was left of this one plus
500, at most 3000, and a timeout -- which types WAIT -- resets it to 3000.

And MATCH_WORD unpacks one candidate per call rather than walking the
bucket itself; the tokeniser comes back in at $6F72 for the next. Its
description said otherwise and is corrected.

events.title: Comment the darkness test and MOVE, and find out what falling does
events.message:
Comment the darkness test and MOVE, and find out what falling does

TOO_DARK and MOVE are commented step by step, and reading MOVE through
turned up what happens when the player walks into a wall in the dark.
Each fall rotates byte 5 of the player's record right, having cleared the
carry first, so it halves; while anything is left the player "falls and
hits your HEAD", and the fall that empties it "smashes your skull" and
goes to PLAYER_DIES ($90D2). Byte 5 starts at $40, so six falls are
survived and the seventh is fatal. Each message was printed through
RUN_MESSAGE rather than guessed from the bytes, and PLAYER_DIES is named:
it says "you are dead.", waits for a key and goes back into the start-up.

events.title: fix: a reset or power cycle no longer swallows the lazy disk write
events.message:
fix: a reset or power cycle no longer swallows the lazy disk write

The drive's reset sequence and power switch flushed the pending track into
disk.bytes and then re-attached the disk, which marked it synced: the flush
report the daemon's lazy host-file write arms on was consumed and lost, so a
write made just before a drive reset, a drive power cycle, a held reset, or a
C64 reset on the IEC reset line never reached the user's file on its own.
"Written into disk.bytes" and "reported" are now two facts: the drive keeps
an unreported-write flag that its reset and power paths set and carry with
the disk, and only flush_disk_writeback takes it. A C64 power cycle carries
the report through the session's media registry, and the lazy write no longer
disarms while the disk sits in that registry.

vic/inspect/origin searched drive 8's disk.bytes without a flush and missed
the latest writes; it now searches disk_as_written().

events.title: Lay out the object record's head: size, weight, description and flags
events.message:
Lay out the object record's head: size, weight, description and flags

Byte 2 of an object's head is its size and byte 3 its weight; for a
character, byte 3 is the most it can carry. Three routines say so in their
own failure messages, printed through RUN_MESSAGE: the one at $8CF1
compares a thing's weight and load with the actor's byte 3 and says it is
too heavy to lift, the one at $93AB says you are carrying too much, and the
one at $A596 compares the actor's size with the room at the thing's byte 2
and says you are too big. Doors, walls and fixtures are $FF in both.

Bytes 14 and 15, where not zero, point at the object's own description:
the map's is the one about symbols you cannot read, the river's describes
a fast black river. Both land on message starts.

Four flag bits are now described from the data and the code together: bit
7 there to be seen and reached, clear only on the secret side door and the
butler; bit 6 a character, set on all twelve and nothing else; bit 5 can be
seen into; bit 1 a liquid. Bytes 4-6 and flag bit 0 are left open.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: jonsole

events.title: Find what an object is held by, and what the player can reach
events.message:
Find what an object is held by, and what the player can reach

Byte 1 of an object's record is what holds it or has it inside, $FF for
nothing. The map's is $3E, Gandalf, on the tape and 0, the player, at the
first prompt -- the opening turn is the one where the game says Gandalf
gives you the map -- and the large key's is $47, the hideous troll, as the
trolls' clearing says. Every object's block now says what holds it when
the game starts.

IN_REACH ($9E34), which the matcher and the darkness test both use, is
built on it. Nothing is within reach whose flags have bit 7 clear.
Otherwise an object is within reach of a character inside it, or shut in
the same container, or -- when neither is shut in anything -- in the
character's location, checking every location the object is in, which is
how a door is reachable from either side. SHUT_IN ($9E7A) follows byte 1
upward through holders that can be seen into and stops at the first that
cannot; the player can be seen into, so carrying a thing does not shut it
away.

Called directly from Bag End with the player as actor, IN_REACH says yes
to the chest, the map in the player's hands, Gandalf, Thorin and the round
green door, and no to the troll's key, the heavy rock door and the short
strong sword -- which is lying in the trolls' cave, where Bilbo finds
Sting.

events.title: Find how the parser decides which object the player means
events.message:
Find how the parser decides which object the player means

A read watchpoint on the command frame's first noun stopped in
COPY_PHRASE ($7C91), which copies a noun and its two adjectives out of
the frame into one of two slots: TARGET_NAME ($7942) or INSTRUMENT_NAME
($7948). The code before it decides which phrase is which by whether the
second phrase's prepositions are the ones the command expects, so in
ATTACK THE TROLL WITH THE SWORD the troll is the target and the sword the
instrument. Those slots and their flags sit in 35 bytes the generated
listing called unused, because they are zeros on the tape; they are the
parser's working space, now described, with the parts still unexplained
said to be.

TRY_TARGETS ($7CFC) then asks FIND_NAMED_OBJECT ($9DD9) for the next
object fitting the target's name, makes it the target, tries the
command, and goes round again if that did not take. FIND_NAMED_OBJECT
walks the object index with the exits' iterator and passes over anything
whose name does not match, anything excluded by a mode on its flag byte,
and anything out of the actor's reach.

What counts as a match was settled by calling NAME_MATCHES ($71F3)
directly on the small curious key. The noun must match; the adjectives
may be left out and are accepted in either order; one that does not
belong rules the object out. So KEY, CURIOUS KEY and CURIOUS SMALL KEY
all match, and LARGE KEY and SMALL LARGE KEY do not. WORD_MATCHES
($722E) is why: an untyped word fits anything, and only the twelve-bit
offset is compared, never the flag nibble.

Also: check_annotations' preliminary pass now keeps sub-block directives
as well as block ones. Without them a data block's comments were checked
against the default eight-byte lines and all reported as misaligned,
though the build itself was right.

events.title: Find the parser's dispatch and the command frame it fills
events.message:
Find the parser's dispatch and the command frame it fills

PARSE_COMMAND dispatches on each token's class: the class nibble shifted
right three places indexes PARSER_CLASSES ($75D2), thirteen handlers from
adverbs to the end of the line, reached through JP (HL). That is why the
table showed as anonymous data -- nothing branches to its entries -- so the
handlers are now named, one per class, and seeded into the code map;
twelve were reached in play, and the thirteenth, IN or INTO, is new. There
is no entry for an unknown word, which never gets this far.

What the parser builds is COMMAND_FRAME ($B9C8), 24 bytes just below the
room pointers, with further commands in a line built in the frames below
it. The v1.0 disassembly credited in the docstring gave the layout; v1.2's
was then confirmed by stopping at OBEY after real sentences. The verb is
at offset 0, with bit 7 of its second byte set by TAKE ALL; an adverb or
direction at 2; and two noun phrases at 4 and 14, each two prepositions, a
noun and two adjectives. Articles are dropped.

The words are stored little-endian, which is what made the first capture
look like nonsense when read as tokens -- and what makes the best finding
here. PUT THE SMALL CURIOUS KEY IN THE WOODEN CHEST leaves A5 03 E1 05 63
01 as its first noun phrase, which is byte for byte the name in the key's
own object record. A noun phrase is written in the same form objects are
named in, so finding what the player means is a straight comparison.

The corrected word classes also widened the verb drill to 59 verbs, so the
playthrough now types 126 commands.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: jonsole

events.title: Watch the tokeniser, and correct what the dictionary's class bits mean
events.message:
Watch the tokeniser, and correct what the dictionary's class bits mean

A word's class is four bits: bits 5-6 of its first dictionary byte and
bits 5-6 of its second, read together. That is what TOKENISE ($6E97) puts
in the top nibble of each two-byte token, and all eighteen tokens captured
from real sentences carry exactly the class this predicts. Bit 7 of the
second byte is not part of it -- it marks the 58 words PRINT_WORD may give
an -s, 53 of them verbs -- and folding it in, as the dictionary blocks did
until now, is what made the verbs look like a class of their own number.
The labels are corrected: twelve classes, from adverbs and directions
through verbs, nouns and adjectives to AND and THEN, with the game
commands SAVE, LOAD, SCORE and QUIT sitting among the quantifiers.

The captures also show the tokeniser at work: synonyms are resolved before
anything else sees them, so GET SWORD arrives as TAKE SWORD; and a closing
quote has a full stop token put in front of it, so what is said to a
character is a complete sentence. An unknown word never reaches the parser
at all.

GET_KEY ($7249) turns out to be where "time passes" comes from. It counts
down while it waits, and when the count runs out it types WAIT into the
line itself -- four letters from $7291 -- and returns ENTER. Which exposed
two bugs in hobbit_drive.py. ready() ran on when the game was already
waiting, so every command it sent was preceded by a WAIT nobody asked for
and the other characters had an extra turn each time; and because the key
scan reports only changes, stopping with ENTER held left the next ENTER
unheard. Both are fixed, and GET_KEY's annotation says why.

events.title: Name the message control codes, and print messages the game's own way
events.message:
Name the message control codes, and print messages the game's own way

Each of RUN_MESSAGE's 23 control codes now has a named handler: the ones
that print a pushed object or word, the actor's or target's name, HIS or
YOUR, a name with IS or ARE, the instrument, a backspace, the three
endings, a jump and a sub-message. Four codes share the do-nothing handler
at $738B, which is the XOR A; RET ending code $02's own.

Codes $02 and $0B take a byte after them -- a signed distance, for the jump
and for the sub-message -- and the decoder had been reading that byte as an
element in its own right. The pointer checks still passed, but one operand
had been taken for a terminator and split a message in two: there are 177,
not 178. It walks them correctly now.

Where the codes' meanings came from the v1.0 disassembly credited in the
docstring, four were then confirmed by running real messages through
RUN_MESSAGE and capturing every character at PRINT_CHAR ($858B).
Location 66's description prints the west bank of the black river and
skips the east, so $02 is the jump and the two banks are one message. And
one message's bytes print YOU ARE NOT CARRYING IT with the player as actor,
GANDALF IS and THORIN IS with them, which is $10; $0C gives YOUR or HIS,
with the verb taking its -s for a character; $06 gives the name.

That capture is now Hobbit.message() in hobbit_drive.py -- the game's own
rendering of any message, for any actor, rather than a decoder's guess.

events.title: Decode The Hobbit's messages, and every way into them
events.message:
Decode The Hobbit's messages, and every way into them

Nearly everything the game says is a message in a compact bytecode, run
by RUN_MESSAGE ($72D3): a byte with bit 7 set starts a two-byte word
reference whose flag nibble can end the message; $60-$7F is one of 32
common words from COMMON_WORDS ($AD3D); $20-$5F a literal character; and
below $20 a control code, dispatched through CONTROL_CODES ($7295) --
below $14 as a subroutine, from $14 up as the end.

It was checked against the screen rather than only read. Location 4's
description pointer decodes to exactly the words the game printed on
arriving there, and so does Bag End's. The v1.0 disassembly credited in
the docstring describes the same bytecode, and is what said where to look.

The messages are stored end to end from $AD7D, straight after the common
words, up to the last room description; zeros and then the variables
follow. 178 of them, walked one after another, and every one of the 92
pointers to messages -- room descriptions, and LD HL,msg before a call
into RUN_MESSAGE, found by decoding the code map's own instructions --
lands on a start or on a known way in. The build stops if one does not.

There are five known ways in. Four enter another message at an element
boundary and share its tail; the last of those is the black river, whose
two banks are one description entered at two places. The fifth begins on
the second byte of the word that ends the message before it and reads that
byte as a control code -- one byte doing two jobs, as the code does at
$8113.

The 23 control-code handlers are code seeds, since a dispatch is what
following branches cannot see through; fifteen were reached in play.

The local disassembly now shows each message's text beside its bytes.
That is gitignored with the rest of the build output, and the docstring
now says so rather than promising the prose never leaves the bytes.

events.title: fix: a checkpoint carries the disk as the drive has written it
events.message:
fix: a checkpoint carries the disk as the drive has written it

The medium a checkpoint embeds for each drive position is now the image a
persist would write at the capture: every written track folded in, the
pending dirty track included, in the mounted format. It is built on a copy by
the write-back's own encoder (Drive1541::disk_as_written ->
Rotation::writeback_image, sharing fold_dirty_track with
drive_gcr_data_writeback). Used for position B's driveB node, drive 8's ring
_ringDriveDiskBytes, the .c64re media payload (and its summary sha) and the
recorder's disk medium. Dumps no longer flush the live drive.

Before, the embed was DiskImage.bytes, which only a flush with a dirty track
pending brought up to date: a track written and then left by a head move sat
in the rotation's write-back image alone, and a restore mounted a disk without
it - lost from every later persist. flush_disk_writeback now also copies the
write-back image out when a head move has folded a track in since the last
copy (Rotation::writeback_gen).

drive_disk_checkpoint_gate: D64/G64 x position A/B(unit 9), SAVE mid-way,
capture, restore - red on all four before; plus the stale-flush case.

events.title: Name every room and object from its own words, and find the only lamp
events.message:
Name every room and object from its own words, and find the only lamp

Rooms and objects are named the same way: three 12-bit word references,
the noun first and then up to two adjectives, which PRINT_WORD expands --
bytes 2-7 of a room's head and 8-13 of an object's. So every room and
object block is now titled from the game's own data: location 5 the
trolls clearing, object 5 the round green door, object $0E the short
strong sword, and all twelve characters from Gandalf to the six goblins.
The order they print in is the stored order of the adjectives followed by
the noun, checked against what the game says on screen.

That named object $0E, which is what made the rest make sense. Bit 7 of a
room's first byte is whether it is lit, and TOO_DARK ($95ED) is where it
is read: characters never need light, the player can see in a lit room or
from inside something, and otherwise only if the sword is with him and
its flag byte has bit 2 set, bit 3 clear and bit 4 set -- tested in one
go by XOR $F7, AND $1C. It starts as $94, so it glows from the first move:
the sword is the game's lamp, as Sting glows in the book. The 26 rooms
with bit 7 clear are exactly the places the story makes dark. In the dark
MOVE throws the direction away for a random one, and CLEAR_CANVAS blacks
the picture out.

The v1.0 disassembly credited in the docstring is what pointed at the
sword; the mechanism, the flag test and the starting value were then read
from v1.2's own code and data. A room's bytes 8-9 point at a longer
description where it has one, which the game prints in place of the name.
A room's byte 1 and most of an object's head are still open.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: Decode The Hobbit's rooms and every exit
events.message:
Decode The Hobbit's rooms and every exit

Each location has a record, found by number through ROOM_POINTERS
($B9E0, two bytes per location, 0-79) by GET_ROOM ($9BB1). A record is a
10-byte head and then its exits, three bytes each -- direction, the object
the way goes through or zero, and the destination -- ending at $FF.

Found by asking the game rather than searching for it. A write watchpoint
on the player's location stopped in MOVE as EAST took Bag End to location
4; rewinding from there to where FIND_EXIT ($9F08) returned found IX on
$BAA1 and the record 03 05 04 -- east, through object 5, to 4 -- and one
step further back, the room lookup returning Bag End's record at $BA97.

The whole table then proves itself: 79 records end exactly where the next
begins, the last exactly where the object index starts, every exit's
direction is one of the ten, every destination a room, and every object an
exit goes through a real object. The build enforces all of that. Doors
agree from both sides: object 5 is listed in locations 1 and 4 and is the
way between them, object 1 in 7 and 6 and the way north from 6 to 7.

The direction codes are settled by what the game prints rather than by
pattern. Location 4's exits are 3, 1, 5 and it says "east north
northeast"; the trolls' clearing's are 8, 7, 1 and it says "southwest
southeast north". With 1-4, 9 and 10 already watched in MOVE, that leaves
6 as northwest -- which the map's round trips had suggested too, pairing
5 with 8 and 6 with 7. An attempt to read the codes by stopping in MOVE
mid-turn gave self-contradictory answers and was not used.

Location 0 is not a room: 13 bytes, an empty head and no real exits.
Three exits lead to location 0, which FIND_EXIT passes over -- ways that
exist but go nowhere until the game writes a destination in. Nothing
addresses those bytes directly, so what opens them is still to be found.

events.title: all: close the code-quality review - seams, protocol, licence and polish
events.message:
all: close the code-quality review - seams, protocol, licence and polish

Everything the code-quality review found, fixed across its fix batches. Structural: pist_core split into module libraries (the graph is now acyclic - seams speak through Host interfaces, control through ControlHost, the theme is an injected value); FloppyTransfer and the profiler models extracted from the widgets. Correctness: CRLF sources round-trip byte-identically, git discovery follows the opened project (no more index.lock in PiST's own checkout), emulator framing/queue invariants pinned (owed-prompt drain, hrdb reply-hold), FAT12/line-map/hex parsing fixes, project files load strictly (project-relative paths, version gate, typed entries). events.title: Find where objects are, and drive the game by handing it whole commands
events.message:
Find where objects are, and drive the game by handing it whole commands

The list after an object record's 16-byte head is where the object is, and
byte 0 of the head says how many places. Watched rather than inferred: over
several turns the one byte that changes in any character's record is the
first of its locations, as it wanders; and walking the player east out of
Bag End and back moved object 0's location 1, 4, 1, matching at every step
the location whose picture DRAW_LOCATION_PICTURE looked up. Object 0 is the
player, which fits $B6EA being zero for sentences about you. Things in
several places are fixtures: object 5 is in locations 1 and 4, exactly the
two rooms that walk went between, so it is the round green door. Its record
does not change when it is opened and closed, so that state is kept
somewhere else -- most likely on the room's exit -- and is left open.

The walk was worth more than its result, because it kept failing. Typed
commands arrived mangled -- OPEN THE DOOR as R -- and the fixed waits that
were supposed to prevent it were guesses. hobbit_drive.py does what the
game does for its own opening LOOK: it puts the command in INPUT_LINE
($6FF9). READ_LINE keeps its cursor only in HL and B, so the driver stops
at $6DF3 just after they are set, writes the text, moves them past it and
presses ENTER; readiness is a breakpoint, not a sleep.

That also corrects an earlier explanation. The first command after the
opening picture was not lost because the drawing ignores the keyboard, or
not only: the game then waits in WAIT_FOR_ANY_KEY, and the first key is
taken as carry-on rather than as a letter. The settle comment says so now.

events.title: Decode The Hobbit's object records, each with its own action handlers
events.message:
Decode The Hobbit's object records, each with its own action handlers

An object record is a 16-byte head, a list whose length is byte 0 of the
head, and then a FIND_RECORD table of [action, handler] triples ending at
$FF -- the object's own handlers for particular actions. The game states
the grammar itself: FIND_OBJECT_HANDLER ($9B81) adds byte 0 and 16 to IX
and calls FIND_RECORD, and it is what runs straight after the action
dispatch, asking whether this object handles this action itself before the
ordinary handler gets it.

The proof is in the fit rather than in any one record. Parsed this way,
all 61 records end exactly where the next begins, the first starts exactly
where OBJECT_INDEX ends, and the last ends exactly where ACTION_TABLE
starts. The build now enforces that and stops if it ever fails.

The handlers are code on the same argument as the dispatch table's: the
same format, reached through a lookup rather than a branch, and 78 of the
143 reached by the playthrough. The other 33 distinct addresses are now
seeds, and they passed the check that no executed address lands inside a
decoded instruction -- which is the evidence that they begin real
instructions rather than just sitting near them. The code map goes from
5832 to 6263 instruction starts. One handler value is $0000, which is not
an address in the game: it is left out as a seed and described as the
object doing nothing special for that action.

The 16-byte head and the list are described by extent only. What their
bytes mean has not been worked out and is not asserted.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: jonsole

events.title: Identify the object index, and credit a third reference
events.message:
Identify the object index, and credit a third reference

$C063 is a FIND_RECORD table of 61 objects. Its keys come in two runs,
$00-$2B and then $3C-$4C, and the upper run is the characters: every one of
the nine seen wandering during a single turn has its number there, and
$B6EA, which says who a sentence is about, holds numbers from that same
run. A character is an object with a number in the upper block rather than
a separate kind of thing, which also explains why the narration's subject
ids looked like object ids.

The records are variable length and what the code does with them is only
partly worked out, so that is where this stops. $95DF tests bit 6 and bit 3
of (IX+$07), consistent with a flags byte at offset 7 of a record from this
table, but the path from one to the other has not been traced and the
annotation says so.

A third reference is credited in the docstring: a complete annotated
SkoolKit disassembly of the v1.0 tape, author unnamed and with no licence
for its annotations. Same treatment as the other two and as the Knight Lore
map -- used to know what exists and where to look, never as text to copy.
It documents v1.0, 37,888 bytes against this one's 40,000, so its addresses
do not transfer and the two disagree about where almost everything lives;
it says the action table is an 8-byte indexed array, where v1.2's dispatch
at $C730 is a keyed table, so they are not even the same structure. The
object index above was settled from the character ids already observed
moving, not from its say-so.

events.title: feat(871): drive position B — a second 1541 on the one IEC bus
events.message:
feat(871): drive position B — a second 1541 on the one IEC bus

Machine gains drive_b beside drive8 (position A; the name stays). B is
built off with its jumpers at 9, so a one-drive machine is the machine it
was: not clocked, not folded, no driveB checkpoint node.

- IecCore carries a slot per position; the device map is what
  iecbus_status_set builds for the true drives present (Conf3 for two).
- At every sync point both drives are fed the bus as it stands, both are
  caught up, then both are written back — the advance order cannot change
  what the bus reads. Each drive's v_iecbus now carries the other devices'
  pulls, as VICE's one global iecbus does.
- ATN edges go to the drive at each unit; the C64's RESET reaches both.
- set_drive_power / set_drive_unit refuse two powered drives at one unit,
  naming the other position. drive()/drive_mut()/position_at_unit()/
  position_for_media().
- Checkpoints carry B (part, core blob, its disk, GCR overlay) as driveB;
  a checkpoint without it restores B off.
- A drive restored from a checkpoint no longer has a pending hardware
  reset: a never-run drive (B while off, or any drive in a freshly booted
  machine) ran its reset sequence over the restored CPU on the first
  catch-up.

events.title: Cutscenes copy only what changed, plus a double_buffer experiment
events.message:
Cutscenes copy only what changed, plus a double_buffer experiment

A scene's shapes are clipped to a 128-row window, yet every page
clear, page copy and screen push moved all 224 rows. Between
ST_pageBandStart and ST_pageBandEnd those work on a row band instead:
the scene starts on cleared pages, so rows outside the band match on
every page and on screen, and each primitive widens the band before it
draws outside it. A clear in a different colour widens it to the whole
page.

Within the band, the two pages that take turns on screen each carry a
box around where they differ from aux, the background every frame is
restored from, and so does the screen. A restore copies only what the
last frame on that page drew over, a new background only where it
moved, and a push only what changed since the last one. One box per
page rather than per-row or per-block masks: on a 68000 the marking
and the split copies cost more than the clean pixels a box takes
along. A temporary self-check compared every restore, copy and push
against a full copy over the intro, the level openings and the whole
credits, with no difference.

Hatari, work with every frame drawn, fit (budget in brackets):
  logo (15.5s)   ST 8.0 -> 2.2s   STE 6.8 -> 2.2s   Mega STE 4.7 -> 1.1s
  intro (27.2s)  ST 40.4 -> 33.2  STE 38.1 -> 32.8  Mega STE 24.6 -> 18.8
With frame skipping, the Mega STE intro drops 42 frames instead of
138. Its jungle stretch still needs about twice its budget: bus-bound
copies cost the same at 16MHz, and the fills and per-shape work there
are the rest.

The palette fade multiplies in 16 bits, not through __mulsi3 on every
palette write.

double_buffer=true (off by default, undocumented) draws on a hidden
page and flips at the VBL, copying what was drawn onto the other page
afterwards. Benchmarked and not worth it: every frame lands on a whole
VBL, so ST and STE fall from about 40ms to 60ms a frame and a Mega STE
from 25ms to 40ms, overscan or not.

events.title: fix(851): the Ultimate holds its C64 at 1 MHz for 2.06 s after a reset
events.message:
fix(851): the Ultimate holds its C64 at 1 MHz for 2.06 s after a reset

v0.8.6 fixed BUG-061 on an assumption: that the firmware applies the turbo after the C64
has booted. It does not. With the real firmware 3.15 the speed strobe arrives 445 cycles
after reset release (`C64::reset()` -> `effectuate_settings()` -> `setCpuSpeed`), so the
applied-flag was cleared by the reset and set again half a millisecond later, and the
KERNAL still booted under turbo. On the emulator driven by the real firmware nothing
changed.

The real mechanism is in the hardware, measured on the owner's device, reset-anchored:
the C64 runs at 1 MHz for 2.06 s after a reset, at 16 MHz and at 64 MHz alike, stable over
three runs each; a strobe inside that window has no effect and the last strobed speed
applies when it ends; a change without a reset applies at once. The KERNAL's PAL/NTSC race
at $FF5E runs ~1.5 s after reset, inside the hold — which is why the device detects PAL at
every speed.

`vic.u64_reset_hold`: armed by every reset on the U64 profile with 2.06 s of PHI2 taken
from the model's clock, counted down once per VIC cycle. `u64_speed_applied` is removed.
Unmeasured and modelled conservatively: whether a program's own $D031 write inside the
hold is honoured — here it is not.

Gate `u64_boot_speed_gate.rs` rewritten to drive the firmware's order (reset, strobe 445
cycles later): 5 tests, the two that matter red without the hold at 16 MHz. The CIA gate's
`booted@64` re-recorded, and it alone — the only workload that resets; every other digest
bit-identical. 350 lib, 92 across seven gates.

events.title: fix(851): a C64 boots at 1 MHz, whatever speed the firmware prefers
events.message:
fix(851): a C64 boots at 1 MHz, whatever speed the firmware prefers

851 treated the Ultimate's preferred speed as a state of the machine: `u64_d031()` fell
back to `u64_speed_prefer` whenever `$D031` had not been written, and a reset clears
exactly that flag — so every reset handed the KERNAL a turbo CPU.

That is not a cosmetic ordering question. The KERNAL works out whether it is a PAL or an
NTSC machine by racing the CPU against the raster: `$FF5E` sets the raster compare to line
311 — a line only a PAL frame has — polls `$D012` until its low byte reads 0, and asks
whether the sticky latch fired in between. A C64 that boots at 16 MHz or faster reaches
line 256 before the raster has crossed 311, reads a clear latch, and `$FDDD` programs CIA 1
Timer A with the NTSC latch $4295. 57.8 jiffies per second on a PAL machine, for the rest
of the session.

Real hardware never does this, at any speed, five runs per step. It boots its C64 at 1 MHz
and the firmware applies the turbo afterwards — measured on the owner's device in a single
run: one program, one boot, work right after the reset exactly as slow at 64 MHz as at
1 MHz, then a factor of 71 in the same boot, changeover 2.62 s after the first instruction.
The CPU is still 56x for everything after, which is what UPic needs and what Gideon's own
REU test reports.

So: `vic.u64_speed_applied`, cleared by every reset, set when the speed is APPLIED — a
`$D031` write, or the firmware's strobe through `set_u64_turbo`. While clear the machine is
a 1 MHz 6510 whatever the setting says.

NO TIMING CONSTANT. The device's ~4.5 s is one observation of one firmware on one machine
and stays in the bug report. What is modelled is the architecture: a reset drops the C64 to
1 MHz, and a speed takes effect when something applies it. 851's own "the divider refreshed
at each instruction boundary" was a convenience with no source and it cost this project
half a picture last week; this is not another one.

One caller needed the firmware's half. `cia_alarm_check_gate` boots ROMs, so its `@64`
workload would have booted AND run at 1 MHz — a gate for the alarm check at 64 MHz quietly
no longer testing 64 MHz. It re-strobes after the boot now, and its digest is BIT-IDENTICAL
to the one recorded before this change. That is the evidence that a turbo machine still
behaves exactly as it did and only the moment the speed arrives has moved.

Gate: `u64_boot_speed_gate.rs`, 4 tests, all four red without the fix. 350 lib tests, 88
across the six U64 and turbo gates.

Found by the UE2 emulator session as "the C64 runs 3.3% slow under turbo". It was not a
clock, not a lost cycle and not a wrong constant — the machine was being told it lived on
another continent.

events.title: Amiga: the credit scroller reads a hires glyph whole
events.message:
Amiga: the credit scroller reads a hires glyph whole

W scrolls the version and score under the flight view. The scroller was built
around eight-pixel cells, one byte per plane with two characters to a word,
but in a 640 screen CHARSET_PTR names the sixteen-byte font. It indexed by
eight and read a byte a line, so it drew half of the wrong glyph, and it fed
a new character every eight pixels while the cell was sixteen wide, so what
did arrive was cut in half again.

A hires cell is now a whole word. SCROLL_CELL takes the cell's width as its
operand size, the way Q_PUSH does, so one line of pixels is written once
rather than once per screen width; the index steps by sixteen, a character
lasts twice as many scroll steps, and SCROLL_WORDS and SCROLL_STRIDE carry the
widths the loops and the buffer need. The 320 screens keep their layout.

events.title: 68030 MMU: MOVES must use the _state accessors in the CE table too
events.message:
68030 MMU: MOVES must use the _state accessors in the CE table too

Table 35 (68030 MMU + caches + cycle-exact) never set xfc_postfix, so its
MOVES stores went through the plain dfc030c_put_* helpers instead of the
_state variants that record the data output buffer for the bus-fault
frame. A MOVES that page-faulted was then completed on RTE with the
PREVIOUS instruction's write data. Tables 32 and 34 already set it.

Seen with Atari System V (UniSoft SVR4) under Hatari: copyout() of the
first user page faulted, the retry stored the previous store's value over
the icode's `moveq #59`, and init's exec became a different syscall.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: slaapliedje

events.title: 68030 data cache: burst fill translates with the access's function code
events.message:
68030 data cache: burst fill translates with the access's function code

dcache030_maybe_burst() translated the line address with regs.s, the
CPU's privilege level, rather than the function code of the access that
missed. A MOVES with SFC=user runs in supervisor mode: the supervisor
translation can match a transparent translation register, come back
untranslated, and the burst then fills a user-tagged line from PHYSICAL
memory at the logical address. Only visible when RAM exists there.

Seen with Atari System V under Hatari with 256 MB of TT-RAM: user data
at logical 0x1003xxxx read back as zeros through copyin() and every
dynamically linked program crashed in the runtime linker; 240 MB (no RAM
at that physical address) was fine.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: slaapliedje

events.title: Amiga: hold the blitter only while the clear runs
events.message:
Amiga: hold the blitter only while the clear runs

AMIGA_ENTRY took the blitter before the game started and kept it to the end.
Booting a fastdraw build from its ADF then hung with an empty screen on a
512 KB A500 under Kickstart 1.3. Holding it is what does it, not the call:
taking it and handing it straight back boots, and so does adding the WaitBlit
the documented sequence asks for while still holding it.

BEGIN_CLEAR takes it, waits for the system's last blit and WAIT_CLEAR hands it
back as the fill ends, so it spans the drawing and never a disk read. DISK.M68
reads a saved commander mid-game, which ownership held that long would hang
the same way.

events.title: Amiga: HORIZ_LINE fills wide spans in longs
events.message:
Amiga: HORIZ_LINE fills wide spans in longs

The fill loop wrote the four plane words one word at a time. From
long_fill_min words up it doubles each plane word into a long and writes two
words per instruction, leaving an odd trailing word to the word path. The
same bytes reach the screen; what goes away is opcode fetch, which on an A500
shares the bus with them.

Narrow spans keep the word loop, because doubling the four words costs twelve
instructions and does not pay back under six.

docking 180 ms of rasterising to 170, a planet 73 to 70.

events.title: Amiga: the blitter starts the clear as the present releases the buffer
events.message:
Amiga: the blitter starts the clear as the present releases the buffer

It ran from CLEAR_IMAGE, so it had only the game logic to finish in, and on
an A500 in hires the drawing still waited a few milliseconds for it.
SWAP_SCREEN now starts it on the buffer the present has just released, which
adds the sky update and the frame budget wait to its head start.

BEGIN_CLEAR programmes the registers for both callers. CLEAR_IMAGE leaves a
blit that is already filling the same buffer alone, and only a frame that
cleared hands the next one on, so a menu screen never inherits one. The frame
that opens a menu drains instead, since it will not clear.

The clear reading follows the wait: WAIT_CLEAR adds what it spends draining
BBUSY, so the number is the delay the clear caused rather than the cost of
programming the registers, which read zero on a 68000 whatever the blit did.

events.title: grm-yflf: a caller-side read-back of a live-bank mirror is a RESTORED_BANK note (megaman2 ca12/d0c3, kicarus, db3, dbz2, dbz_saiyan)
events.message:
grm-yflf: a caller-side read-back of a live-bank mirror is a RESTORED_BANK note (megaman2 ca12/d0c3, kicarus, db3, dbz2, dbz_saiyan)

The classification half (6ecacdd) covered a helper whose own prologue reloads the bank.
This is the mirror image: the reload is in the CALLER -- `LDA $29 / PHA / JSR c96b / PLA /
JSR c000`, or the bare `LDA $29 / JSR c000` in an interrupt tail -- and the scanner already
walks to it; what was missing was evidence that $29 is a bank mirror and a stop reason that
says "unmodified read-back of one" instead of the generic ANALYZER_LIMIT.

Discovery first, because megaman2's mirror set was EMPTY: $29 has one write-through store
(c000 STA $29) and no route could corroborate it. Route (b) now records an argument load
`LD<reg> C / JSR helper` as a write-through load too when the CALLED helper's body holds one
of C's write-through stores -- route (a)'s two-sided rule with a call boundary in the middle
(scanArgumentCells, 3-arg form; the 2-arg form is unchanged for the derivation tests).

Then the scanner: Hooks.isLiveBankMirror (a KIND query, deliberately separate from the
resolveMirrorLoad VALUE channel, which answers null both for "not a mirror" and "a mirror I
refuse" -- serial-shift refuses every WRITE_THROUGH, memory-latch a stale one). A plain
non-indexed load of a live-bank mirror under identity accumulators stops RESTORED_BANK with a
ReadBack(cell, readAt, carriedAcross). Only the engine's call-site path answers the query
(OracleHooks, from the strategy's new observedMirrors()), so direct sites -- grm-p9y's NMI
restores at megaman d571 / wizwarr ffa6 -- are byte-identical; filed as grm-rd6h.

The note names the cell and its kind without promoting a shadow to the live bank (in an NMI
tail the shadow is stale by design, and the restore is right BECAUSE it is), the read, the
carried-across call, and -- only when readsEntryBank proves the read straight-line from the
function entry -- that it is each call site's own bank, already tracked there. The
description's "one frame out" propagation turns out to be what the engine's non-helper call
transparency already does; the note now says so at the site.

cb60 did not move: a BPL copy loop sits between the calls and its PLA, so this is grm-mej.3's
open cross-block pairing shape (recorded there with the listing). d0c3 gets the cell-level
note, not "unchanged from handler entry": NMI's own chain and JSR $8000/$8003 precede the
read, and the coherence proof the bead flags as subtle is not establishable structurally.

Goldens: megaman2 warnings 8->6, kicarus 5->3, db3 5->4 (grm-mej.6's db80), dbz2 3->2,
dbz_saiyan 3->2 -- every diff a warning->note flip, no value or reference moved; blessed
after review. Full gate SUITE OK; 12 new Tier-2 cases in CallerSideRestoreProgramTest.
Real-ROM `check nes` pass=24 fail=9: the five above, the documented dodge/lwings/rcproam,
and megaman -- which ab-test.sh --dirty HEAD showed failing on the UNCHANGED side at a third
state (grm-g73 jitter), not blessed.

events.title: grm-mej.3 increment 3: call-crossing PHA/PLA pairing, resolved against the state at the push
events.message:
grm-mej.3 increment 3: call-crossing PHA/PLA pairing, resolved against the state at the push

findMatchingPush now steps over a call while pairing a PLA to its PHA (the depth counter is
exact across JSR/RTS by construction -- reaching the fall-through is the witness, the same
argument increment 1's restoresEntryBank crosses its inner JSR on), and the walk that resumes
from the push resolves against the tracked state AT THE PUSH, not at the store: in
`LDA <mirror> / PHA / LDA #n / JSR helper / ... / PLA / JSR helper` the store-site state is
the bank the first call installed, a confidently wrong value.

The state comes through a new defaulted Hooks.stateAt(Address); only the call-site recovery
path gets a real one (BankDataflowEngine hands recoverCallArgument a recording StateOracle),
and with it two obligations: a fixpoint dependency edge (stateDependents -- a change at the
push re-enqueues the call, since both calls typically deposit the same fields and the
store's own in-state never sees it) and no callSiteRegCache memo for an oracle-dependent env.
A pairing that crossed a call with NO state available ABANDONS -- measured, not guessed:
withdrawing to unknown let MemoryLatch's effectDependsOnPriorState probe reach ironsword
FUN_ffc0's LDA $C5 under our own blindness and declare a requirement on six call sites
already proved no-ops. Direct-site strategies therefore stay byte-identical to increment 2.

Also fixes a bug found by the new tests: a JSR's own p-code writes S, so the stack-pointer
guard aborted every crossing; the crossed call is now exempt from that check.

nesmmc3idtest ID1/ID2 flip (e212 resolves r6=2,r7=3; JSR $A000 retargets to WA000_B3),
golden blessed. Real-ROM `check nes`: pass=30 fail=4, all four the documented stale/bistable
signatures (dodge, ff1, lwings, rcproam); rcransom's mainline restores did not move --
listing read filed in docs/human-research-todo.md.

events.title: fix(vic): the VIC reads the cartridge under ultimax, as the chip does
events.message:
fix(vic): the VIC reads the cartridge under ultimax, as the chip does

A MAX-machine cartridge (GAME=0, EXROM=1) has RAM only at $0000-$0FFF, so its charset
cannot live in memory. The VIC reads it out of the cart: under a real ultimax board the
chip's own fetches at $3000-$3FFF of EVERY bank come from ROMH at $1000 + (addr & $0FFF),
and the CHARGEN shadow does not apply there at all. VICE does both (vicii.c:842-875,
vicii-fetch.c:410-452); `VicMemView` did neither — it read RAM and still laid the character
ROM over $1000-$1FFF.

Found on Jupiter Lander, which renders as a picture with the right shape and not one
glyph: screen codes and colour RAM arrive correctly, because both live in real memory, and
every character cell is blank. RAM at $3000-$3FFF holds the power-on pattern, and under
ultimax the CPU cannot even write there.

Note what the chip reaches: `0x1000 + (addr & 0x0fff)` of an 8 KiB window, so only the
cart's UPPER half — A13 is not driven out to the expansion port. That asymmetry is the
hardware, not a shortcut, and a test says so.

`CartMapper::vic_romh()` answers the window, default None = VICE's NULL
`ultimax_romh_phi1_ptr`, where the fetch falls back to the ordinary map. Implemented for
the classic families (only when the header's lines put ROMH at $E000 — a 16K cart's ROMH
is at $A000 and the VIC never sees it), EasyFlash and C64MegaCart. Deliberately None for
GMod2 and MegaByter, whose ultimax mode exists only to open a flash programming window and
whose `read` answers $8000-$9FFF and nothing else, and for the fake-ultimax carts, which
resolve their own windows and must show the VIC the ordinary map exactly as they show it
to the CPU.

`vic_romh_window` is a free function rather than a method because `&self` borrows the
whole bus and the view is built beside a `&mut self.vic` — the same reason `VicMemView`
exists at all.

Why nobody missed it: EasyFlash and GMod2 are in ultimax only long enough to fetch a reset
vector, then their boot code switches to 8K or 16K and copies to RAM, after which the VIC
reads ordinary memory. Only a cart that never leaves ultimax puts the VIC on the cart's
bus, and the corpus had none.

350 lib tests (4 new), 43 across the VIC, cart-mapper and expansion-port gates.

events.title: fix: a tool's bulk costs something to register, and there is a way back
events.message:
fix: a tool's bulk costs something to register, and there is a way back

project_inventory_sync reported "2747 tool-produced file(s) are on disk and
registered by nothing" and handed over an inventory-patterns.json skeleton in
the same answer. The caller wrote a `patterns` entry for the bulk, registered
2732 per-sector .bin dumps, and S12 coverage fell from 22.2 % to 7.6 % without
a single byte becoming less understood — their bytes joined the denominator and
nothing joined the numerator. Moving the glob to `intentional` afterwards
stopped only NEW registrations: the rows stayed, the next sync said "Files
registered: 0", and registration had no inverse.

A number a caller can act on wrongly has to carry what the action costs, and an
action a caller can take wrongly has to have an inverse.

So the tool-output line now says what the files ARE (machine output; the run's
manifest is the artifact that stands for them), what registering them COSTS
(the bytes, and what those bytes do to coverage), and which key settles it —
`intentional`, which silences, never `patterns`, which registers. No `patterns`
skeleton is offered for such a bulk. howToSilenceToolOutput is the one place
that answers for it, so project_inventory_sync and scan_registration_delta say
the same thing, and the byte totals are measured in the shared scan rather than
guessed at by the reporter.

And unregister_files(glob=…) is the way back. It never deletes a file — the
bulk it exists for is a tool's output and the tool will read those bytes again
— and it refuses any row somebody has written about: cited by a finding,
entity, relation, flow or open question, sitting in a lineage, carrying a
version history, or whose subject holds more than one version. Each refusal is
named with its reason. It is on the DEFAULT surface, because the sync names it.

Gate: npm run e2e:inventory-truth, section 10 — it registers the bulk and
measures the coverage denominator before, after, and after the undo
(4096 → 34336 → 4096).

Also records BUG-060 and brings the generated tool surfaces in line.

events.title: fix: a disk file and its listing are one subject, not two
events.message:
fix: a disk file and its listing are one subject, not two

extract_disk files a stock-DOS row under the CBM directory name (`p`) and
writes its bytes into `03_p.prg`. Every analysis producer files that file's
graph rows under the FILE stem (ownerFromAnalysisPath → `03_p`), and so does
the S12 coverage measure (stemOf(relativePath)). A payload's owner stem is
derived from its NAME, so the payload stood under ram/p and its own
disassembly under ram/03_p: the payload node read as nothing-known although
the listing was fully annotated and rebuilt byte-identically. All seven
side-1 DOS files on Neuromancer, and a coverage number counting the same
bytes under a name the graph did not use.

The file wins, because it is what the rest of the system already counts. So
the manifest importer names a disk row after the file it was extracted into.
The CBM directory name is not lost: it becomes an alias, so search and
lookups by the directory name still land, and it is stated in the summary.
Where there is no extracted file the CBM name is still all there is.

Naming is the whole of it. Deriving the owner from the payload's SOURCE
ARTIFACT was tried first and is wrong: on a real corpus payloadSourceArtifactId
points at `_disasm_rebuild_check.prg` byproducts, at /tmp paths, and at a
different side's charset, so the stem it yields is not the payload's file at
all — it split 97 entry nodes and 34 segment nodes off their owners and merged
six payloads that are not the same payload.

The row also carries the path it was written from, so the importer registers
the blob and points the row at it itself. That replaces a content-hash match
back from files to rows, which two byte-identical files on one disk get wrong;
Spec 752's linkExtractedPayloadFiles stays as the catch-up path for rows
imported before this and now finds them linked.

Gate: npm run e2e:subject-identity, section 5 — a real D64 through
extract_disk, the import, and the payload node's owner against
ownerFromAnalysisPath for its extracted file. e2e-752 and e2e-832-disk follow
the rename: they asserted the catch-up door's return count and looked rows up
by the CBM name, so they assert the outcome and look up by alias.

events.title: fix: the reader half of the graph lock, and its check stops being a note
events.message:
fix: the reader half of the graph lock, and its check stops being a note

GraphStore gives every connection a busy timeout; the pipeline's own graph
reader is the one connection it does not make, and it opened with none. In
WAL mode the last connection to close checkpoints and unlinks the `-wal`
under an EXCLUSIVE lock, so a reader opening inside that window has nothing
to wait with. Measured side by side under four concurrent writers, 1920
reads each: 4 lost without a timeout, 0 with.

The gate's 5c printed that residual as prose because the file belonged to
another branch. It asserts it now, from the source — the untimed reader
stays as the CONTROL and its error count is reported, never asserted: the
race does not fire every run, so a green on it would mean "the race did not
happen", not "it is fixed". This run it fired, 3 of 240 against 0.

events.title: fix(822 D9): name the reader-side residual instead of letting the gate flake
events.message:
fix(822 D9): name the reader-side residual instead of letting the gate flake

Section 5c asserted that a reader with no busy timeout of its own never loses the
race. It does, about once in 240 reads: in WAL mode a reader is not blocked by a
writer, but the last connection to close checkpoints and unlinks the -wal under
an EXCLUSIVE lock, and a reader that opens in that window with timeout 0 has
nothing to wait with. No amount of writer discipline closes that; a busy timeout
on the reader does — measured side by side, 0 errors of 240 with one, 1 of 240
without.

Everything under src/ opens through GraphStore, which passes one; the shape that
does not is pipeline/src/analysis/graph-reader.ts, one argument in a file this
branch does not own. So 5c asserts the half that is in hand (from the source, and
from four real readers through the race) and prints the residual as a loud RESID
line naming the exact fix, rather than a green that hides it or a red that is
somebody else's.

npm run e2e:store-concurrency — 34 pass, 0 fail, three runs in a row.

events.title: fix(822 D9): the graph gets the lock discipline the JSON stores got
events.message:
fix(822 D9): the graph gets the lock discipline the JSON stores got

`ERR_SQLITE_ERROR: database is locked` at store.ts's
`PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL`, with four subagents writing at once, cured by a
single retry. The line is the whole bug: a journal_mode change needs an
EXCLUSIVE lock and SQLite does NOT run the busy handler for it, so the
connection's 5 s timeout bought nothing — and every writer ran the pragma on
every open, whether or not the file was already WAL.

  - ask what the mode IS first; when it is already `wal`, no exclusive lock is
    attempted at all, which is every open after the first
  - when the switch is really needed, retry it a bounded five times with backoff,
    and if it still cannot be had, open anyway: another connection has the file,
    so another connection is about to set WAL, and rollback-journal mode is
    slower, not wrong. Failing an open over it is the one outcome that is wrong.
  - busy_timeout is set BEFORE anything else, so the DDL and every statement
    after it is covered
  - `BEGIN` -> `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` in replaceGenerated and in the 826.0 resolve
    pass: the write lock is taken where the busy handler applies, not half-way
    through where a deferred upgrade fails outright. store.ts has claimed
    IMMEDIATE in a comment since 822 D9; the statement did not say it.

Gate: e2e:store-concurrency section 5, the way section 1 does it —
5a is deterministic (a writer holds the file, the mode is not WAL yet) and
reproduced the reported error at the reported line; 5b is eight real writer
processes creating one graph, six times over, proved overlapping from their own
timestamps; 5c is four readers shaped exactly like the pipeline's
graph-reader.cjs, which cannot be fixed from here and no longer has to be.
3 fail before, 32 pass / 0 fail after. A 20-trial probe of the original race went
from 3 dead writers to 0.

events.title: feat: a LUT descriptor can say the table is in a loaded payload, and that a side is not a bank
events.message:
feat: a LUT descriptor can say the table is in a loaded payload, and that a side is not a bank

`declare_lut_descriptor` defined `at` as an address in the MEDIUM's own
terms, and the only readers were medium readers. A game whose index tables
live inside a payload the loader has already pulled into RAM has no such
address — and a .g64 holds flux-level tracks with no usable byte offset to
count from at all, so for a custom-GCR disk the medium framing is not
merely awkward: it cannot be true.

A run got correct probes anyway. It pointed `medium_path` at the extracted
.prg and hand-offset every column by two for the CBM load-address word.
The numbers were right and the record was a lie: a descriptor asserting
"offsets into this medium" about a file that is not a medium, with an
off-by-two folded into every address by hand and nothing saying so.

So the framing is now part of the record. `frame` defaults to "medium" and
every descriptor written before this means exactly what it did. Passing
payload_path + payload_load_address makes the column addresses RUNTIME
addresses inside that payload; payload_header_bytes is inferred from the
bytes when omitted, by the same rule the disassembly doors use (if the
first two bytes ARE the load address they are a load word), and the answer
says which reading it took. payload_origin carries the provenance a medium
with no offsets cannot give. Naming both framings is refused rather than
quietly preferred, and resolve_lut_rows finds a payload-framed table's
bytes from the descriptor — no medium_path, no second telling.

And a disk side is its own column role. The run used `bank` because there
was nothing else, which is not a cosmetic mislabel: `bank` is handed back
to the reader as the bank a deref reads through, so a side number there
addresses a cartridge bank that does not exist. `side` is data about the
row and never a bank override.

Gate: npm run e2e:750-lut, new §17 (payload framing), §18 (side vs bank)
and §19 (both over MCP) — 26 checks, red before this commit on 15 of them
(payloadReader did not exist, `side` was not a role, the door had no
payload_* argument, resolve_lut_rows required a medium_path). Green after,
with §1-§16 unchanged and still green. e2e:750-cart-payload-slots,
e2e:tooling-defects, probe:tool-surface, check:wiki, check:docs-current
stay green; the knowledge doc and the tool-surface inventory follow.

events.title: fix: two annotation segments may not share a start, and say which two
events.message:
fix: two annotation segments may not share a start, and say which two

An autonomous run's answer carried one line under a green rebuild verdict:

  Annotations import: FAILED — migration_log: annotations:s1_t01s02_core_4300/segment:43a8 logged twice

The listing rebuilt byte-identical, so everything else said the call had
worked. It had not: the import was rolled back whole and the graph got
nothing. A segment row is keyed on its START (`segment:<hex4>`), two
entries sharing one start mint that id twice, and the ledger threw after
rows had already been written.

The contradiction was in the FILE the whole time, and nothing looked at it.
`segmentsByStart` silently kept the LAST of the two while
`segmentAnnotations` kept BOTH, so the listing was overlaid with two claims
about one range as well.

Now the file is refused at parse time, before a byte is rendered and before
a row is written, with the offending pair named as the file wrote it:

  REFUSED — the annotations file contradicts itself. Nothing was rendered and nothing was imported.

  core_4300_annotations.json

  2 segments declare the same start $43A8:
    - $43A8-$43AF  data  "tbl_lo"
    - $43A8-$43BF  pointer_table  "tbl_all"

Three places, because there are three ways in:
  - `loadAnnotations` checks the starts as WRITTEN;
  - the renderer checks them again once Spec 842 has resolved the address
    spaces, since a relocation can map two entries onto one address;
  - the graph importer checks the RESOLVED address — the id it actually
    uses — so a migration run names the pair instead of dying at the ledger.
    That one is a deliberate ESM mirror of the pipeline's CommonJS body, the
    way `src/cost/cycles.ts` and `src/knowledge-graph/windows.ts` carry theirs.

Overlap is not this: two ranges that overlap at DIFFERENT starts are legal
and useful, and are not refused.

The refusal gets its own error class so the pipeline CLI prints it as prose
and exits 1, instead of handing the caller a Node stack trace.

Gate: `npm run e2e:bug060-dup-segment` — the reported file driven through
the real door, plus the importer called on it directly, plus a control with
distinct but overlapping starts. Against the old code: 3 pass, 8 fail, with
`migration_log: annotations:core_4300/segment:43a8 logged twice` reproduced
verbatim beside `rebuild verified byte-identical`.

events.title: fix(845 D2): nesting counts toward membership
events.message:
fix(845 D2): nesting counts toward membership

`model_assert` answered "contains: nothing yet — no analysed nodes fall in this
range" for a system-level boundary (`resident engine $3E00-$C0FC`) whose whole
content is the containers nested inside it, and `project_critique` followed up
with "an empty container is a guess wearing a name". The nodes were exactly
where the asserter said; membership was reading the innermost-wins tally, which
answers a different question.

ModelMembership.members now counts every member node inside the boundary's
range, nested ones included — that is what "contains" means to a reader. The
innermost-wins tally keeps its own field, `direct`/`directByKind`, and D4 still
rolls the fine edges up by it, so nothing is counted twice in the edge view and
the orphan count is unchanged. `nested` names the boundaries strictly inside —
strictly, because two boundaries over an identical range are the overlap the
critic already reports, not a parent and a child.

The "contains:" sentence moves into rollup.ts as `describeContains` so the tool
and the gate say the same thing, and so it can name WHERE the nodes are instead
of implying they are missing. The critic needs no change: it reads `members`.

Gate: npm run e2e:845-model — "members=0 (expected 9)" before, all green after,
including project_critique no longer flagging the boundary and still flagging a
genuinely empty one.

events.title: fix(818 D5): `orphaned` is about the address, not about the id string
events.message:
fix(818 D5): `orphaned` is about the address, not about the id string

`orphaned: Boolean(human && !generated)` compared ONE id. A human `label:09b8`
whose generated twin at the same address is a `segment:09b8` is a different id,
so the row read `orphaned` while $09B8 was covered twice over — by 822's segment
and by 819's routine. A peer session read the flag the way its name reads and
spent hours concluding the graph had lost their prose layer. Nothing was wrong
with the graph.

Decision (stated in the code): keep the name and fix the meaning. The flag is
false as soon as the generated layer has any node of its own standing at this
node's address, in the same space, under the same owner and bank. Exact address,
not containment — a human row INSIDE a generated routine's extent is 826.0 T3's
split, and `graph boundaries` exists to keep that visible. `addr` nodes are
excluded: a reference to an address is the question, not the answer.

`mergeRows` stays pure and answers the id half; `Graph.merge` finishes it against
the address, so every verb (resolve, nodesAt, find, byKind) gets the same answer.
One prepared-statement lookup, and only for rows that would have been flagged.

Gate: npm run e2e:818 — 3 fail before, 31 pass / 0 fail after. The four
guard cases (split, addr-only, nothing-there, other-owner) were green before the
fix and stayed green.

events.title: fix: a block chain that stops early stops loudly
events.message:
fix: a block chain that stops early stops loudly

extract_disk walked a CBM file's chain and broke out of the loop on a
revisited sector or one the image could not deliver, then handed the caller
a bare link list. The Spec-784 manifest built one span per walked link and
said nothing — so a file whose chain loops back after one block, or links on
to a sector that is not there, was published as a clean one-sector payload.
extractFile stops at the same broken link, so the blob is short by exactly
as much as the spans are and chainCoverageWarning sees a perfect match. That
is the Pawn 168/1329 bug with the one guard that exists for it blind.

Neuromancer side 2: both directory entries link on to 149/72 and 210/3,
which the image does not hold. Both were declared as 254-byte one-sector
files. The run's agent re-walked every chain by hand in Python.

walkFileSectorChain returns the links WITH a verdict — complete, empty,
cyclic, unreadable, malformed-terminator (link track 0 with a byte count of
$00, which no CBM last sector carries) — and a note naming the track/sector
that stopped it and how much was walked against the directory's block count.
traceFileSectorChain stays the link list for callers that only want it.
extract_disk carries chainStatus/chainNote per file into manifest.json, the
Spec-784 row carries chainNote, and the tool's own output lists the affected
files. A chain that ends cleanly gets nothing: side 1's seven files and the
motm sample stay silent.

The builder's no-chain fallback no longer invents 254 bytes at the directory
start and presents it as an extent — it says what it is.

Gate: scripts/e2e-disk-chain-spans.mjs (npm run e2e:disk-chain-spans), a
synthetic 35-track D64 with one clean file and three broken chains, checked
against a chain walker the gate owns, plus the real Neuromancer sides
read-only when present. 12 failures before, 30 pass after. e2e-disk-spec784
was in scripts/ but in no npm script; wired up.

events.title: feat: one call, many paths — a bulk door on disasm and analyze
events.message:
feat: one call, many paths — a bulk door on disasm and analyze

A run over one game extracted 217 payloads and then had to put each one
through `analyze` and `disasm` on its own: 400+ round trips through two
doors that each take exactly ONE path. `disasm_menu` was not the missing
door — it wants an extract_disk manifest, not a list of payloads. The run
answered a door problem with a scheduling trick and spawned eight
subagents.

`paths` is the door. Each path goes through exactly the body a
single-path call goes through, so nothing can be true in a batch and
false alone. A path that fails is NAMED with its reason and the rest keep
going — one unreadable file may not sink 216 good ones. And the answer is
one line per path: 217 full listings is megabytes, and a report nobody can
read is the same defect as no report.

The whole batch is ONE background job, not one per path — a job per path
would hand back N job_ids and be the round-trip arithmetic again.

Refused rather than guessed: paths with path/artifact_id (the bytes named
twice), paths with output_asm/output_json (one name cannot hold N
results), an empty list, and more than 512 paths.

Gate: npm run e2e:060-bulk — 38 checks, red before this commit on 28 of
them, green after. e2e:866, e2e:865, e2e:disasm-family, probe:tool-surface,
check:wiki, check:docs-current stay green; the tool-surface inventory is
regenerated for the two changed descriptions.

events.title: fix: the PRG load header is not a missing sector
events.message:
fix: the PRG load header is not a missing sector

Spec 784 GAP 4's chain guard compared the extracted blob's size on disk
against the sector spans, and a payload an extractor writes as a `.prg`
carries two bytes the medium never held: the load-address header the file
format requires. A Neuromancer run was told its complete 49-span chain
"looks incomplete (start-only?)" and silenced it by declaring the first
sector's span from offset 0 with length+2 — a span claiming the payload
starts inside the sector's T/S link bytes, which is false for every other
loader. A guard that can only be satisfied by a lie is worse than no guard.

The guard now accounts for the header itself: for a payload the manifest
declares `prg`, a shortfall of EXACTLY two bytes is the header. Three bytes
still warns, a start-only chain still warns, and the warning text now says
the header is already allowed for so nobody pads a span again.

Gate: npm run e2e:chain-coverage (newly wired; it had bit-rotted on a
missing initProject and did not run at all).

events.title: fix: a code segment may end mid-instruction, and say where
events.message:
fix: a code segment may end mid-instruction, and say where

Ten payloads of one autonomous run carried
`WARNING: rebuild diverges from … at body offset 0x8FD`. The cause is one
line in the renderer, not the classification the caller wrote down.

Bytes carved out of a bigger file stop where the carve stopped, not where
an instruction does. `decodeInstruction` already refuses to invent the
operand bytes it does not have and degrades such an opcode to a 1-byte
`.byte` fact. `renderCodeSegment` then took that fact down the INSTRUCTION
path, where `operandTextFromFact` has nothing to say for mode `impl` and
`renderMnemonicAsm` emitted the mnemonic alone:

      .byte                             // probable code

`.byte` with no value assembles to nothing. The byte vanished and the
rebuild came out short — leaving the caller to guess a data-tail length or
to drop the `code` classification of the whole body, which is what cost the
coverage the classification was for.

Now the code ends at the last instruction that FITS, the rest of the range
renders as data, and one line names both ends of the boundary:

// CODE ENDS at $430D, the last instruction that fits: $430E (1 byte) opens an
// instruction whose operand bytes are past the end of these bytes, and renders as data.

The boundary is derived from the decode, never from a length. The sibling
case Spec 830.1 already handled — an instruction crossing a declared segment
end — now says so through the same line, and the loop is bounded by the last
byte of the image as well as by the segment, so a segment end past the image
cannot read bytes that are not there.

Gate: `npm run e2e:bug060-code-tail` — three truncation shapes plus a
complete-tail control, each asserted for a valueless `.byte`, for the stated
boundary, for the surviving `code` classification, and for a byte-identical
KickAssembler rebuild. Against the old renderer: 6 pass, 12 fail.

- a successful click speaks too: 'Collecting — continue, then Profile

  the success feedback rather than surviving it;

  this file — never a bare blank that reads as broken.

The guided-flow test now clicks the actual buttons (refusal, then the
real run) and captures every observable before host->stop(): the
capitalisation mismatch on 'Collecting to' proved that a late
assertion failure with a live session is the documented teardown
crash.
