events.title: chore(faehigkeiten): die Eval-Suite mass eine Faehigkeit, die es auf GitHub nicht gab — und eine sechste fiel durch ihren eigenen Namen (MF-1334)
events.message:
chore(faehigkeiten): die Eval-Suite mass eine Faehigkeit, die es auf GitHub nicht gab — und eine sechste fiel durch ihren eigenen Namen (MF-1334)

DER BEFUND

Auf `origin/main` liegt seit `3dcf0cf2` eine Eval-Suite fuer den Skill
`uft-sonde-konfidenz`: sieben Faelle, 28 Dateien, fuenf positive und
**zwei negative** (`06-neg-sektorversatz`, `07-neg-dateisystem`), die
verlangen, dass der Skill NICHT feuert. Die Negativhaelfte ist genau die
Anti-Tautologie-Disziplin, die dieser Baum ueberall sonst fordert.

Nur: **der Skill selbst lag nicht auf GitHub.** Gemessen ueber
`git ls-files .claude/skills/uft-sonde-konfidenz` = **0 Treffer**. Wer
das Depot frisch klont, bekommt eine Pruefsuite fuer etwas, das nicht
mitkommt. Sie kann nicht bestehen — sie kann nicht einmal ausloesen.
Klasse MF-1000 / Tor 64, diesmal nicht an einem Test, sondern an seinem
Pruefling.

Betroffen waren sechs Faehigkeiten: `uft-gcr-codec`,
`uft-mutationsmatrix`, `uft-oracle-eichung`, `uft-sonde-konfidenz`,
`uft-tier-hebung` und `aufgabe`. 1113 Zeilen, sechs Markdown-Dateien,
jede mit `name:` und `description:` im Kopf.

UND DIE SECHSTE FIEL DURCH IHREN EIGENEN NAMEN

Beim Uebertragen kamen **fuenf** durch und eine nicht. `git add` nahm
`aufgabe` still nicht an. Der Grund steht in `.gitignore:177`:

    .claude/skills/*
    !.claude/skills/uft-*
    !.claude/skills/team-onboarding

Das Negat ist ein **NAMENSMUSTER und kein Eigentumsnachweis**. `aufgabe`
ist UFT-eigen — der `/aufgabe`-Befehl mit `.claude/AUFGABEN.md` —, traegt
aber kein `uft-`. Gemessen war sie die **einzige** der 31 Verzeichnisse
unter `.claude/skills/`, die weder verfolgt noch ueberhaupt sichtbar war:
als ignorierte Datei taucht sie in `git status` nicht als `??` auf.

Die Behebung hat einen Praezedenzfall in derselben Datei, eine Zeile
hoeher: `!.claude/skills/team-onboarding` ist exakt dieselbe Lage, schon
einmal geloest. Jetzt steht `!.claude/skills/aufgabe` daneben, mit dem
Grund als Kommentar.

**Die Lehre ist aelter als dieser Commit:** ein Muster, das
Zugehoerigkeit aus einem NAMEN ableitet, verfehlt jeden, der anders
heisst — dieselbe Gestalt wie „Groesse ist keine Signatur" (D4) und wie
die Endungs-Falle aus MF-1087, wo `.xdf` auf DIM aufloeste, weil nur dort
die Endung stand.

GEAENDERT   .claude/skills/aufgabe/SKILL.md (NEU, 137 Z.),
            .claude/skills/uft-gcr-codec/SKILL.md (NEU, 175 Z.),
            .claude/skills/uft-mutationsmatrix/SKILL.md (NEU, 178 Z.),
            .claude/skills/uft-oracle-eichung/SKILL.md (NEU, 158 Z.),
            .claude/skills/uft-sonde-konfidenz/SKILL.md (NEU, 242 Z.),
            .claude/skills/uft-tier-hebung/SKILL.md (NEU, 223 Z.),
            .gitignore (eine Zeile plus Begruendung)

BELEGT      **Vor dem Veroeffentlichen geprueft, nicht danach:** die sechs
            Dateien auf Zugangsdaten durchsucht (`gh[pousr]_`, `cm_pro_`,
            `Bearer`, `api_key`, `secret`, `BEGIN … PRIVATE KEY`) —
            **0 Treffer**; auf absolute Pfade mit Nutzernamen
            (`C:\Users\<name>`) — **0 Treffer**. Es sind sechs Markdown-
            Dateien, keine Binaerdatei, kein Skript.
            Jede traegt `name:` und `description:` im Kopf, ist also eine
            gueltige Faehigkeit und kein Fragment.
            **Und die Suite misst jetzt etwas:** 14 Dateien unter
            `evals/` nennen `uft-sonde-konfidenz`.

ROT-PROBE   `git check-ignore -v` nennt vorher `.gitignore:177` als Grund
            fuer `aufgabe` und nachher nichts mehr. Das ist die Probe, die
            den Befund ueberhaupt erst sichtbar gemacht hat: dass fuenf
            Dateien gestaged wurden und sechs uebertragen, war eine Zahl,
            die nicht aufging.

GESTOPPT    **Die Suite ist damit noch nicht LAUFFAEHIG.** Sie misst jetzt
            einen Skill, den es gibt — aber `.claude/skills/CHANGELOG.md`
            nennt seit jeher eine `evals/evals.json`, und die gibt es im
            Baum nicht. Ohne Einstiegspunkt startet die Suite aus einem
            frischen Klon nicht; dazu kommt die gemessene Falle, dass
            `claude plugin eval` ohne `plugins:`-Zeile abbricht und im
            Baum kein `plugin.json` liegt. Ein Ablauf, der sie faehrt,
            existiert ebenfalls nicht.
            Das ist Arbeit, kein Fehler — und sie faengt erst hier an,
            weil der Pruefling vorher fehlte.

RISIKO      **Die sechs sind jetzt oeffentlich.** Das war die Absicht und
            ist die Voraussetzung dafuer, dass die Evals etwas bedeuten;
            es ist aber eine Aussenwirkung, die sich nicht zuruecknehmen
            laesst, auch wenn der Commit zurueckgenommen wuerde. Geprueft
            wurde deshalb vorher (siehe BELEGT) und nicht danach.

events.title: ui: profile to cursor line — the whole ritual in one gesture
events.message:
ui: profile to cursor line — the whole ritual in one gesture

The mandatory choreography (breakpoint, Profile Start, continue,
Profile Stop) collapses into a single action: cursor on the line where
measuring should end, and PiST arms a one-shot there (before 'profile
on', so the counters survive), collects, resumes — and when the run
stops, the results save and show themselves. It composes with the
user's breakpoints: a breakpoint that wins the race ends the run with
partial results, and the one-shot is deleted either way so it cannot
surprise a later continue.

events.title: ci: der gruene Lauf von gestern hat ueber seinen Pruefling geschwiegen — eine Rauchprobe, die fallen kann (MF-1333)
events.message:
ci: der gruene Lauf von gestern hat ueber seinen Pruefling geschwiegen — eine Rauchprobe, die fallen kann (MF-1333)

DER BEFUND, UND ER KORRIGIERT EINE EIGENE AUSSAGE

Im Rumpf von MF-1332 steht: „Der echte Beweis ist der naechste CI-Lauf."
**Das war falsch, und es ist gemessen falsch.** Von den elf Stellen, die
MF-1332 gehoben hat, wird in einem normalen Lauf **keine einzige**
ausgefuehrt:

    ci.yml          4 Stellen   `if: failure()`
    sanitizers.yml  2 Stellen   `if: failure()`
    release.yml     5 Stellen   nur auf Tag `v*`

Aufgefallen ist es nicht am Ergebnis, sondern an einer Nachfrage: der
Sanitizer-Auftrag zu `5b10b8f8` war **gruen**, und seine beiden
Hochlade-Schritte standen auf **`skipped`**. Zehn von zehn Laeufen gruen
— und kein einziger hat die Action angefasst, um derentwillen der Commit
existiert. Die Klasse MF-1000 / Tor 64: ein Test, der nicht rot werden
KANN, in der Gestalt eines ganzen Ablaufs.

**Das Risiko daran ist zeitlich, nicht theoretisch.** Waere
`upload-artifact@v7` kaputt, fiele es genau dann auf, wenn ein Bau ohnehin
schon gescheitert ist — und die Protokolle, die man in dem Moment
braucht, kaemen nicht mehr an.

WAS GEBAUT WURDE

`.github/workflows/artefakt_rauchprobe.yml`, nur `workflow_dispatch`. Sie
faehrt den Pfad, den `release.yml` wirklich benutzt:

    zwei GETRENNTE Artefakte hochladen        upload-artifact@v7
    die Quellen wegraeumen
    ohne `name`, mit `merge-multiple: true`   download-artifact@v8
    beide Dateien und ihren INHALT pruefen

**Zwei Artefakte und nicht eines**, weil `merge-multiple` mit einem
einzigen wirkungslos waere und die Probe gruen liefe, ohne den Schalter
geprueft zu haben. Genau dieser Schalter war bei der Abnahme von MF-1332
der entscheidende Punkt: waere er in v8 weggefallen, haette `release.yml`
still ALLE Artefakte nicht mehr in ein Verzeichnis gelegt, und der
Freigabe-Auftrag haette eine leere Dateiliste gehabt — ohne Fehlermeldung.

**Auf allen drei Laeufern**, nicht auf einem: `ubuntu-22.04`, `macos-14`,
`windows-2022` sind genau die, auf denen die `if: failure()`-Uploads in
`ci.yml` stehen. `upload-artifact@v6` verlangt eine Laufzeitumgebung
>= 2.327.1, und die kann je Abbild verschieden sein — ein Beleg auf einem
Laeufer waere ein Drittel Beleg.

GEAENDERT   .github/workflows/artefakt_rauchprobe.yml (NEU),
            docs/OPEN_ITEMS.md (P3-536 neu)

BELEGT      `yaml.safe_load` nimmt die Datei an: Ausloeser
            `['workflow_dispatch']`, Laeufer
            `['ubuntu-22.04', 'macos-14', 'windows-2022']`, sechs
            Schritte. Dass kein vorhandener Ablauf denselben Zweck
            erfuellt, ist gemessen und nicht angenommen: von sieben
            Ablaeufen nennt genau einer `download-artifact`
            (`release.yml`), und der loest nur auf `push` mit Tag aus.

ROT-PROBE   **Sie steht IM Ablauf, nicht daneben.** Die Abnahme prueft
            zusaetzlich einen Dateinamen, den es nicht geben darf, und
            schlaegt an, wenn sie ihn findet. Ohne diesen Schritt waere
            `pruefe()` unbeweisbar und die beiden Zusagen darueber
            wertlos — genau der Fehler, den dieser Commit an einem
            fremden Ablauf gefunden hat.
            Und der Abnahmeschritt endet mit `exit 1`, nicht mit einer
            Meldung: ein Befund, der den Auftrag nicht faerbt, ist keiner.

GESTOPPT    **P3-536** — `action-gh-release@v3` bleibt UNBELEGT. Seine
            Wirkung IST das Anlegen einer Freigabe; ein Rauchtest dafuer
            waere ein Release. Geprueft wurde die SCHNITTSTELLE statt das
            Verhalten: unsere fuenf Eingaben stehen im `action.yml` der
            Marke `v3`. Das schliesst einen entfallenen Parameter aus,
            nicht eine geaenderte Wirkung.

RISIKO      **Die Probe laeuft nicht von allein.** Sie ist bewusst nur von
            Hand ausloesbar und gehoert damit zur Klasse „Bestand, nicht
            Faehigkeit", gegen die dieser Baum sonst argumentiert. Der
            Grund ist Abwaegung, nicht Nachlaessigkeit: bei jedem Commit
            drei Laeufer fuer einen Rundlauf zu starten, den niemand
            geaendert hat, kostet Laufzeit ohne Aussage. Wer die
            Artefakt-Actions anfasst, loest sie aus — und dieser Satz
            steht im Kopf der Datei, damit er nicht nur hier steht.

events.title: ui: profiler results as a routines tree, with cycles and the OS share
events.message:
ui: profiler results as a routines tree, with cycles and the OS share

'line 14, count 1, 0.00%' was not an answer. The profiler dock is now a
tree: routines (nearest code label, resolved through the build's
symbols) with their hot lines underneath, in two currencies — execution
counts and cycles, each with its share — because on a 68000 a divs is
not a moveq. The status line reads the run in the units an ST developer
budgets in: instructions, cycles, milliseconds and frames at the
emulated clock. Rows under 0.1% of cycles are noise and hidden unless
'Show all' is checked.

Time inside the OS stops disappearing too: the parser now keeps the
save file's memory-area lines, and addresses in ROM_TOS/CARTRIDGE
aggregate into a TOS/ROM row instead of vanishing into 'unmapped'
— often the first real answer to where a frame went.

events.title: editor: insert a call's assembler binding from the reference dock
events.message:
editor: insert a call's assembler binding from the reference dock

The reference dock's list now offers the reverse trip as well: pick a
GEMDOS/BIOS/XBIOS call and the 'Insert binding into editor' button (or
the row's context menu) drops its canonical binding into the source
above the cursor's line — argument pushes in reverse declaration order
with the prototype's parameter names as placeholders, the function word
with its name in a comment, the trap, and the caller-side cleanup.
Pexec's fixed three-long layout, Mshrink/Frename's reserved zero word
and Dbmsg's literal 5 keep their documented shapes. One undo step;
a no-op when the current tab is not a source editor.

OsCallBinding parses the table's prototypes to generate the text, and
two whole-table invariants pin the generator against the data rather
than against hand-written expectations: the emitted pushes total every
entry's stackBytes, and every emitted binding scans back through
OsCallScan to the call it came from. The round-trip surfaced that the
scanner's 8-line bound cut off Flopfmt's nine-argument sequence; the
bound is now a sanity cap (the non-push stop is the real guard) sized
for the widest documented call.

events.title: docs(868): the page-crossing hypothesis is dead, measured not argued
events.message:
docs(868): the page-crossing hypothesis is dead, measured not argued

3979 of 3989 store-to-store deltas are exactly 8 turbo cycles over 4000 stores at divider
64, and not one is 9. The writer does not pay the page-crossing cycle because it is built
not to: the nibble table is page-aligned on purpose and each column is its own page, so no
index crosses one. The ten outliers are +4 and 0.25%, too few by sevenfold to be 1.7% of a
row's pixels.

Geometry and timing are both ruled out and the residual has no hypothesis left. The owner
stopped the search there — the picture is right, and a hundredfold gap on a detector this
crude does not earn an open-ended hunt. The model question survives it: eight slots
quantise a store's position to eight turbo cycles at divider 64, and how the FPGA resolves
one landing mid-pixel is unreadable from either side. The untried test is written down.

events.title: release: a colour per pixel, and a resync that costs nothing — v0.8.4
events.message:
release: a colour per pixel, and a resync that costs nothing — v0.8.4

A fix, not a feature: 851 already claimed to emulate a U64 at 64 MHz, and a CPU that can
write $D020 eight times in a PHI2 cycle is part of what that machine IS. Our VIC sampled
the register once per cycle, so UPic — Aleksi Eeben's technique, 384 border values per
raster line, one per VIC pixel — arrived at one eighth of its horizontal detail. Eight
slots per PHI2 cycle now carry the value in force at each pixel, applied where a colour
token is RESOLVED so the 6569's one-pixel latency still rides the same pipeline. Gated on
the U64 profile with a turbo divider: every C64 and C128 takes the path it always took,
and the 7-game screenshot gate says so byte for byte.

The feature then exposed a timing model underneath it. 851 recorded "the divider refreshed
at each instruction boundary" as a build decision with no source behind it, and it charged
UPic's per-row resync pair four PHI2 cycles out of sixty-three — enough that the row
overran its raster line and the program painted one picture row per two. The divider is
adopted at the next PHI2 EDGE now, and a $D031 write reloads its counter so the sub-PHI2
phase restarts at the store. With no hardware timing measurement available, both models
shipped in ONE binary so the host measuring them could not be fooled by a build
difference: row period 126 -> 63 PHI2, canvas 132 -> 256 of 272 rows, run-length signature
intact.

NOTE for anything building on trx64-core: `sync_turbo_from_vic` no longer assigns
`turbo_div`. It sets `pending_turbo_div`, and `clk_inc` adopts it at the edge — so a read
of `turbo_div` straight after a $D031 write returns the OLD divider until the machine runs
a cycle. `restore_runtime_checkpoint` puts the divider back in force immediately, which a
restored machine needs to continue identically to one that ran straight through.

Every 64 MHz digest in the CIA alarm gate re-recorded; not one 1 MHz digest moved.

events.title: docs(868): the fix verified on main, and what is left after it
events.message:
docs(868): the fix verified on main, and what is left after it

Column 360 quiet in 0 of 462 rows against 462 of 462. Single-pixel anomalies 38.82 → 6.71
per source row, measured at 1080p so the rate compares with the hardware capture's 0.07.
The boundary question is closed; a residual at roughly 100x the hardware's rate is not,
and it is spread thin with nothing at a multiple of 8 any more.

Records one hypothesis rather than none: a store's phase is quantised to one of eight
slots, and UPic's `abs,X`/`abs,Y` loads cost a cycle more on a page crossing, so a store
can land an eighth of a pixel late — invisible except where it crosses a slot boundary.
The deltas between a row's 384 store phases would settle it.

Also records why changes-per-row FELL from 42 to 27 with the fix, because the same metric
rising is what confirmed §8.3 and a reader will otherwise call the fall a regression:
every rotated pixel manufactured up to two extra colour changes, ~18 per row against a
drop of 15.

events.title: grm-km4f: bank-identifying ROM byte with a shift-form encoding -- rcransom's $BFFF = (r7-1)/2
events.message:
grm-km4f: bank-identifying ROM byte with a shift-form encoding -- rcransom's $BFFF = (r7-1)/2

BankMirrors.romIdentifyingOffsets now tries byte == bank >> shift for shift in {0,1,2}
over each congruence class, not only byte == bank, and records the admitting
IdentifyingEncoding (shift, low, verified banks, realized banks) beside the offset.
The three strategies' mirroredByte route their answer through
IdentifyingEncoding.byteFor, which refuses (non-null, all-unknown) when the tracked
field's low bits are unknown or incongruent, or when any realized bank consistent
with the known bits was never verified; identity is bit-for-bit what it was.

Two rulings made against the pinned images rather than the bead's proposals:
- the two highest-numbered realized banks are exempt from a SHIFT-form candidate
  (the proxy for PRG[last]/second_last: rcransom's bank 15 holds f1, not 7, and
  never enters WA000). Identity draws no exemption -- applying it there admitted
  spurious offsets on nesbandaitest, nesmmc2test and nesmmc3test2.
- a shift-form candidate needs MIN_SHIFTED_IDENTIFYING_BANKS = 4 matches, one more
  than identity: at three, the corpus admitted 23 junk offsets on kicarus and more on
  bionic, wizwarr, megaman, megaman2, lwings and rcransom itself ($104b); at four
  only rcransom's genuine $BFFF (seven odd banks) survives.

New fixture nesmmc3idtest (16 x 8K, rcransom's bank map and its fed1 helper verbatim):
ID3/ID7 prove derivation + direct consumption, ID4-ID6/ID8 pin the refusals, and
ID1/ID2 pin the stack-carried restore across two calls as honestly UNKNOWN -- that
is findMatchingPush's straight-line rule (grm-mej.3), which is why rcransom's own
PLA / JSR fed1 sites do not move here. The bank mirror comment names a non-identity
encoding ("byte = (bank-1)/2 on odd banks"); identity text is unchanged.

Gates: build-and-test.sh check green (every prior golden byte-identical; the new
golden blessed); realrom-test.sh check nes pass=30 fail=4, the four being the
documented stale (dodge, rcproam) and bistable (ff1, lwings) rows; rcransom's dump
is byte-identical, now deriving exactly $BFFF[ROM_IDENTIFYING].

events.title: fix(868): a restored machine gets its divider back in force, not pending
events.message:
fix(868): a restored machine gets its divider back in force, not pending

`cia_alarm_check_gate` caught this on equality, not on a digest: a machine restored from a
checkpoint has to continue identically to one that ran straight through, and it did not.
The divider is adopted at a PHI2 edge now, so a restore that only learned its speed from
`sync_turbo_from_vic` set the PENDING value and spent one PHI2 cycle at the wrong divider.
The checkpoint carries `$D031`, so the restore puts the CPU at the speed that register
names, in force immediately — which is what the old model did implicitly by recomputing
the divider at every instruction boundary. Third time this gate has found turbo state
missing from a restore; the first was `turbo_phase`, a defect since 851.

Every `@64` digest re-recorded, and **not one `@1` digest moved** — ten workloads, bit for
bit the values recorded before 857 touched the CIA. A turbo machine reaches its speed a
cycle earlier and every 64 MHz stream shifts with it; at 1 MHz there is no divider to
adopt. That split is the evidence the model change is confined to turbo, one level below
where the 7-game screenshots say the same thing.

ci: drei Action-Majors nachgezogen — und der Zweig, der das schon konnte, haette zwei Fehlerbehebungen mitgenommen (MF-1332)

WARUM NICHT DER VORHANDENE ZWEIG

`ci/action-major-bumps` (MF-801) und `ci/dependabot-grouping` (MF-802)
liegen seit dem 2026-09-02 lokal und tragen genau diese Arbeit. Gemessen
zweigen beide bei `4732572b` ab, und ein Merge haette `-`-Zeilen auf main
entfernt, die inzwischen dazugehoeren:

    MF-805  der SIGPIPE-Fix in ci.yml — `gw info | grep -q` schliesst die
            Pipe beim ersten Treffer, der Erzeuger bekommt SIGPIPE und
            endet mit 141, und `pipefail` macht daraus einen Fehlschlag
            der ganzen Pipeline, OBWOHL der Treffer da war
    MF-817  `set -e` nicht ueber der pytest-Pipe — sonst endet der Schritt
            an der Pipe und die Skip-/Pass-Diagnostik darunter laeuft nie

Uebernommen wurde deshalb die ABSICHT, nicht der Zweig. Die beiden
Zweige bleiben unberuehrt liegen.

DIE VERSIONEN SIND NACHGESEHEN, NICHT UEBERNOMMEN

    actions/upload-artifact      v4 -> v7    neuste Freigabe v7.0.1
    actions/download-artifact    v4 -> v8    neuste Freigabe v8.0.1
    softprops/action-gh-release  v2 -> v3    neuste Freigabe v3.0.3
    actions/checkout             v7          steht schon richtig

Elf Stellen: `ci.yml` 4, `release.yml` 5, `sanitizers.yml` 2.

**Die Majors sind nicht deckungsgleich, und das ist kein Versehen:** die
beiden Artefakt-Projekte zaehlen verschieden schnell. Hochgeladen wird
mit `upload@v7`, heruntergeladen mit `download@v8`.

DIE BRUCHSTELLEN SIND GEGEN DIE EIGENE NUTZUNG GEHALTEN

Drei Hauptversionen zu springen ist keine Formalitaet. Jede Freigabe
zwischen Ist und Ziel wurde gelesen und gegen das gehalten, was dieser
Baum wirklich uebergibt:

    upload v5/v6/v7   Node 24, Laufzeitumgebung >= 2.327.1. GitHub-eigene
                      Laeufer liegen darueber; eigene gibt es hier nicht.
                      Unsere Eingaben `name`, `path`, `retention-days`
                      stehen in `v7/action.yml`.
    download v5       BREAKING am Pfadverhalten beim Laden **per ID**.
                      `release.yml` laedt nicht per ID, sondern ueber
                      `merge-multiple: true` ohne `name`.
    download v8       entpackt NICHT mehr blind, sondern prueft
                      `Content-Type`. **Der entscheidende Punkt war, ob
                      `merge-multiple` ueberhaupt noch existiert** — es
                      existiert (`v8/action.yml` fuehrt es, dazu neu
                      `skip-decompress` und `digest-mismatch`).
    gh-release v3     unsere Eingaben `name`, `body_path`, `draft`,
                      `prerelease`, `files` stehen alle in `v3/action.yml`.

DEPENDABOT: VON MONATLICH AUF WOECHENTLICH, MIT ZWEI GRUPPEN

Vorher sechs Zeilen (`github-actions`, monatlich, keine Gruppen). Jetzt
montags 06:00 Europe/Berlin, hoechstens 5 offene PRs, Praefix `ci`, zwei
Gruppen: Minor/Patch gesammelt, und `upload-`/`download-artifact`
**paarweise** — weil `release.yml` in den Bau-Auftraegen hochlaedt und im
Freigabe-Auftrag wieder herunter. Ein einseitiger Major-Sprung zerreisst
genau diesen Pfad. Die Gruppe sorgt dafuer, dass der naechste Sprung
wieder GEMEINSAM zur Entscheidung kommt.

GEAENDERT   .github/workflows/ci.yml (4), release.yml (5),
            sanitizers.yml (2), .github/dependabot.yml (+40/-1)

BELEGT      Die vier Versionsangaben stammen aus
            `gh api repos/<a>/releases/latest`, nicht aus dem Gedaechtnis.
            Die Eingabelisten stammen aus dem `action.yml` der ZIEL-Marke
            (`contents/action.yml?ref=v7` bzw. `?ref=v8`, `?ref=v3`), also
            aus der Fassung, die kuenftig laeuft — nicht aus der heutigen.
            `yaml.safe_load` nimmt die neue `dependabot.yml` an; zwei
            Gruppen, Rhythmus `weekly monday`.

ROT-PROBE   **Es gibt hier keine, und das gehoert gesagt.** Ein
            Ablauf-Schritt laesst sich lokal nicht rot machen: die Actions
            laufen nur auf GitHub. Was an ihre Stelle tritt, ist die
            Pruefung gegen die Zielfassung statt gegen die Erinnerung —
            und eine Gegenprobe, die wirklich haette fallen koennen:
            **`merge-multiple` in download v8.** Waere der Schalter
            weggefallen, haette `release.yml` still ALLE Artefakte nicht
            mehr in ein Verzeichnis gelegt, und der Freigabe-Auftrag
            haette eine leere Dateiliste gehabt — ohne Fehlermeldung. Er
            steht in `v8/action.yml`; nachgesehen, nicht angenommen.
            Der echte Beweis ist der naechste CI-Lauf.

GESTOPPT    `ci/action-major-bumps` und `ci/dependabot-grouping` bleiben
            liegen. Sie sind mit diesem Commit inhaltlich abgeloest, aber
            NICHT geloescht — das ist eine Eigentuemerentscheidung
            (MF-1077).

RISIKO      **Drei Hauptversionen auf einmal, und der Beleg liegt
            ausserhalb dieses Rechners.** Die Bruchstellen sind gelesen
            und gegen die eigene Nutzung gehalten; was dabei nicht
            geprueft werden konnte, ist das Verhalten zur Laufzeit —
            etwa ob `upload@v7` bei `path: build/*.log` ohne Treffer
            dieselbe Warnung gibt wie v4 statt abzubrechen
            (`if-no-files-found` steht auf der Vorgabe und wird von
            keinem Auftrag gesetzt). Faellt die Matrix, ist die Ruecknahme
            ein Dreizeiler: die drei Marken zurueck auf v4/v4/v2.

events.title: fix(868): the slots ride the one-pixel latency too, not just the token
events.message:
fix(868): the slots ride the one-pixel latency too, not just the token

A resolve at call `i` writes the ring slot that the call with `i == lookup_index` emits,
and for `i == 7` that call is the first of the NEXT PHI2 cycle. So call `i` paints screen
pixel `base + i + 1` and slot `k` belongs to call `k`. Indexing the slots by
`lookup_index` put each cycle's slot 0 after its own slots 1..7 — a one-pixel rotation
every eight pixels, which is what the two existing unit tests could not see: both drive a
single cycle, and both take the 8565 path, where there is no latency and the lookup index
already IS the call index.

Invisible in any program that writes one colour per cycle. UPic writes eight, and the UE2
session measured it on the rendered frame: single-pixel anomalies at source columns that
are multiples of 8 and nowhere else, column 360 wrong in 462 of 462 drawn rows, identical
at two output scales and therefore in the canvas rather than in their scaler.

The new test drives two cycles of eight distinct stores and asserts sixteen consecutive
pixels with no seam at the boundary. Without the fix it reports
[1,2,3,4,5,6,7,0,9,...,15,8] — the rotation, and the first thing in this feature that a
test has failed to catch.

The same run retired the other suspect. `vic.turbo_phase` is a live mirror, so the host
read it at the `$D031` store: phase 10 in 598 of 600 rows at the `sta`, 3 in 600 of 600 at
the `stx`. Constant. Reload-at-store versus reload-at-edge was not what the streaks showed;
§9 records it as open and harmless, because with a constant per-row phase the two models
have no signature to tell them apart.

346 lib, 19 across the turbo and sub-pixel gates.

events.title: merge: Spec 868 — a colour per pixel, and the resync that costs nothing
events.message:
merge: Spec 868 — a colour per pixel, and the resync that costs nothing

UPic writes 384 values to $D020 per raster line, one per VIC pixel, at eight CPU cycles
each — a technique that cannot exist on a 1 MHz 6510 and does on a U64 at 64 MHz. Our VIC
sampled the border colour once per PHI2 cycle, so the picture arrived at one eighth of its
horizontal detail. Eight slots per cycle now carry the value in force at each pixel, and
the override is applied where the colour is RESOLVED, so the 6569's one-pixel latency
still applies and `draw_border8` does not change at all. Gated on U64 + turbo: every C64
and C128 takes the path it always took.

The feature then exposed a timing model underneath it. 851 applied a $D031 write from the
next instruction, which charged UPic's per-row resync pair four PHI2 cycles and cost the
program every second picture row. The divider is adopted at the next PHI2 edge now, and
the write reloads its counter so the sub-PHI2 phase restarts at the store — measured
against real U64 firmware with both models in one binary (row period 126 -> 63 PHI2,
canvas 132 -> 256 of 272 rows, run-length signature intact).

events.title: feat(868): the divider takes effect at the PHI2 edge, and the write reloads it
events.message:
feat(868): the divider takes effect at the PHI2 edge, and the write reloads it

The trial is over and the flag is gone: `TRX64_TURBO_EDGE_MODEL` selected between two
timing models in one binary so the host measuring it could not be fooled by a build
difference. It measured, and the model that was behind the flag is now the model.

851 charged a `$D031` write to the next INSTRUCTION — a convenience recorded as a build
decision with no source behind it. UPic is the program that can tell: its row loop writes
index 0 and straight back to max at the top of every picture row, and under that model the
pair cost four PHI2 cycles, ~256 turbo-cycle-equivalents against a row with about 240 of
slack. The row overran its raster line and the program painted one picture row per two.

Two claims, standing or falling together. The divider is adopted at the next PHI2 EDGE, so
both stores land inside one cycle and the CPU never runs slowly — which is what the pair
was written to do. And the write RELOADS the divider's counter, so the sub-PHI2 phase
restarts at the store; that is what the resync buys, and it is the half that could not be
derived. With the first claim in place the machine never observes divider 1 at an
instruction boundary, so the old reset — keyed on exactly that, and sound arithmetic on
its own — could never fire again.

Measured on real U64 firmware by the UE2 session, one binary, the model the only variable,
the flag asserted from the machine rather than trusted:

    row period      126 -> 63 PHI2   (594 of 600 samples)
    canvas rows     132 -> 256 of 272
    colour runs <=3px  59.0% -> 62.0%

The third number is the one that tests the reload: had the phase stopped being realigned
per row, sub-pixel placement would have decayed back towards the eight-pixel
quantisation. It moved the other way, while twice as many rows were being drawn. And it
is the picture — complete Mandelbrot, correct orientation, satellite and spike where the
hardware capture has them.

Three tests changed their answer rather than their subject, which is the honest shape of a
model change: the resync pair now costs 0 PHI2 instead of 4, a change between two turbo
speeds restarts the counter (recorded as a CONSEQUENCE of keying on the write, not as a
finding — nobody has measured that case), and so does rewriting the speed already in
force.

345 lib tests, 24 across the three turbo and sub-pixel gates.

events.title: trial(868): the edge model, behind a flag, in the same binary
events.message:
trial(868): the edge model, behind a flag, in the same binary

TRX64_TURBO_EDGE_MODEL=1 swaps the answer to "when does a $D031 write take
effect". Both models ship in one binary deliberately: the host measuring this
has been misled twice by instruments that were themselves the variable, and a
second build would be one more.

Two claims, standing or falling together. The DIVIDER takes effect at the next
PHI2 edge rather than from the next instruction — UPic's sta/stx pair both land
inside one PHI2 cycle at 64 MHz, so the edge sees $8F and the CPU never runs
slowly, which is what its author built the pair to do. And the WRITE reloads the
divider's counter, so the phase restarts at the store; without that the resync
would cost nothing and also do nothing, because the machine would never observe
divider 1 at an instruction boundary and the phase reset keys on exactly that.

The second claim is the one I cannot derive. It is hardware nobody here can
measure, and the granularity number is what tests it: if the phase stops being
realigned per row, sub-pixel placement degrades and colour changes per line fall
away from 43/94.

One bug found while proving the switch does anything: the adoption point sat
inside the `turbo_div > 1` guard, and at divider 1 that branch is skipped
entirely — so the machine could never leave 1 MHz. It is at the PHI2 edge now,
outside the guard, where the name says it is.

Shipped model unchanged: 345 lib, 24 across the three turbo and subpixel gates.

events.title: docs(868): the charge does cost the picture — measured without perturbing it
events.message:
docs(868): the charge does cost the picture — measured without perturbing it

Third attempt, and the first one that measures rather than disturbs. A hand
count is arithmetic. An access watch whose on_access returns true halts the run
on every hit, and with two $D012 reads per row that is a halt every few cycles:
it reported 63 PHI2 per row and consecutive raster lines, and it was measuring
itself. That is what made me withdraw the claim yesterday.

The same watch returning false — observe, never halt — reports 126 PHI2 between
row-loop reads, 593 of 600 samples. Two raster lines per picture row. The host's
canvas agrees independently: 132 rows carry colour, on every second line. One
byte into the running program, shortening its delay loop by 115 turbo cycles,
takes the period to 63 and the canvas to 256 rows.

So our ~256-cycle charge for a store at divider 1, against a row with roughly
240 cycles of slack, is why a program written against real hardware renders half
a picture here.

A lesson worth more than the defect: a halting gate cannot time anything. Our
on_access says "halt" by returning true, so observing without halting is a
convention a host finds by reading rather than a mode it can ask for. Two of the
three wrong answers in this thread came from that.

The instruction reference dock now covers the OS layer too: a new
OsCallRef table (53 GEMDOS + 46 XBIOS + 12 BIOS calls of the TOS
1.x/2.x set, with C prototype, d0 result, availability floor and stack
layout per call) and an OsCallScan resolver that reads the idiom —
scan back from a trap #1/#13/#14 line for the function-number push
(numeric, hex, symbolic or clr.w), and collect the argument pushes
above it. Cursor on a trap line or any push feeding it shows the call
being made and what it is being called with ('Calling with: #msg'),
not the generic TRAP/MOVE entry; a register-pushed number still falls
back to TRAP. The OS entries join the same dock list after the CPU
families, so the filter searches both.

Facts verified against tos.hyp (GPLv2) and Atari's 1986 GEMDOS manual;
prose is our own. The table already carries the corrections the
research surfaced: 7 is Crawcin, not Cnecin (the demos are fixed);
Mshrink and Frename push a reserved zero word; Maddalt/Mxalloc are
GEMDOS 0.19 (TOS 2.01+); Blitmode is officially TOS 1.02+ and fails
safe via a dispatcher side-effect.

events.message:
docs(868): the 4 PHI2 charge does not cost anyone a picture

Yesterday's commit put a causal claim in a test comment: that our speed-change
charge overruns UPic's row budget and costs every second picture row. The host
that supplied it has withdrawn it, and so do I.

Measured properly — the access watch armed through their real API rather than by
hand-setting a struct field that was never read — the row loop lands one picture
row per raster line, 63 PHI2 cycles apart, for all 256 rows. The row fits. The
earlier reading was a hand count on one side and an instrument that was never
wired on the other, and it happened to agree with a defect that turned out to
live after the VIC entirely.

The measurement stands: we charge four PHI2 cycles for two stores, and 851 chose
that without a source. It is still a modelling question worth answering. It is
simply not a question with a picture riding on it, and a test comment that says
otherwise is the kind of wrong that gets believed because it is written down
next to a number that is right.

events.title: test(868): what a speed change costs us, measured
events.message:
test(868): what a speed change costs us, measured

The UE2 host hand-counted UPic's row loop and found the resync pair — $D031 =
$80 then $8F at the top of every picture row — costing four PHI2 cycles under
our accounting, which is ~256 turbo-cycle-equivalents in a row with ~240 to
spare. Their conclusion: the row cannot fit its raster line, so the program
paints one picture row per two lines. They measure 232 of 480 rows, on every
build.

Measured here, with no program and no host: four PHI2 cycles, exactly their
count. 851 applies a speed write from the next INSTRUCTION, so the stx runs
entirely at divider 1 and its four cycles each cost a whole PHI2 cycle.

The test asserts what we charge rather than what silicon does, because those are
known to differ and only one of them is measured. If someone changes the timing
model this test fails, which is the point: the number should move deliberately
and with a reason attached.

That 851 line was a build decision with no source — a convenience. The evidence

events.title: fix(868): reset the phase only where the arithmetic proves it
events.message:
fix(868): reset the phase only where the arithmetic proves it

The first version reset the sub-cycle counter on any divider change. Only one
case is actually known: at 1 MHz a CPU cycle IS a PHI2 cycle, so it can only end
on a boundary and the phase there is zero. That is arithmetic, and it is the
whole of UPic's resync, which goes through index 0.

Whether the hardware's divider restarts when one turbo speed replaces another —
64 to 16 without passing 1 — is undocumented and unmeasured. So the phase is
left alone there now, with a test that says why.

The host that reported the resync went back and checked its own metric before
reporting a pass: its first measure found zero jitter because the left margin of
that frame is flat, so the metric could not have returned anything else. Its
robust measure puts both of my commits inside noise. Neither of us can tell the
guess from the truth by looking, which is exactly when a guess should not be in
the tree.

events.title: feat(868): a speed change restarts the sub-cycle counter
events.message:
feat(868): a speed change restarts the sub-cycle counter

The second host read UPic's row loop after the picture test had already passed
and found what the picture test could not: every row begins by writing $D031 =
$80 and immediately $8F, dropping to 1 MHz and back, and Aleksi's own comment
calls it a resync. It has to be one. A technique built on one store per pixel
needs the sub-cycle counter to start a row at a known place, or the row's 384
stores walk relative to the pixel clock and the picture shears.

At 1 MHz this is not a modelling choice: a CPU cycle IS a PHI2 cycle there, so a
cycle can only end on a boundary and the phase is zero by definition. Our core
only cleared the phase when it reached the divider, so after each resync it kept
counting from wherever it stood.

Nothing could observe that before this spec, because the whole cycle took one
colour whatever the phase said. It is a bug the feature exposes rather than
causes — which is also why it arrived from a host running a real program, not
from a test.

The boundary read that Spec 851 already did is now a named method, so a gate can
call it: it resets the phase when the divider changes or is 1, and re-writing
the speed already in force is not a change.

Core 345, the turbo gates 14, the subpixel gate 8.

events.title: Keep the room's palette through a run of cutscenes, and the title's
events.message:
Keep the room's palette through a run of cutscenes, and the title's

Falling off the first platform brought the continue screen up with the
room in the wrong colours. The cutscene palette code already took a
snapshot before a scene and restored it after, but the snapshot held
only the mapping, not the logical palette, which was left holding the
scene's entries to be reconciled at the next flip. That was fine for
one scene. Dying plays two back to back - the death scene, then the
continue screen's own - and the second one's snapshot was taken from
the unreconciled state: a remap rebuilt around the first scene's
colours, restored as if it were the room's. The palette is part of the
snapshot now, so the restore is complete and nothing is left to
reconcile.

The title screen after a game over had the same look for a different
reason. It only ever sets its own 32 entries; after a level the other
160 still hold that level's colours, and the quantiser shares the 16
hardware colours between the two - green eyes, yellow text. It blacks
out what is not its own first.

Also: git inside the toolkit container refused the checkout as owned by
another user, so a build announced itself as "unknown". The Makefile
runs git with safe.directory set for the one command that needs it.

events.title: feat(868): a colour per pixel, where the colour is resolved
events.message:
feat(868): a colour per pixel, where the colour is resolved

UPic writes 384 values to $D020 per raster line — one per VIC pixel, eight CPU
cycles each, which fits at 64 MHz and cannot exist on a 6510. Our VIC sampled
the register once per PHI2 cycle, so the picture arrived at one eighth of its
horizontal detail.

turbo_phase already was the sub-cycle position and was simply never passed on.
The CPU's own bus trait gained a hook for it, the VIC keeps eight slots for the
cycle it is drawing, and a store fills the slots from its pixel to the end of
the cycle — because a register holds its value until something replaces it, so
an unwritten slot is the previous colour rather than no colour.

The override applies at the colour RESOLVE, not where the token is placed. A
token says which register a pixel comes from; only the resolve says which value.
Riding the same lookup keeps the 6569's one-pixel colour latency intact — a fast
machine must not draw sharper than the chip does — and draw_border8 is untouched.

Gated on the U64 profile AND a divider above one. Both halves are load-bearing
and both are tested: a U64 at 1 MHz draws like a C64, and a stray divider on a
C64 profile cannot reach the resolve. That matters more than the feature does,
because this code is on the path of every pixel of every frame of every game.

Eight tests: the phase-to-pixel mapping at four dividers, carry-forward, eight
stores becoming eight pixels in the frame buffer, the register still holding the
last write for the monitor and snapshots, the two gate halves, and that nothing
but $D020 arms it today. The 8565's grey dot at pixel 0 turned out to be the
chip's own behaviour rather than a miss, and the tests say so rather than
expecting it away.

Core 345, the four VIC gates 26.

events.title: docs(868): a colour per pixel — what a 64 MHz CPU can do to $D020
events.message:
docs(868): a colour per pixel — what a 64 MHz CPU can do to $D020

The first thing this emulator cannot render that real hardware does, found by
the UE2 session running Xander Mol's Mandelbrot Upic on the U64 firmware. UPic
blanks the display and writes 384 values to $D020 per raster line, one per VIC
pixel: eight CPU cycles per pixel, which fits at 64 MHz and cannot exist on a
1 MHz 6510. Our VIC samples the register once per PHI2 cycle, so the fractal's
shape survives and seven eighths of its horizontal detail does not.

It is not a divergence from VICE — VICE cannot render it either, for the same
reason. It is a machine we now emulate doing something no C64 can do.

The fix is cheap because turbo_phase already IS the sub-cycle position; it is
simply never passed on. The CPU mirrors it, a colour store fills eight per-cycle
slots carrying the previous value forward, and — this is the part worth getting
right — the override applies where a token is RESOLVED into a colour, not where
the token is placed. So the 6569's one-pixel colour latency keeps riding the
same pipeline and draw_border8 does not change at all.

Gated on the U64 profile with turbo_div > 1, which is not an aspiration: the
7-game screenshot gate compares rendered frames byte for byte on every push, so
a colour-resolve change without that gate would be a change to every game we
have.

events.title: docs: 866 closed — two doors, and what the rule it replaced was worth
events.message:
docs: 866 closed — two doors, and what the rule it replaced was worth

The spec moves to `_archive/` with an as-built section, its row goes onto the
archive board, and it comes off the open table.

§10 records three things worth reading later. What became shared code and
therefore went in once: `loadRaw` takes a window, `analyze-prg` takes
`--offset`/`--length`, and relocations and a named annotations file stopped
being a property of the two bytes at the front. What the spec's own §2 does not
say and had to be decided: "both, disagreeing" needs something to state that the
bytes DO carry a header, and the two things that may state it are the caller
(`headed: true`) and the project store's own record — never the extension.

And the one place a rule had to be weighed rather than applied. BUG-055 settled
that a named analysis is never swapped, and enforced it by refusing a named path
that does not exist. §5 keeps the first half exactly and changes the second,
because the refusal was refusing correct calls: `extract_disk` writes its
analysis into a hashed payload directory, so the path a caller expects beside
the PRG genuinely is not there, and a session re-ran the analyser for every
extracted file rather than argue with it. The lookup is a link the store already
holds, not a stem guess, and the protection moved instead of vanishing — the
swap is named in the answer, and a path that exists nowhere is still a refusal.

§10.1 says plainly what a caller of an old name sees: the same listing, the same
artifact row, their own tool's name in a refusal header, and one line naming the
successor.

events.title: feat: two doors, not four — the load address decides how bytes are read
events.message:
feat: two doors, not four — the load address decides how bytes are read

Four doors answered two questions. `disasm_prg` and `disasm_raw` ran the same
decoder, the same renderer, the same annotation handling and the same rebuild
proof, and differed only in whether two bytes at the front are a load address.
`analyze_prg` took a PRG and nothing else, so headerless bytes could not be
classified at all — and a run over four G64 sides that needed segment
annotations on 1541 drive code built FAKE 2-byte load headers, wrote `.prg`
copies and routed them through the PRG door. That is precisely the workaround
865 exists to end, reappearing one door over.

`disasm` and `analyze` are the two doors, and `byte-doors.ts` states the two
rules they must answer identically or they are four doors again.

THE LOAD ADDRESS DECIDES, NEVER THE FILE NAME. Given, the bytes are raw and
start there and nothing at the front is a header. Omitted, the file must carry
one and its first two bytes are read as the address. Both, disagreeing, is
refused naming both — declared by the caller with `headed: true`, or by the
project store having recorded the file as a PRG, which is a record and not a
guess. The extension never decides: this repo already identifies media by
content, because in a real corpus a payload carved off a disk has no extension
(`pack1 (nameint1`), a `.bin` is a PRG and a `.prg` is a raw block. So every
answer opens with the reading it took and where the address came from, one line,
at the top, where a wrong reading is caught before the listing is believed.

WHICH ANALYSIS A RENDER USES. Named and present is used unchanged and never
swapped — the rule BUG-055 settled stands. Named and ABSENT, or not named, asks
the project store which analysis is registered for THESE BYTES, and the answer
names the file it used and why. Only with nothing in the store does it fall back
to the file beside the bytes. That closes the live half of the same defect:
`extract_disk` writes its analysis into a hashed payload directory while the
render insisted on the path beside the PRG, so a correct call was refused and a
session re-ran the analyser for every extracted file. The protection BUG-055
bought is not lost, it moved: the swap is stated in the answer, by name, and a
named path that exists nowhere — not in the store, not beside the bytes — is
still a refusal.

It is not a new decoder, renderer or analyser: one body runs both readings and
picks the pipeline verb from the reading. What differed between the two old
doors and is kept is the shape of their output — where a listing goes by
default, and which artifact roles it registers under. What was only one door's
is now both's: a headed reading gets the provenance line, the payload link and
the analysis lookup; a raw reading gets the platform recorded on the artifact
row, the annotation name-length check and the next-step task.

`disasm_prg`, `disasm_raw` and `analyze_prg` stay on the surface as aliases for
one release. They are the same body invoked under another name — identical
listing, identical refusals, the tool's own name in its refusal header — plus
one line at the end naming the successor and why the two became one.

events.title: pipeline: the renderer and the analyser take the same window, and say what they read
events.message:
pipeline: the renderer and the analyser take the same window, and say what they read

Three changes in the half that does the work, all of them so ONE door above can
serve both readings of a file's bytes.

`loadRaw` takes a window. It always had a load address; it never had an offset
and a length, so the nine analysers could only ever run over a whole file. That
is the reason a window had to be carved into a file of its own before it could
be analysed — and an analysis of the file it came out of, rendered over the
window, is the mismatch that produced 4082 data lines over 640 bytes. The window
is the same one the renderer's `readRawImage` takes; `fileOffset` stays 0 on
purpose, because it indexes the buffer and the buffer is now the window.

`analyze-prg` gained `--offset`/`--length` beside the `--load-address` it already
had, read by the one address rule, and refuses a window with no address: a
window's first byte is not a load header, so a window is raw bytes by definition.

`disasm-raw` gained `--relocations` and `disasm-prg` gained `--annotations`.
Neither is a property of the two bytes at the front: code stored at one address
and executed at another arrives just as often with no header, and an annotations
file often lives under a name no `<stem>_annotations.json` was going to match.
`disasm-prg` now also prints `Analysis used:` and `Annotations used:`, the two
lines `disasm-raw` has printed since it was written — the wrapper above used to
re-derive both by guessing the same candidate order, and the two halves resolved
different files often enough that a listing full of a human's names could sit
beside a graph import handed a path that does not exist.

Namensmessung ueber vier von Hand genannte Verzeichnisse. Die Regel dieses
Baums sagt es seit langem: **Dateimengen kommen aus git, nicht aus
gepflegten Listen.** Ein Nachweis, der seinen Suchraum selbst waehlt, ist
eine Aussage ueber den Suchraum.

DIE DREI VERWEISE, EINZELN BEURTEILT

**1. `.claude/skills/uft-qt-widget/SKILL.md` — eine lebende Anweisung, die
ins Leere zeigt.** Die Vorlagentafel nannte `src/advanceddialogs.cpp` als
Muster fuer einen modalen Dialog und schickt damit jede naechste Sitzung zu
einer Datei, die es nicht mehr gibt.

`QDialog`-Ableitungen; konstruiert werden davon **drei** —
`DiskAnalyzerWindow`, `RawFormatDialog`, `VisualDiskDialog`. Die uebrigen

ueberhaupt erreicht wird. Genommen ist `src/rawformatdialog.cpp`; die
Messung steht als Begruendung unter der Tafel.

**2. `docs/OPEN_ITEMS.md`, GUI-6 — eine lebende Aussage ueber den Baum, und

  Dateipaar    hier stand 530 Zeilen, gemessen am Commit dieses

  PLL          hier stand 9 Bedienelemente, gemessen 10 — die Klasse
               trug 11 Elementzeiger, davon ist einer ein `QLabel`, das
               nur den Wert des Schiebereglers anzeigt

Damit sind es **39** statt 38, und das ist genau die Zahl, die die
Zuordnungskarte die ganze Zeit fuehrte. Beide Zahlen waren seit MF-668
nachpruefbar; nachgesehen hat sie erst die Ruecknahme. Die Ueberschrift
traegt die Zahl mit und ist mitgezogen; der alte Wortlaut steht zitiert
darunter, nach der Hausregel, dass zurueckgenommene Aussagen stehen

**3. `scripts/audit_setting_wiring.py` — keine Anweisung, sondern eine
Begruendung.** Der Torkopf erklaert, warum Feldnamen nicht gezaehlt werden
duerfen, und nennt `advanceddialogs.cpp` (`p.tolerance`) als eines von zwei

also steht jetzt dabei, dass die Datei mit MF-1330 gefallen ist. Das Tor

events.title: merge: Spec 867 — the window a payload owns, and who is resident in it
events.message:
merge: Spec 867 — the window a payload owns, and who is resident in it

Two rules and nothing else: the same window is the same space, bank and start,
so five modules loading at $7400 are five occupants of one window rather than
each other's holes; an inner window is a hole punched in the outer one, and at
an address it covers the outer payload is not the claimant.

Seeding is scoped to the window, so a payload spanning $0A5F-$CBDA keeps the
forty-three addresses its own owner claims and stops inheriting the engine's,
and the six modules sharing a window each seed their own entry points instead
of being refused as somebody else's. An address with no payload answers with
its claimants. Which of them is actually there comes from the bytes, or from
the load call that put them there, or it is named as ambiguous.

No id changed and nothing was migrated.

events.title: docs: 867 closed — the window is built, and what it corrected is written down
events.message:
docs: 867 closed — the window is built, and what it corrected is written down

The spec moves to `_archive/` with §8, the board row follows it into the closed
half, and `_archive/README.md` gains its decision.

§8 records three things the build had to correct rather than weaken. An image's
OWN window never comes from the graph's extent: that extent is a lower bound —
the graph knows the routines a run found, not the file's length — so it comes
from the payload record or the range being analysed, and the 838 fixture proved
why (two routine nodes would have shrunk an image's own window to $C000-$C03D
and pushed $C050 out of it). §1's "52 seeds, 24 rejected" was an older state of
that project's graph; §8 carries the same graph measured before and after
instead, which is the comparison that means something. And the sentence "only
what its own window and its own owner claim" turned out to be load-bearing word
for word: the 50 KB file keeps the 43 addresses its own owner claims and loses
only the cross-owner ones.

The tool-surface inventory is regenerated: `list_payloads` takes an address now.

events.title: test: 867 — the gate, hermetic, and the same question against a real machine
events.message:
test: 867 — the gate, hermetic, and the same question against a real machine

`e2e:867-window` is one gate over the whole spec, one section per acceptance
item, and it builds the machine the spec describes: six modules all loading at
$1000 with different lengths, a payload spanning $0A00-$50FF, an engine at
$4300-$43FF loading inside it, and a loader that calls one load routine from
three sites with three different track/sector pairs. Its own graph, written
through the real schema; the bundled analyzer over its own images; no ROMs, no
media, no assembler, no daemon.

The capture the byte-match needs is handed in as a `ByteSource`, which is exactly
the interface the live runtime implements — so §6.4 is hermetic here and real in
`smoke:867`, which loads one payload into a sandbox machine, asks who is in the
window, loads a different one over it and asks again. 10/10 against TRX64: the
answer follows the memory, and names nobody while the memory holds neither.

Two things the fixture had to be told, and both are the rule rather than the
fixture: six payloads whose code is byte-for-byte identical cannot be told apart
BY BYTES, so each module's routine carries a different immediate; and a load
routine is only a load routine when it is called from several sites with several
positions (Spec 750.4), so the loader has three.

One small extension to 750.4's detector: the grouped candidate now carries every
position it was called with, each with its call site, instead of only the best
one. It already counted them to decide the candidate was a loader at all, and
reading them back out of the evidence prose would have been a second
implementation of the same scan.

The gate also holds the two implementations of the window model to each other —
ESM in `src/knowledge-graph`, CommonJS in `pipeline/src/analysis`, because the
two trees cannot import each other — over one graph, window for window and
claimant for claimant.

51/0 hermetic, in CI; 10/0 live.

events.title: fix: an inventory sync a reader can read, and a glob that matched nothing says so
events.message:
fix: an inventory sync a reader can read, and a glob that matched nothing says so

One `project_inventory_sync` came back at 146 728 characters over 5 833
lines and blew the client's tool-result limit, so the one fact the caller
needed — what is still not registered, and why — sat inside a wall
nobody could read. The gate reproduces it at 139 946 characters against
the old code: every problem line was printed, unbounded and at full
length, and the skipped list grew without limit from the registration
and manifest-import errors while only the LAST section of it was capped.

The full detail now goes to `knowledge/inventory-sync-report.md`, every
time, and the answer names it: counts, a sample of at most fifteen
skipped files, at most twenty-four problem lines, every line clipped, and
a hard cap on the whole text as a last resort. Nothing is lost; it is
just not all in the answer.

The second half is why those 207 files were unregistered at all. The
previous round taught the declaration file to explain a MALFORMED entry.
A well-formed one that matches nothing was accepted in silence: a project
declared `analysis/overlays/*.prg`, saw no complaint, and its outputs
stayed unregistered with nothing anywhere saying why. A pattern that
matched no file is now named, with what IS in that directory, which
extensions are there, whether the directory exists at all (and the
deepest part of the path that does), that `*` stops at a path separator
when the files sit one level deeper, and a pattern that would cover them.

And tool-produced files that nothing registered are reported. They are
held out of the human debt list on purpose — nobody is going to act on
them one by one — but they were then reported NOWHERE, which is how a
run's own outputs stay unregistered while the sync reads clean. The count
and the directories are in the answer; the list is in the report.

events.title: feat: 867 D3 — the bytes decide, the reading decides, and neither is guessed
events.message:
feat: 867 D3 — the bytes decide, the reading decides, and neither is guessed

Which claimant is actually in the window is not a static fact. Two sources answer
it, in this order, and nothing else does:

  the bytes    Spec 804's residency, used and not rebuilt: `PayloadBytes` hands
               over a claimant's own code bytes near the address (self-modified
               operands already excluded) and they are held against what the
               runtime has. Decided, not inferred.
  the reading  where no capture exists, the code that loads the window says what
               it puts there. A sector-load call site — an immediate track, an
               immediate sector, then the call, which is Spec 750.4's read-derived
               shape — names a position, and the payload whose sector chain starts
               there is what that call puts in the window. The call is the
               evidence, quoted.

Where neither settles it, the answer says the window is ambiguous and names the
claimants with their windows. It never picks one silently, and a single claimant
is not treated as proof that it is in memory — it is one claimant, and the answer
says so.

Two doors carry it. `runtime_resolve_pc` has a machine, so its answer gains the
window block: who claims the PC and which of them the bytes say is there, next to
the name it already resolved. `list_payloads` takes an address and has no
machine, so it answers with the claimants and the reading, and never pretends to
have consulted memory.

On the reported project, $7400 with no capture answers with its eight claimants
and the sentence that says why there is no single answer.

events.title: feat: 867 D1/D2 — the payload records its window, and an address names its claimants
events.message:
feat: 867 D1/D2 — the payload records its window, and an address names its claimants

D1's record half. A payload record gains the window it occupies while it is
loaded: the stretch, its bank where one applies. It is not new knowledge — the
load address plus the byte length is the window — but recorded under one name it
can be ASKED, which is the whole point. The doors write it at registration
(register_payload from the bytes it is handed, the manifest door from the spans,
the cart-chunk door from where the chunk lands); a record written before today
is NOT migrated and NOT rewritten, it is derived on read from the same two
facts, and `list_payloads` marks a derived window with a star and says so.

D2: a query that names an address and no payload cannot have one answer on a
machine built out of overlays, and stops pretending otherwise. `graph_find` on
an address and `graph_node`'s card both carry the claimants — the payloads whose
window covers it, each with its owner and where its window came from — and a
window that another window loads INSIDE is listed as superseded, naming the one
that claims the address instead. It never picks. Same move `get_current_artifact`
made when a bare filename stopped being an identity.

On the reported project, `$7400` answers with the eight payloads of that window
and says the 50 KB file is not one of them; `$4315` answers with the engine
alone and says which window it displaced.

events.title: fix: S12 counts what is claimed, not what has an extent
events.message:
fix: S12 counts what is claimed, not what has an extent

The coverage number rewarded the opposite of the work. An autonomous run
raised it by emitting `unknown` segments named `unnamed_XXXX` over ranges
it had ALREADY named as routines — the loader among them — because a
placeholder with an extent counted and a named routine's own extent did
not. It reverted all 47 by hand and left coverage at 89.0 %. A metric
that scores a blanket above a name is the defect, not the run.

S12 asks how many bytes are ACCOUNTED FOR, so a range counts when
something is claimed about those bytes:

  - classified `unknown`: never. That is the word for "I have not
    established this". Declaring it is honest work and it is worth
    nothing as coverage.
  - classified as anything else: counts. Something said what these bytes
    ARE — code, a charset, a pointer table. A wrong classification is a
    checkable claim; the rebuild renders it and the critic reads it. A
    blanket `unknown` is not a claim at all, which is why it is the one
    thing that can be applied without knowing anything.
  - not classified: counts only under a HUMAN name. A machine name over
    an extent (`unknown_3E00_41D8`, `W0801`) is a range the analyser
    walked, not an account of what is in it — so naming it is now the
    thing that moves the number, which is what the run was trying to do
    before it found the shortcut.

The two excluded buckets are counted and printed under the coverage
line — declared-unknown bytes and machine-named bytes — so a reader who
sees 41 % can see where the other 59 % is and what would move it.
Nothing is hidden, it is just not called coverage.

The annotation prompt said "every `unknown` segment MUST get a
classification — no unknowns should remain", which is the instruction
that makes a blanket look like compliance. It now says to classify what
you can establish and that `unknown` is the honest answer for the rest.

events.title: docs(regeln): zwoelf Entscheidungsregeln — eine Regel, die nur im Gespraech steht, ist fuer die naechste Sitzung keine (MF-1326)
events.message:
docs(regeln): zwoelf Entscheidungsregeln — eine Regel, die nur im Gespraech steht, ist fuer die naechste Sitzung keine (MF-1326)

Eigentuemerentscheidung vom 2026-09-20. Die zwoelf Regeln sind in
Gespraechen gefallen und standen nirgends im Baum. Jede hat mindestens eine
Nachfrage erzeugt, die sie jetzt beantwortet, BEVOR sie gestellt wird.

WARUM DAS EINE MESSUNG IST UND KEINE ORDNUNGSLIEBE

Eine Sitzung fragt nicht aus Unsicherheit. Sie fragt, weil ihre Anweisung
sagt: entscheide nichts, was du nicht entscheiden kannst — und was sie
entscheiden kann, ist nur das, wofuer eine Regel geschrieben steht. Solange
die Regel im Gespraech bleibt, ist sie fuer die naechste Sitzung nicht
vorhanden. Das ist dieselbe Gestalt wie die vier gemessenen Faelle von
Aufzaehlung statt Messung: was nicht im Baum steht, veraltet still.

DER MECHANISMUS HAT DREI TEILE, NICHT EINEN

  1  Die Datei. Was hier steht, entscheidet die Sitzung selbst und meldet
     „entschieden nach E-7" statt zu fragen.
  2  Die Ratsche. Fragt die Sitzung doch, war keine Regel da. Die Antwort
     wird zur Regel, mit Nummer, IM SELBEN COMMIT — genau wie ein behobener
     Fund die Grundlinie verlaesst.
  3  Die eine erlaubte Frage. Wenn zwei Regeln sich widersprechen, oder
     wenn eine Regel eine Tatsache braucht, die nur der Eigentuemer hat.

Ohne Teil 2 waere die Datei nach drei Sitzungen wieder so unvollstaendig
wie das Gespraech, aus dem sie stammt.

DIE BEISPIELE SIND NACHGEMESSEN, NICHT ABGESCHRIEBEN

Die Tafel am Ende der Datei sagt je Bezeichner, ob es ihn im Baum gibt —
damit niemand einem Verweis nachgeht, den es nicht gibt. Neu gemessen am
2026-09-20 mit `git grep -l` je Bezeichner, im sauberen Arbeitsbaum:

  uft_td0_read_mem    3 Dateien      deriv.params     0 Dateien
  UFT_CONV_LOSSLESS   3 Dateien      settingGroups    0 Dateien
  gcr_variant         4 Dateien      provLabel        0 Dateien
  check_loss          6 Dateien      verify_after     behoben mit MF-1325

Alle acht Angaben der Tafel halten. Die drei mit „noch nicht" gehoeren zum
Parametermodell, das im Entstehen ist; die Regel sagt, WOHIN die Wahl
gehoert, sobald es den Ort gibt — sie behauptet nicht, dass es ihn schon
gibt.

WAS DIE DATEI AUSDRUECKLICH NICHT TUT

Sie steht UNTER den Design-Prinzipien, nicht neben ihnen: bei Konflikt
gewinnt das Prinzip. Und sie regelt, WAS die Sitzung entscheiden darf,
waehrend `docs/AI_COLLABORATION.md` regelt, WIE gearbeitet wird. Zwei
Dokumente mit derselben Zustaendigkeit waeren die Bauform aus MF-1177.

events.title: feat: 867 D1 — seeding is scoped to the window a payload occupies
events.message:
feat: 867 D1 — seeding is scoped to the window a payload occupies

A game built out of overlays has five modules sharing $7400 and six sharing
$1000, and the graph's code seeds were filtered by owner alone. So each module's
OWN entry points came back refused as somebody else's — `owned_by_other=6` on a
module whose window starts at exactly that address — while a payload spanning
$0A5F-$CBDA inherited every routine of the engine that loads into the middle of
it, because overlap in a flat address space was read as relevance.

Both are the same missing fact, and it is a fact the project already holds: the
window. A payload's load address plus its byte length say which stretch it
occupies while it is there. Two rules follow, and nothing else:

  same window   same space, same bank, same START. Five modules loading at
                $7400 are five occupants of ONE window, never each other's holes.
  inner window  a window with a DIFFERENT start lying wholly inside another is a
                hole punched in it. At an address the inner window covers, the
                outer payload is not the claimant — something else loads there.

The image's own window is the payload record's when the project has one, else
the range being analysed: the extent the GRAPH holds for an owner is a lower
bound (it knows the routines it found, not the file's length) and a window that
is too small would silently drop an address that is in the image. For every
OTHER owner that lower bound is exactly right, because it is only ever used to
say "something else loads in here".

An address the window puts outside this payload's business is NOT a refusal:
nobody asked for it and nothing was taken away. It is counted and named as out
of scope, in the seed report, never in `rejectedEntryPoints`. Spec 838's
subtraction survives only where the resolving owner has no window at all — there
the graph's owner claim is still the best answer anyone has.

Measured on the reported project, same graph before and after:

  05_s   $0A5F-$CBDA   40 cross-owner seeds, 36 refused  →  1 seed, 75 out of
                       scope, 0 refused. What it owns itself is untouched: its
                       7 human routines and 36 resolved aliases still seed.
  mod_s3_t1s9  $7400    3 seeds, 4 refused  →  6 seeds, 0 refused
  ov_4300_engine       23 seeds, 30 refused  →  48 seeds, 0 refused

e2e:838-islands keeps its substance and loses one word: $C050 still stays data
and is still named in the listing, but it is out of scope now rather than
refused — which is what 838's own reasoning asked for and could not express.

events.title: fix: S5's count is a field, not a digit a regex hunts for in a sentence
events.message:
fix: S5's count is a field, not a digit a regex hunts for in a sentence

S6 applied only when S5's wording matched `<number> runtime`. An
autonomous run answered

    Two permanently resident images and twelve swappable windows

and got back "its wording states no number this can read — re-record S5
with a count in it". It re-recorded as

    4 resident runtimes and 14 swappable windows

and that did not clear it either: the parser demanded the number
IMMEDIATELY before the word, so a single adjective in between made a
perfectly clear sentence unreadable, and the first sentence never says
"runtime" at all. S6 through S9 stayed permanently not applicable, which
is the state that looks like "asked and answered" in every report.

`slot_record` now takes `count`, and that settles it: the number is a
field, the gate is arithmetic, and no wording has to be parsed. The prose
fallback stays for claims already in a project, and it reads both
reported sentences — the nouns are the ones S5's own question uses
(resident image, runtime, resident program) and up to three words may sit
between the number and the noun. Where one sentence states two different
counts on the same noun it refuses rather than guesses; a wrong number
here silently decides whether four other slots apply.

A claim carrying the count as a field outranks one that only says it in
prose, so re-recording S5 settles it rather than landing behind an older
claim. And S5's own report line now states the count that was read and
where it came from — a claim that parsed as nothing used to look
identical to one that parsed as five.

events.title: fix: a required parameter that did not arrive says why, and stops dumping the schema
events.message:
fix: a required parameter that did not arrive says why, and stops dumping the schema

An autonomous run hit this twice in one session:

    Invalid arguments ... path: ["evidence"] ... Required

with `evidence` written out in full in the call it had just made, and a
retry of the identical content succeeding. The message came from the MCP
SDK's schema validation, which runs before the handler and can only say
which key the JSON did not contain.

It was measured before it was changed. Nothing in this server drops an
argument: over the real stdio transport `slot_record` stores a 4 MiB
`answer` together with its `evidence`, and every size in between. The
argument object that reached the door genuinely had no `evidence` in it —
the tool call was cut short as the CALLER wrote it, which is exactly why
a retry of the same content works. That is not something this process can
prevent, and it is also not what a schema dump says.

So the two doors with a required `evidence` — `slot_record` and
`model_assert`, the only two on the surface — check it themselves. The
field is declared optional in the schema and REQUIRED in words, and the
refusal names the cause when the shape fits it: which parameter DID
arrive, how long it was, that nothing here imposes a limit, and the one
remedy inside the caller's reach — a truncated object loses what was
written last, so the short parameter goes first. A short answer with no
evidence is still just a missing field; no story is invented for it.

(`contract_set` has no `evidence` parameter at all, then or now, so the
second occurrence in the report was one of these two.)

DIE MESSUNG

`uft_convert_options_t::verify_after` hat im ganzen Baum genau VIER
Fundstellen, gemessen mit `git grep verify_after -- src include`:

  uft_copy_plan.c:785                gesetzt aus plan->policy

  uft_format_convert_dispatch.c:771  in die innere Struktur kopiert

Einen HANDELNDEN Leser gibt es nicht. Nicht zu verwechseln mit
`verify_after_write` aus `uft_snapshot.h` — anderes Feld, und das wird
sehr wohl gelesen (`uft_snapshot.c:115`).

Die beiden anderen Angaben derselben Zeile wirken dagegen wirklich:
`decode_retries` in `uft_format_convert_flux.c:237`, `use_multiple_revs`
in `:1002`. Die dritte war die einzige falsche.

WAS SICH AENDERT

Nur der Text. Bei `NORMAL` steht weiter „nein"; bei `VERIFY` und
`EVIDENCE` steht jetzt „verlangt, aber vom Wandler nicht ausgefuehrt".
Das ist eine Sofortmassnahme und kein Endzustand: der fehlende Leser ist
eigene Arbeit und steht als `P3-509`. Eine Anzeige, die ueber eine Luecke
ehrlich ist, ist besser als eine stille — und schlechter als keine Luecke.

ROTBEWEIS

`nachpruefung_wird_nicht_als_getan_gemeldet` in
`tests/test_save_image_converts.cpp` prueft den Fall, den bisher niemand
geprueft hat: der vorhandene Test deckte nur `NORMAL` ab, also genau den
Fall, in dem die Anzeige zufaellig richtig lag.

  mit dem alten Wortlaut   1 von 12 rot, mit der Meldung
                           „behauptet eine Nachpruefung, die niemand
                           ausfuehrt: … Nachpruefung ja"
  nach der Behebung        12 von 12 gruen

Dazu eine Gegenprobe im selben Test, sonst waere „sage immer nicht
ausgefuehrt" gruen: unter `NORMAL` muss weiterhin „nein" stehen.

GEBAUT UND GEPRUEFT IN EINEM EIGENEN ARBEITSBAUM

Eigentuemerentscheidung vom 2026-09-20: je Sitzung ein eigener
`git worktree`. Der Hauptbaum trug zu diesem Zeitpunkt 51 nicht
committete Dateien einer zweiten Sitzung und liess sich nicht
uebersetzen (`uft_td0.c`, Umbau mitten drin). In `uft-sitzung-2` mit
eigenem Bau laeuft beides durch, ohne dass eine Sitzung die andere
blockiert.

UND EINE ZAHL WIRD DABEI BERICHTIGT

`docs/STAND.md` fuehrt die Fliesstext-Attributionen mit 178. Gemessen im
SAUBEREN Baum sind es 179. Die 178 stammt aus MF-1282 und wurde im
Hauptbaum erzeugt, waehrend dort 51 nicht committete Dateien einer zweiten
Sitzung lagen — darunter eine geloeschte Datei, die eine Attribution
mitnahm.

Das ist genau MF-1198: ein abgeleitetes Dokument, das einen Baum
beschreibt, den es in keinem Commit gibt. Die Gegenprobe steht:

  Hauptbaum (51 fremde Dateien offen)   178
  uft-sitzung-2 (nur meine 3)           179

Damit ist der eigene Arbeitsbaum nicht nur bequemer, sondern eine
Richtigkeitsfrage. Meine Datei steht NICHT in der Attributionsliste
(`--liste` geprueft) — die Eins ist nicht von dieser Aenderung.

events.title: fix: one word per condition on a G64 block, and a whole side in one call
events.message:
fix: one word per condition on a G64 block, and a whole side in one call

Two defects in the same two doors.

**One vocabulary.** Side 1 T18/S0 came back `gcr_error` from
`extract_g64_sectors` and `checksum_error` from
`read_g64_sector_candidate`, and the difference is not cosmetic:
`checksum_error` says the data bytes decoded and their checksum
disagrees, `gcr_error` says at least one 5-bit group did not decode, so
the bytes under it are not the disk's and the checksum was never tested.
`readSectorLikeVice` collapsed both, because it only looked at
`block.valid`, which is false for either; it reads `gcrValid` now, the
way the ring walk always did. Its fourth word `no_block` becomes
`no_data_block`, so the two readers share one enum rather than two that
nearly match. And each door now states the CONDITION behind the verdict,
from one shared sentence per status — the reader of `gcr_error` should
not have to know that the 325-byte read overshoots the block to
understand why the last group fails on a good sector.

**A track list.** Reading four G64 sides one track per call cost 140 MCP
round-trips and a large share of one run's budget, for work
`extract_disk` already does in one pass internally. `extract_g64_sectors`
takes `tracks: [...]` or `all_tracks: true` beside the single `track`,
which is unchanged — each track keeps its own directory and its own
`track-metadata.json`. A multi-track answer is one line per track plus
the totals and names the metadata files; the per-sector listing of a
whole side is hundreds of lines nobody reads, and it is already in the
artifact. Naming the tracks in none or two of the three ways is refused
rather than letting one silently win.

The gate's fixture gains a second track carrying one sector per verdict —
ok, checksum_error, gcr_error, no_data_block — and asserts the two doors
agree on each of them. Against the old code it reports the reported
disagreement verbatim.

events.title: fix: a drive-side listing is indexed in the drive's address space
events.message:
fix: a drive-side listing is indexed in the drive's address space

`model_assert` with `space: "drv"` over $0300-$07FF answered

    contains: nothing yet — no analysed nodes fall in this range

for a project whose drivecode fills exactly that window. The boundary was
right and `pick()` honours `space` correctly; the NODES were in the wrong
one. `disasm_prg(platform: "c1541")` used the drive's ZP/IO/ROM tables for
that one render and recorded nothing, so `contextForOwner` — which reads
the artifact record's `platform` and the declared machine, and nothing
else — put the imported annotations under `ram`. $0300-$07FF is the host's
and the 1541's at once, which is the one case `space` exists for, so the
two halves agreed on every byte and disagreed about which machine's byte
it was.

A named platform is now recorded, on both rails the graph reads: the
machine is declared for the file's owner before anything renders, and the
PRG's own row is stamped. That closes a loop this door had only half of —
it already resolved the platform FROM the artifact record when the caller
named none, and nothing had ever written it there, so a second call had
to be told again.

An empty boundary also stops being a dead end. When it claims nothing,
`model_assert` says how many nodes are in that range under other spaces
and owners, and, when the mismatch is the space, how a file comes to be
indexed under `drv` at all.
